Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The Essence of Ritual Action (Kriyāsāra)
Introduction:
Homage to the venerable Gurus. Homage to the venerable Lord of the Gaṇas.

One should contemplate in one's mind Śaṅkara, the Lord of Ambikā— the beginningless and endless auspiciousness, whose nature is unborn and equal, who is the primordial universe, ageless and free from disease, the knower of the Self, the five-faced one, the powerful one, and whose nature is the play of the five.
On Kailāsa, the treasury of arts dwells joyfully adorning his crest;
he unites with the masculine nature of the Daughter of the Mountain King as she opens her eyes;
and he sports with immeasurable servants, his body shimmering with the application of musk and shimmering camphor pasted upon half of it.
Salutation to him, the source of auspiciousness.

I bow to those servants of Śiva, who have made their necks radiant with abundant, pure, and auspicious rudrākṣa beads; whose divine limbs are smeared with ashes; who possess immense laughter born of supreme bliss;
who are worthy of honor; and who, through the grace of Śiva, have attained the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, which shatter the mountain of obstacles.
I shall employ those [arrows] which are more effective at piercing than the thunderbolt itself. || 3 ||
I bow to my father Mallaya, the preeminent teacher of the gods, whose mind is bound with enthusiasm for the worship of Śiva according to the methods taught in the authentic Śaiva Āgamas;
he is never satiated by the appropriate rites performed at dawn, midday, and evening, nor by day or night, as these are natural to him.
The entire wave of the yoga of devotion has been expanded.
I bow daily to that mother Cennamāmbā, who, through noble expressions of devotion and constant weeping, perfectly fulfills her wifely fidelity in the service of worshipping Śiva;
she who attains a state of loving friendship with the two supreme Śivas and purifies all who behold her.
I [salute] my nurse, who emulates the conduct of Śīlā, and who respectfully endures the actions of others; she is my mother. || 5 ||
O Lord, master of Kailasa, who has assumed the form of a parrot; O treasure-house of compassion, at the close of this night, protect me with your abundant and auspicious clusters of eloquent verses.
With the collections of words gathered from all the scriptures, you, O child of pure intellect, should compose a treatise named *Kriyāsāra*, for your stainless wisdom is expanding.

Thus commanded by him, Nīlakaṇṭha, having attained a subtle intellect blossomed by his own inspiration, composes this *Svaravikāsita*, the essence of the ritual service for the virtuous in this world, for the sake of greater joy— a compendium of all the scriptures and the words of Paraśiva.
Remembering again and again that mantra received as instruction in a dream, contemplate it repeatedly.
If a human being were to possess the limbs of Śiva—
possessing the deer as his mark, having lotus-hands that touch the feet of Pārvatī, having eyes that have rendered the God of Love powerless,
and wearing the serpent as his supreme ornament clinging to his body— then he would be like the waves of the Gaṅgā.
One whose head is adorned with the fragments of a deer's horn from a royal grove shall become supreme. || 8 ||
From the ocean of the mouth of Nīlakaṇṭha, he, who is Nīlakaṇṭha himself, brings forth this profound essence of Śiva through the path of the Vedas and Agamas.

The paths of devotion have been trodden by the ancient teachers, by all the Vedas, and by the Āgamas; they have been explored by those of sharp and powerful intellect who have attained the realization of reality,
through concise expressions and the composition of unartificial speech for the sake of living beings.
May there be an ever-increasing growth of devotion in those whose minds are stainless. || 10 ||
Those who follow the Śaiva Āgamas, who reject the words of the Vedas, and who oppose the doctrine enjoined by the *Khilasaṃhitā-sūtra*, are seen to possess [only] power.

Among these, the practice of the path of action proclaimed by the Vedas is indeed primary; however, others who have fallen away from the conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti also possess eligibility. || 11 ||

In this Śaiva [system], I shall not demonstrate its being rooted in the Vedas, its conformity with the Sūtras of Vyāsa, and its suitability for the practice of Vaidikas, without first refuting those [objections]. 12.
Maheśvara is the teacher of all scriptures without exception;
even regarding these Vedas, there is no room for doubt concerning their authority. (13)
Validity is established without distinction through the path of the Nigamas and Āgamas;
various Āgamas are to be known as those that do not contradict the Vedas. (14)
And these [practices], which follow the path of the Śruti, are not contradictory therein,
just as the Vedic rites beginning with plowing and ending with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) are performed.
In the same way, the Āgamas of the Vīraśaivas are considered Vedic;
their Vedic nature is proclaimed because they are not in contradiction with the Vedas. (16)
If that which is stated in the Vedas alone were considered Vedic in the ultimate sense,
then [the status of] rites enjoined by the Śruti, such as the vow of Ekādaśī and others, would be lost.
Because they are non-Vedic, all [such practices] would become unenforceable; furthermore, by performing what is not opposed to the Vedas, one would incur a fall from one's status. || 18 ||
If the eleventh day and other such observances were indeed to be practiced by the wise, then the Śaiva Āgamas, their practices, and the Vedic injunctions would all be authoritative. (19)
Those who are initiated according to the Smṛtis and the Purāṇas are indeed Vaidikas;
they would not be Vaidikas at all if they were not ordained within the Śaiva Āgamas.
(5) Since it is not said that those [practices] mentioned in the Smṛtis are Vedic, why do you not feel any hesitation?
If those mentioned in the Smṛtis were indeed Vedic, then those mentioned in the Āgamas would also be Vedic. (21)
For this very reason, all learned Vedic scholars who possess the highest knowledge of the scriptures perform these rites, such as temple festivals and rituals, for the sake of liberation.
They say that the Kāpāla and other such systems, as well as whatever other Śaiva doctrines there may be, are all non-Vedic; a follower of the Veda should not practice them.

One should completely avoid the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, those with matted hair and those with shaven heads, as well as those who bear the sectarian mark (liṅgin), those under religious vows (vratī), and heretics (pāṣaṇḍa).
Thus, how can it be that the Kāpālika and other systems, though prohibited by this [scripture], are not to be censured when they have entered the path of Vīraśaivism? (25)
When the mere act of killing is prohibited by the statement "one shall not kill," there would be no prohibition regarding the slaughter of animals for sacrifice and the like. (26)
The restriction of the word "all" on the basis of dharma is logical in other cases;
in that regard, the injunction "one should sacrifice" is cited as the restrictive factor. (27)

In the Śaiva [tradition], those other than Vīraśaivas are censured as "non-Śaivas" and so forth; this is a contraction of the word "Śaiva," just as [the term] "all" (sarva) is contracted when applied to specific instances. || 28 ||
Furthermore, the scripture that establishes this is heard repeatedly there, as well as in the *Amṛtabindu* and other such primary texts that constitute the essence of the Vedānta. (29)
Alternatively, these Śiva-āgamas are superior to the Śiva-niśvāsa and the Śruti,
for they have issued directly from the mouth of Śiva himself.
The Nigamas and Āgamas spoken by Śiva have mutually contradictory meanings;
those of small intellect imagine contradictions between them. (31)
The authority of the Nigamas and Āgamas, by virtue of being the instruction of the supreme authoritative teacher, is to be understood without distinction by those who perceive reality. (32)
The contradiction is clearly resolved through many arguments;
however, fearing excessive prolixity, I shall proceed with the subject at hand.
The sequence of the treatise, however, follows immediately after this introduction.
These thirty-two instructions have been declared;
in the first instruction, they are in accordance with the Sūtras of Vyāsa. (34)
When the omniscient and omnipotent [Brahman] is thus established as the efficient cause and the material cause of the world, the Vedānta statements are properly connected [to it]. (35)
In the second instruction of all the Vedānta texts. || 36 ||
When objections concerning memory and so forth arise, a refutation is now presented; the independence from the positions of opponents has been established through detailed elaboration. (37)
The refutation of the scriptural prohibitions has been elaborated;
the non-produced nature of the individual soul (jīva) and its causes have also been demonstrated. (38)
And in the third instruction, the withdrawal [of the elements] into the individual soul (jīva) augmented by the instruments (karaṇa), as well as its other states, was proclaimed. (39)

Likewise, there is the state of Brahmanhood through the transcendence of both difference and non-difference; furthermore, there is the collection of qualities as well as the non-collection of those qualities.
The accomplishment of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) through knowledge has been described therein;
that knowledge consists of the primary [mantras] and their auxiliary parts, together with the assistance of dhāraṇā and so forth. (41)
The various divisions of the ritual procedure, the determination of liberation as the fruit, and the investigation of the means have likewise been described in their proper sequence. (42)
In the fourth instruction, the consideration of the fruits has been completed;
indeed, the primary rites beginning with the cleansing of the teeth have been described.
In the fifth [chapter] is the instruction; in the sixth, the birth of the ash;
in the seventh, its wearing; and in the eighth, its display.
The origin of the rudrākṣa is declared in the ninth chapter; furthermore, its wearing and its praise are described in sequence in the tenth and eleventh chapters respectively. (45)
In the twelfth chapter, however, is the procedure for the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra;
in the thirteenth, its praise, followed by the ritual for the worship of Śiva.
In the fourteenth instruction, the characteristics of flowers, leaves, and so forth are presented;
in the fifteenth and sixteenth instructions, they are described in sequence.
Then, in the seventeenth [chapter], the procedure for the worship of the Guru and its praise with devotion are described, as well as the praise of the devotee.
Among those, in the eighteenth [chapter] there is the gift (dāna), and again in the nineteenth,
the liṅga, sāmarasya, and the wearing of the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa).
In the twentieth instruction, its praise has been told in brief;
however, the characteristics of the primordial reality, the Great Liṅga, are found in the twenty-first.
In the twenty-second [chapter], the excellence of power (śakti) is proclaimed along with its authoritative basis;
in the twenty-third, there is the description of the slipping of the *golaka* and so forth. (51)
In the twenty-fourth [chapter], there is the description of the six sites and specifically the initiation (dīkṣā);
then, in the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth, the meditation on the Sakala [deity] is proclaimed.
The method of meditation on the partless (niṣkala) has been declared in the twenty-seventh [chapter];
however, in the twenty-eighth instruction, there is the reception of the Guru’s grace (prasāda).
Furthermore, in the twenty-ninth [chapter], the consecration with water from the feet is mentioned;
thus, the intrinsic validity of the scriptures has been declared in their proper sequence.
The power of Śiva-dharma has been respectfully declared in thirty chapters;
in the thirty-first, that which occurs when an offense against Śiva is committed is fully explained.
In that case, atonement generally consists of thirty-two recitations of the teaching on the greatness of Śiva, accompanied by devotion, while listening to it being narrated. (56)
This sequence has been described as the attainment of a succession of higher states;
these thirty-two instructions have been compiled from the Śiva Āgamas. (57)
One must investigate the mutual consistency among the paths of the Vedas and Agamas, as well as the resolution of their contradictions through valid means of knowledge. 58.
The Vīraśaiva Āgamas, however, possess a particularly uniform character;
fourteen sciences (vidyās) have been proclaimed, and their agreement with that [Vedic] teaching was declared of old. (59)
The auxiliary sciences, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Śikṣākalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Jyotiṣa, as well as Chandas and Viciti— by these, the Veda is said to have six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 61 ||
Śiva, the Supreme Lord, is the primordial speaker from whom these [Vedas] were extracted:
the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda.
The Rigveda has twenty-one divisions; the Yajurveda has one hundred and one;
the Sāmaveda is said to have one thousand divisions, and the Atharvaveda nine.
In this regard, these groups of Upaniṣads are the heads of the Veda-puruṣa:
the Śrī Rudra, Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Śvetāśvatara, and Muṇḍaka.
Kaivalya, Kālāgnirudra, Kaṭhavallī, Bāṣkala, Haṃsa, Paramahaṃsa, and also Brahmanārāyaṇa; || 65 ||
The Kātyāyanī, Brahmabindu, Āruṇi, Amṛtabinduka, Pañcabrahma, Jābāla, Tejobindu, and Maudgala. (66)
The Bodhāyanīya, the Carca, the Śravaṇa, the Parākrama, the Prācya, the Śaunakīya, and the Śivasankalpa as well. || 67 ||
The Āsurāyaṇa, the Maitrāyaṇīya, the Vājasaneyaka, the Vedāntasāra, the Praṇava, the Vajrasūcī, and likewise the Ambaka; || 68 ||
The Sāṃkhyāyanīya and others are the most excellent among all branches of knowledge;
those eighteen Purāṇas have been fully sung. (69)
The first is known as the Brāhma, then the Pādma; the third they know as the Vaiṣṇava;
the fourth is declared to be the Śaiva, and the fifth is devoted to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavat).
The sixth is the Nāradīya, while the Mārkaṇḍeya is the seventh; the eighth is known as the Āgneya, and they recognize the Bhaviṣya as the ninth.
The tenth is the Brahmakaivarta; the Laiṅga is considered the eleventh;
one should know the Vārāha as the twelfth, and the Skānda as the thirteenth. (72)
The fourteenth is the Vāmana, while the Kaurma is considered the fifteenth;
the sixteenth is declared to be the Mātsya, and after that follows the Gāruḍa.
The eighteenth is the Brahmaṇḍa; after that are the Upapurāṇas. Sanatkumāra has spoken [the Sanatkumāra], and after that is the Nārasiṃha.
After that, the Skanda [Purāṇa] was narrated by Sanatkumāra.
The fourth is the Purāṇa known as Śivadharmākhya, composed by Nandin;
likewise, the Nāradīya was proclaimed by Dūrvāsas, following that.
As well as that of Kapila, of Manu, and likewise that composed by Uśanas. || 77 ||
Beyond that is the meritorious Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, and after that the Vāruṇa;
then there is the Purāṇa known as Kālika, which describes Kālakhaṇṭha.
Then there is that known as the Vāsiṣṭha, and by name the Māheśvara;
thereafter is that called the Sāmbapurāṇa, which is proclaimed to be very subtle. (79)
Furthermore, the Parāśara, the Mārīca, and that which is called the Bhārgava—these indeed are the Upapurāṇas that bestow the knowledge of Brahman. (80)
Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsā, the Nyāya-śāstra, the Purāṇas, as well as the Smṛtis and the Vedāṅgas, were proclaimed there by the sages. (81)
Mīmāṃsā is traditionally held to be twofold, distinguished as Pūrva and Uttara;
likewise, Tarka is traditionally held to be twofold, distinguished as Nyāya and Kāṇāda. || 82 ||
(11) Eighteen Smṛtis have been proclaimed, composed separately by sages;
among them, Manu is said to be the first, and Bṛhaspati follows immediately after.
The third shall be Dakṣa by name; then Gautama, Yama, Aṅgiras, Yogīśvara, Pracetas, Śātātapa, and Parāśara. (84)
Saṃvarta, Uśanas, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Atri, Viṣṇu, Āpastamba, and Hārīta are the founders of the Dharmaśāstras. (85)
All eighteen Smṛtis are marked by his name:
Jābāli, Nāciketa, Skanda, Laugākṣi, and Kāśyapa; (86)
Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra, Śaṃtanu, as well as Janaka, Kratu, Kātyāyana, Jātūkarṇi, and Kapiñjala; || 87 ||
Bodhāyana, Kāṇāda, Viśvāmitra,
as well as Paiṭhīnasi and Gobhila, are the authors of the Upasmṛtis.
The eighteen Upasmṛtis are marked by their respective names;
thus, fourteen [Smṛtis] have been declared in accordance with the path of the Vedas. (89)
Preceded by the motionlessness of the palate and lips, those spoken by Śiva, numbering twenty-eight, are the Śivāgamas declared by Śiva. (90)
The Lord of the World, the Master, having condensed the *Prābhṛtatantra*— which consists of three categories and four chapters—
into a single aphorism, expounded it in detail.
Indeed, through its divisions such as the Kāmika and others, it is split into many parts;
the Śiva-āgamas, beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Āvatu, were spoken by Śiva. (92)
(12) These should be known as the Siddhāntas, endowed with [divine] instruction:
Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, and likewise Kāraṇa and Ajita. || 93 ||
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Āpya, Śumān, Suprabhedaka, Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, and Anala. (94)
Vīra and Raurava, as well as Makuṭa and Vimala; Candrajñāna and Bimba, and likewise Prodgīta and Lalita. || 95 ||
The Siddhasantāna, the Śarvokta, the Pārameśvara, the Kiraṇa, and the Vātula—these are designated as the twenty-eight [Tantras]. (96)
In this way, other tantras were spoken by Śiva many times:
the Mahāmāyā-śambara and the Yoginījāla-śambara. (97)
Therein are indeed the Śambaraka, the Bhairavāṣṭaka, the Bahurūpāṣṭaka, and the Yāmalāṣṭaka. || 98 ||
Candrajñāna, Vāsuka, and likewise Mahāsaṃmohana;
Mahocchuṣma, O Mahādeva, Vātula, and Vātulottara. (99)
The Hṛdbhedatantra, the Mātṛbhedatantra, the Guhyatantra, the Kāmika, the Kalāpāda, the Kalāsāra, and likewise the other, the Kubjikāmata. (100)
And the Māyottara, the one called Vīṇā, Trotala, and Trotalottara; Pañcāmṛta, Rūpabheda, and Bhūtoḍḍāmara as well. (101)
The Kulāsāra, the Kuloḍḍīśa, and likewise the Kulacūḍāmaṇi; the Sarvajñānottama and also the Mahāśivamata. (102)
The Mahālakṣmīmata, the Siddhayogīśvarīmata,
the Kurūpikāmata, and the Rūpikāmata as well. (103)
The doctrine of all heroes, the supreme Vimalāmata, the eastern, western, southern, northern, and unsurpassed [teachings]. (104)
The specialized knowledge of Tantra, as well as the supreme Vīrayoga;
Aruṇeśa, Mohaneśa, and Viśuddheśvara as well. (105)
In this way, these tantras and others likewise by the millions—all among all the sciences, Vīraśaiva is preeminent. (106)

Thus ends the introductory chapter in the *Kriyāsāra*, which is the essence of the Vedas and Agamas, composed by Nīlakaṇṭha, who is proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secret of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
The First Instruction:
Now I shall declare the Vedic foundation of the heroic Śaivas, in accordance with the meaning and intent of the Sūtras composed by Vyāsa. (1)
By the word "vi" (vi-), the knowledge that awakens to the unity of Śiva and the individual soul is expressed;
those Śaivas who delight in that [knowledge] are proclaimed as Vīraśaivas. || 2 ||
The word *vi* has the sense of "option" (*vikalpa*), and the word *ra* has the sense of "devoid" (*rahita*).
They declare that which is devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to be Vīraśaiva, the Śaiva [state]. (3)
The prefix *vi-* signifies opposition, while the word *ra* signifies being devoid of;
the wise know that Śaivism which is free from opposition as Vīraśaiva. (4)
In that regard, concerning the majesty of wearing the *liṅga* as spoken in the words of Amṛta,
and regarding the state of identity between the *liṅga* and the body, they declare the fruit to be liberation (*mokṣa*). (5)
One who desires to know, preceded by devotion, the hundred and one stages beginning with *piṇḍa* and ending with *jñānaśūnya*, as well as the six stages and the classification of the *liṅga*.
He should be known as the qualified candidate who has himself renounced all desires, who practices the eightfold yoga, who possesses wisdom, and who is devoted to the fivefold conduct. || 7 ||
Eager to hear the majesty of the devotee, desiring to perform the means for liberation, devoted to service to the guru, learned, and free from taint.
There is no mother equal to the guru, nor is there a father equal to the guru;
for it is he who delivers one from the cycle of existence through the instruction of the supreme truth.
By approaching the Guru alone, the gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and others attained the state of the identity of the Liṅga and the body (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya), freed from all affliction.
Led by Sanatkumāra, those illustrious ones devoted to knowledge,
bearing the marks and limbs of their spiritual state, shine forth eternally with joy.
Led by Ḍuṇḍinandin and Mahākāla, these leaders of the Gaṇas number fourteen thousand; they are indeed the lords of the enclosure of Kailāsa. (12)
All these initiators, who have ascended the seat of the Guru, stand near Maheśvara, bearing tridents in their hands. || 13 ||
Agastya, Jaimini, Viśvāmitra, Kāśyapa, Bharadvāja, Aṅgiras, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Romaharṣaṇa. || 14 ||
All these highly fortunate ones, who are devoted to that which transcends the [ordinary] castes and stages of life, are known as Vīraśaivas; they are liberated while living, without a doubt. (15)
For them, however, this will be their final birth, and they shall possess supreme intelligence;
they are blessed and of noble lineage, being the promoters of the knowledge of Śiva. (16)
By these [means], all phenomena have been set in motion throughout all the worlds;
for Śiva alone is the primordial teacher of all, higher than the highest. (17)
Because he is not limited by time, that auspicious Śiva is the teacher of the predecessors;
from his mouth issued the Vedas and those known as the Kāmika and other [Tantras].
There were also various other sciences demonstrating their respective rituals;
among them was Vyāsa, who had received initiation and was solely intent upon the knowledge of reality.
Through devotion to Śiva, he obtained the knowledge of the Paśu, the Pāśa, and the Pati; he also mastered the various Śiva-knowledges which yield solely the fruit of liberation. (20)
They were taught by Śiva himself and were maintained by him;
thereafter, he indeed composed the Sūtras which are devoted to the ultimate reality (tattva).
The meanings of these [texts] are not clear because even a true guru has not seen them;
their meanings have been depicted in many ways through logic and harsh arguments. (22)

When the identity of the individual self and the supreme self is understood as the meaning of the word "knowledge," the falsity of the world will be declared, like the delusion of a snake in a rope. (23)
Some maintain that the scriptures have as their object those possessed by ignorance;
for Brahman is destroyed solely by knowledge, whereas the fruit born of *prārabdha* karma [persists]. (24)
Thus some describe it; others declare something else:
"The individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—these two principles are established. (25)
The reality of Brahman is immediate; the impermanence of the phenomenal world arises from modification.
Likewise, the Supreme Lord possesses the nature of being the witness of all. (26)
Primarily, liberation from worship is known as *sālokya*;
for the supreme Brahman indeed possesses the form of auspicious knowledge. (27)
Although such doctrines had been widely propagated throughout the world many times over,
Vyāsa then approached Śaṅkara and made this request.
O Śaṅkara, various doctrines indeed have arisen; and the sūtras composed by me have been interpreted incorrectly. (29)
Deciding thus, O Śaṅkara, they engage in mutual strife over this web of threads obtained solely through your grace.
"Since you previously requested that the meaning of my sūtras be analyzed,
the compassionate Lord of Pārvatī, being thus entreated by him," (31)
Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya composed a commentary by name that provides an excellent exposition of the Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine. (32)
I too shall compose all of its essential meaning in the form of *kārikās* in proper sequence, for the sake of the easy understanding of the listeners. (33)
The liberation from bonds is attainable solely through the state of perfect equilibrium between the Linga and its limbs;
Śiva alone is the supreme reality, and Śiva alone is the supreme light.
Śiva alone is the supreme light; Śiva alone is higher than the highest.
That which Vyāsa declared as the Supreme Brahman in his own Sūtras is Śiva himself. (35)
Śiva alone is indeed the liṅga, and Śiva himself is the one who possesses the form of the liṅga;
Śiva himself is the object to be established by all the statements of the Vedāntas.
He is the support of all reality, the imperishable cause of the universe;
he is himself partless, the very essence of the meaning of such statements as "That thou art. (37)
Brahman is one and secondless, consisting of truth, knowledge, and bliss;
it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), stainless, pure, beyond birth, and untainted.
Rudra is the primordial source of the Vedas, the Lord who transcends the universe;
he is omniscient, the creator of all, and the sovereign cause of everything.
The reality is without beginning or end, devoid of high and low;
it is the nature of the Supreme Self and the very essence of the Supreme Brahman.
"The Vedāntas declare that Śiva, the supreme cause, is the ultimate reality to be attained, immeasurable and incomparable. (41)
"He who is Śaṅkara is this very form of the Great Liṅga, he is Sadāśiva"—those devotees who know Śiva thus through the compassion of their Guru [attain him]. (42)

Listen to those who say that it is not logical for Brahman to be characterized by the form of a *liṅga*, because the relationship of primary and subordinate is established even through contradiction with the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*). (60)

If [one claims] that [the practice] of Vīraśaiva and others is not [Vedic], how could there be immediate succession (ānantarya) for those who are diligent in the performance of wearing the sacred ash, rudrākṣa beads, and the liṅga as prescribed in the Vedas? (67)
Brahman, known by the mark [of the Self], is the object of inquiry; thus, there is no contradiction with the immediate sequence.
An object contrary to the meaning of the prior section is said to be what is taught in the prior section. (68)
Whatever dharma belongs to the Pūrvakāṇḍa, or even anything else whatsoever, quickly becomes [attained] by one who has undergone the initiation (upanayana) through entry into the Vedāntas. 69.

"However, some describe that [the result occurs] immediately after the attainment of the four means; that is not very useful. (71)

They say that knowledge which is eternal and immediate, the sole means to liberation,

That dharma which is performed with contentment and without desire for the severing of one's own bonds—that indeed they declare to be the *patidharma* (the duty toward the Lord) in the scriptures. (79)
Through curd, one gains the sense-faculties...
[and so forth]. Here too, at the beginning of all rites, the wearing of ashes is indeed the primary factor that bestows eligibility, as established by the *Kālāgnirudropaniṣad* and other such texts.

The object of the two is the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman; otherwise, how could that which is within the sphere of "you" (the object) become otherwise than that which is within the sphere of "I" (the subject)? Limited knowledge constitutes the state of being an individual soul, while omniscience constitutes its opposite.
If it is asked, "How can impermanence and permanence be joined in one and the same thing?",
then let your vision be directed toward the reality of the object.

And just as the property of being silver ceases when the mode of being mother-of-pearl is present,
so too here, in the case of the omniscient one, the state of being a knower of only a little [ceases].
Liberation is declared to be the purpose by virtue of its commonality.

Just as there is no difference between fire and its sparks in terms of their essential nature.

Therefore,

Indeed, conduct becomes perverted in accordance with the nature of the age;
for even a wealthy man, afflicted by stomach disease, does not eat excellent food.
Their minds will no longer be [confused] regarding the true meaning of the scriptures;
and having assumed the external marks of our order, they will be free from all feverish distress.
Beginning with "Then, therefore, [one should] desire to know Brahman" and ending with "non-return," the inquiry into Brahman has been conducted within the *Vyāsasūtra*.
Having determined that which is to be upheld, the wise, intent upon trust in their guru,
should maintain that absolute Brahman described by the words of the secret Upaniṣads.
Its glory is uninterrupted, beyond the reach of speech and mind;
it is partless, stainless, pure, free from conceptual construction, and untainted.
Having known [the Self] as that which is devoid of the characteristics of duality, how indeed is it to be worshipped?
For the establishment of a reality is always declared to be by means of its defining characteristic and valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the causality of the origin and so forth of the worlds is indeed the defining characteristic of Brahman;
all Vedānta statements are the authoritative means of knowledge for this, without a doubt.
Having determined Brahman through these means, such as hearing and so forth, at first glance,
that person who knows thus, being Brahman itself, attains Brahman.
Indeed, the second aphorism was established by Vyāsa for this very purpose:
"From which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world]," since the birth of the primordial Viṣṇu occurs from Him.
That agency of the world is held to belong directly to Śambhu, who is Brahman;
or else, it is the birth and so forth of Viṣṇu—who is denoted by the syllable *A*—that [proceeds] from Śiva.
The characteristic of Brahman is said to be the causality of all conceptual proliferation.
The subject matter of the passages beginning with "yato vā" has been illustrated;
through the natural force of the sentences, Brahman is ascertained as that which is to be held in mind.
Because all this— beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra,
along with all the elements and the senses— is first brought forth by him.
This god is to be known as Mahādeva, he is Maheśvara;
no state superior to his is ever found.
By this act of painting, the world is first created;
and at the time of its end, it shall again undergo dissolution within this very same [canvas].
And he who is the sustainer of causes, the meditator, is the supreme cause.
He is never produced from anything else, nor does he ever arise from any source whatsoever;
he is complete with all sovereignty, and is himself by name the Lord of All (Sarveśvara).
(26) Śambhu, who dwells in the midst of space, is to be meditated upon by all those seeking liberation;
he alone is Śiva, the agent, the Puruṣa, and the supreme cause.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the Moon, the Sun, Śakra, and the gods along with their progeny—
[it is he who] creates and indeed devours this world which has become darkness.
At that time, when the entire world was unmanifest, the one Great Lord, the Moon-crested One,
first created Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all the others.
And Śiva, O Hero, initiated them in the sequence of the Śaiva Krama;
through the state of essential identity between the Liṅga and the body (liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya), they became fulfilled.
From that time forward, Viṣṇu and the others, empowered by the command of Śiva, the Supreme Self, attained renown throughout the worlds.
By whose command Viriñca is the creator of the world, Hari is the protector,
and Śiva— known as Rudra, accompanied by Ambā and eternal— is the destroyer at the time of dissolution.
He whose nature is solidified bliss, consciousness, and existence like clarified butter;
subtler than the subtlest, the Self of all, greater than the greatest, the Lord.
The Lord Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer;
they are known to possess inseparable consciousness-power (cicchakti), like sparks from a fire.
Indeed, there is no state of absolute difference, nor non-difference, nor both;
rather, difference and non-difference were previously intermingled in the case of the individual soul and Brahman.
The Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, as well as the Kāmika and other Āgamas,
indeed reveal that which is to be approached through worship, consisting of both difference and non-difference.
(27) Having indeed placed Śiva, together with Ambā, eternally within their hearts, they speak thus;
for the scripture is the primary authority regarding His being the cause of this world.
The status of having the scripture as its source is attributed to that which has the scripture as its source;
or rather, it is the established position of those who know reality that [Brahman] is the source of the scriptures.
Since Brahman has the scriptures as its source, it is determined therein that the subject matter consists of the Upanishads;
the subject matter is the contemplation of Brahman.
The concordance of these Vedic statements is recorded as being in Brahman;
because of this concordance, that very Brahman alone is to be held and worshipped by those seeking liberation.
This word "tu" (but) has been employed to indicate a distinction;
therefore, there is no doubt that the subject sentences possess manifold meanings.
In this regard, having cited a single point of meaning according to their own individual intellects,
people are constantly deluded, disputing with one another.
Furthermore, deluded by this wheel of saṃsāra,
people on earth wander about, subject to the control of others due to curses pronounced by Kaṇva and others.
Having abandoned the path of the virtuous, those who resort to another path all fall perpetually and certainly into the Taptanaraka hell.
What is the use of saying more? Human birth is difficult to obtain;
even within that, birth in the family of some devotee of Śiva is rare.
Birth within the lineage of Vīraśaiva is considered supremely difficult to attain;
all men born therein are Vīraśaivas, the best among men.
Because he is the protector of the assembly of gods beginning with Viṣṇu, he is Sadāśiva;
he is celebrated as Vīraśambhu, and his *liṅga* is called Śiva.
Having worshipped the Vīra-liṅga,
those heroic Śaivas who always desire liberation for the worlds attain its very nature.
Radiant with rows of triple-tilaka marks, wearing garlands of rudrākṣa beads around their necks,
they were devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and were worshippers of the devotees of Śiva.
Those who are constantly devoted to the five syllables and intent upon the service of the Guru should be praised, saluted, and diligently sought after for a vision.
They have descended from the world of Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
Through the state of essential identity with the Liṅga and Gaṅgā, they are liberated while living and remain composed in meditation.
Therefore, with every effort, the wise should wear the *liṅga* for the sake of attaining the nature of Śiva and for the cessation of the bonds of the bound soul (*paśu*).
That man who desires liberation while abandoning the wearing of the *liṅga* truly makes himself immortal by drinking poison;
he who, having abandoned the wearing of the *liṅga*, becomes devoted to the scriptures of the bound (*paśu*).
Having abandoned the milk-rice (pāyasa) held in his hand, he licks his own elbow;
now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Brahman, whose birth is from Śiva and from whom [all things] arise.
Therefore, because that [Brahman] has its source in the scripture, and because it is further established through the harmony [of all Vedānta texts],
he himself composed this work, which consists of the essential portions of the logic supporting the cognition derived from the Vedānta.

29) According to the principle that "the part is not [identical to] the whole," that very [reality] is thus proclaimed: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others are portions (aṃśa) of Śiva; the Lord Śiva is remembered as the possessor of those portions (aṃśin).
Mahādeva is the object of worship for all, and all are remembered as worshippers;
how then can there be non-difference between those two—the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)?

It is certain that attributes such as omniscience belong to Śiva, the Supreme Self, while attributes such as limited knowledge belong to individual souls (jīvas). How can there be absolute non-difference when difference and non-difference are thus established?
How could Brahman’s being the source of the scripture not be its own inherent nature?
For the Veda has action as its purpose, whereas Śiva is beyond action.
If it is argued that the manifestation of the agent and other factors does not belong to the activity of Brahman,
we shall address this in the section defining the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*).
Attributes such as omniscience and others are understood through the Vedantas;
indeed, the statements within the Vedantas are firmly established in their coherent unity.
By this, the fact that Brahman has the scripture as its source is firmly established;
for, beginning from the point "Because [Brahman] sees, it is not that which is not based on scripture," this is maintained exclusively.
Up to the end of the first chapter, the reconciliation [of the scriptures] is stated here;
for in various places, scriptural passages such as "Existence alone, my dear," are heard.
And there arises the doubt as to whether the word "Sat" refers to Brahman or to Pradhāna; what, then, is the initial position? Some maintain that it is Pradhāna.
The material cause of the insentient world must itself be insentient; furthermore,
according to the supporting examples, it cannot be something different in nature from that which is sentient.
For by the word "Śat," the Supreme Brahman is understood, just as it is by the word "Ātman."
Because the act of seeing is an attribute of Brahman, it cannot belong to the Pradhāna;
for the Pradhāna is not based on scripture, as there is no Vedic text denoting it.
The analogy of clay and so forth that was stated is indeed dissimilar and not logical;
in passages such as "That fire thought," the term "fire" is used figuratively.
Thus, even with respect to the Pradhāna, "seeing" is said to be figurative;
this has been firmly established by the sūtra: "If it be argued that it is figurative, no, because of the word 'Self'."
For the act of seeing on the part of water and fire is indeed secondary (gauṇa), and not otherwise;
whereas here, the act of seeing belonging to the Seer denoted by the word "Sat" is primary (mukhya).
Because of the reference to the word "Self" in the passage beginning with "That is the Self," the act of seeing must likewise be understood as primary for water and fire as well.
For that designation of "seeing" belongs to the Lord who possesses the conceit [of agency],
just as the word "self" is applied to a servant who accomplishes all the king's purposes.
Thus, the word "Sat" is appropriately applied to Pradhāna, as is the act of seeing it;
for here, liberation is ordained through instruction for one who is established in that.
Indeed, being established in that is being established in Brahman, and they alone are the qualified seekers of liberation.
Therefore, that which was stated—that it is the Pradhāna—is false;
for Brahman alone is the cause of the world and is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation.
By the statement "This is not the Self," there is the rejection of the body of Śiva.
Rejection, indeed, is the assumption of that [divine] form according to the path of injunction (vidhi).
By the statement beginning with "liṅgāṅga," those who are solely intent upon the path to liberation [are addressed];
by the statement "of the nectar," the act of wearing [the mark] is established.
Those devoted to that alone, who thus disregard the distinctions of caste and stage of life,
are indeed the great-souled ones described as being established in Brahman.
Having attained the state of Brahman through the perfect union of the Linga and the body,
they achieve liberation in the form of Sārūpya, which is difficult even for others to obtain.
They indeed become those who have accomplished their purpose, constantly enjoying the bliss of Śiva;
thus, by the statement beginning with "Om," the wearing of the Liṅga is established as certain.
That merit which is the means for its liberation must be held within the lotus of the heart;
therefore, there is no doubt that it is indeed Brahman alone, denoted by the word "Sat" (Being),
inseparable from its power of consciousness, just as coldness is inherent in water.
The claim that Māyā is the primary cause is not logically tenable;
for [the world] arises from the Supreme Self, who is endowed with the power of consciousness (cicchakti) through the mantra "ajā" (the Unborn).
The Lord’s playful creation and dissolution of the universe is described in the Kaṭha,
Kaivalya, Māṇḍūkya, Praśna, and other Upaniṣads.
Alas! The meanings elucidated in the Vedāntasāra, the Praṇavavajrasūcī, and other such works have all been forgotten by some.

Those intent on liberation, being certain that there is nothing else besides this, do not seek anything other than this; what need is there for much speaking? For this alone is the meaning of the Sūtra.
In this regard, the point to be noted from the natural sense of the Sūtra is as follows:

Immediately following these three Sūtras,
the intended meaning as expressed by the word "sautra" is seen to apply precisely to the categories (padārthas) as declared in Vīraśaivism.
For indeed, since the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the worlds proceed from him,
that is the defining characteristic of his Brahman-hood.

In that regard, there is this much difference in the analysis of the words of the Sūtra.

The lack of contradiction with the statements regarding creation has already been refuted,
since the terms "maintenance" and "dissolution" are expressed by the word "sthala" (place/abode).
That place where all principles abide and dissolve is the *sthala*;
the triad consisting of maintenance (*sthiti*), dissolution (*saṃhāra*), and birth (*janma*) is also a *sthala*.
For it is not the case that [the meaning of the passage] beginning with "from which" (yato vā) is consistent with the sense of the subject matter;
rather, it is examined at length by means of the word *sthala* in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures.
Alternatively, the birth of Viṣṇu, who is denoted by the suffix *kāra*,
from Śiva is established by the *Atharvaśiṣṭha Upaniṣad*.
Because it is the author of the teaching of the scriptures and so forth, it is therefore supreme.

The syllable *a* signifies Viṣṇu; because it is His source, the *liṅga* is of the nature of the cause. That reality (*tattva*) is the regulating principle, as heard in the essential meaning of the Sūtra.
Whether it means "that which has the scripture as its source" or "the very fact of having the scripture as its source," or "the source of the scriptures"—
for us, all these interpretations are consistent.
The means for accomplishing all goals exist within all the scriptures;
nevertheless, whatever the helpless gods may say, it is indeed [true].

all other styles have not been made to conform with the Sūtras.
That which others maintain— the superimposition of the world upon Brahman—
is entirely unestablished by the Sūtras and is merely imagined through ignorance.
Fools are constantly deluded without that supreme path;
is it not then said, according to the scriptural injunctions, "Brahman is known," and so forth?
From such statements as "Brahman is one and Brahman alone [is the cause] through its own ignorance," non-difference alone is taught; how then could there be difference-in-non-difference?

If this is argued, it is not so; for it has been determined by both the Śruti and the Sūtras that the statement "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" refers to that [knowledge] which is an auxiliary to meditative worship (upāsanā).
For one who is devoted to that alone, liberation here is indeed certain through instruction as the supreme;
for Brahman alone is denoted by the word "Sat," and nothing other than that has ever come into being.

And because it is so heard [in scripture], the Pradhāna and other such principles can never be the cause.
Is the word "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) used in the Taittirīyaka due to repetition?

For the actual connection of being a limb of the Beloved is not intended here;
rather, that connection in the *Ānandavallī* is imagined for the sake of strengthening the intellect.
The suffix *mayaṭ* may signify modification (*vikāra*), its own meaning (*svārtha*), or abundance (*prācurya*);
however, this *mayaṭ* here does not signify modification, because that would contradict what precedes and follows.
In this context, the introduction is stated using the word "prāṇa" and so forth in silence;
however, in the concluding statements, it is proclaimed with the suffix "-maya."
Therefore, the suffix *mayaṭ* is established as having its own primary meaning in the sense of "abundance," as seen in the Bhṛguvallī;
and if it is argued that [Brahman] is not [the cause] because of the word "modification" (*vikāra*), we say no, for Brahman alone is intended in the sense of abundance.
Nor is it anything else, because of the abundance [of such usage] in words like *anna* (food) and *prāṇa* (life-breath).
Therefore, casting aside envy, one should investigate the wearing of the sectarian mark (*liṅga*).
For this reason as well, it is certain that [the suffix] does not have the sense of a modification (vikāra), but rather denotes its own primary meaning (svārtha);
this is established by the mantras beginning with "satya-jñāna," and by the statements of the Sūtras and the Brāhmaṇas.
Because of the identity of Mantra and Brahman, and because nothing else is taught,
it is certain that Brahman alone is the denoted meaning of the word "Ānanda," and nothing else.
35) In this Taittirīyaka [text], that which is based on the wording of the mantra is indeed what is sung;

How could he be called "Mālī" (the garlanded one) for that reason?

Furthermore, because of the designation of its distinction, the Supreme Lord consists of the bliss of Brahman;

For by the passage beginning with "another within," the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is intended;
and because of the mention of desire, the Pradhāna cannot be [meant], as has been stated.
Because there is no hearing of a desire for that [bliss] in the statement "it does not exist" regarding the insentient,
the Supreme One consisting of bliss teaches its connection with that [sentient being].
Neither the transmigrating soul nor primordial matter (pradhāna) exists; how could they exist within this teaching of Yoga?
For it is certain from the scriptural statement, "When indeed he [sees] in this," that fearlessness is the supreme liberation; therefore, one must be attentive to the knowledge thereof.
The Supreme Brahman, consisting of bliss, is that which is to be attained and maintained within the lotus of the heart;
this was previously investigated on the grounds of the teaching of its internal attributes and other reasons.
(36) All that regarding living beings is determined as the concentration on Brahman;
hereafter, however, the concentration on Brahman concerning the gods must be considered.
Abiding in the solar orb, may the Lord of the Universe inspire us;
likewise, the Lord of Gods is to be worshipped in the right eye, and no other should be so.
Because there is a designation of difference, it is certain that the other is the Supreme Self;
by the statement "He who is beyond the sun," the Supreme Lord is also the object of meditation.
Likewise, space [is Brahman] because of its characteristic marks; for space is indeed the absolute Brahman.
Likewise, for this very reason, it is heard in scripture that "the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed Brahman";

There is doubt because the term "prāṇa" occurs as a recurring designation and because of various indicative marks;

What is the cause, from where were we born, or by what do we live? Where is our firm foundation, and by whom have we been nourished? By what do we constantly abide, whether in pleasures or in miseries?

Is it time, inherent nature, destiny, or chance that exists here?

for time and the like are insentient, whereas the self possesses sentience.
Because they were overwhelmed by pleasure and pain and lacked self-mastery, they reflected;

thus, with their bonds severed, they [attain] the cause of all causes.
Beholding with divine vision the omnipotent Mahādeva,
who is the cause of all things without exception, together with Time itself as his very self.
By means of his immeasurable power, he alone exists as one with them;
he is the Lord, free from duality and free from conceptual construction, whose form is like that of a star.
The extremely beautiful Liṅga, which shines within the space of the heart, is the primary object of worship; indeed, its meditation alone is investigated here.

Having joyfully held the Śiva-linga within the center of the lotus of the heart,
it is declared everywhere in the Vedāntas that this is indeed the Śiva-linga.

nevertheless, foolish men have pointlessly established it as something else.
Indeed, the attainment of liberation through direct perception is considered difficult for all to achieve,
as is well known throughout the Vedāntas by way of traditional instruction.
Endowed with qualities such as being born from that [Brahman], peaceful, and higher than the highest, he is the one to be worshipped;

In the statement "all this indeed," it is the individual soul alone that is the Supreme, and nothing else.

That which was previously established by the sūtra beginning with "jīvamukhya...
is indeed Brahman, the creator of the universe, who should be worshipped with devotion by those seeking liberation.
Because it originates from that and because it is produced by that, the meditation is that "everything is Brahman.
Or rather, the word "this" (idaṃ) refers to the Lord, as indicated by the proximity of the phrase "the vital breath is his body," which sets aside the [ordinary] meaning;

And because the intended qualities and so forth are logically established,
it is firmly and correctly determined that Brahman alone is the supreme object of meditation, and nothing else.
For this reason as well, because of the impossibility [of the qualities], the embodied soul can never [be the subject];
for "one whose desires are true" and "one who is true" refers to the supreme Śiva, the source of all qualities.

And because of the teaching that the individual soul (jīva) is the agent and the Supreme is the object— expressed in the passage, "Having departed from here, one reaches this"— the meditation [is on the Supreme].
The difference between the embodied self and the Supreme Self is understood even from Smṛti;
for attributes such as "consisting of mind" pertain exclusively to the qualified [Supreme Self].
From this and from the distinction in the words used, the difference between the two is understood;

If it is argued that this is the attainment of the *saṃbhoga-kāya*, we say no; because of its difference [from the heart-lotus], for since that [lotus] is free from sin, pleasure, pain, and so forth do not exist there.
Because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving, the Supreme is said here to be the giver;
therefore, by virtue of this context as well, it is the Supreme alone who is to be understood as the recipient.
Although the two selves— the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*)— have entered the cave,

Because of the qualifying attributes, from such statements as "the one who moves within the heart" and so forth,

That destination known as the Devayāna, which is well-established [in scripture], resides within the lotus of the heart.
Furthermore, through austerity, celibacy, and speech,

The Person within the eye is established as Brahman alone,

For qualities such as being the controller and so forth are indeed possible for the Supreme;
therefore, He is the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmī) because of the possibility of His possessing all powers.
That which was stated—that the Pradhāna is the Inner Controller—is not accepted;
nor is that Pradhāna of the Smṛti [the intended referent], because its attributes are described as being other than those [of the Pradhāna].
Attributes such as "not being a seer" (adraṣṭṛtva) and so forth are not possible in the Pradhāna.
For both [the individual soul and the intellect] are possible as conscious entities primarily characterized by seeing and meditating;
indeed, in my view, both are perceived by me as distinct from the Supreme.
The Kāṇvas and Mādhyandinas know that the Inner Controller is not the embodied self;
because of the teaching of attributes such as invisibility and so forth, He is indeed the Supreme.
Neither the individual soul nor primordial matter [is the cause], because their attributes are absent;
for the scripture teaches that the mark of the Supreme Lord is omniscience.
For the divine Person is formless; he is both outside and inside, for he is unborn.
He is without breath and without mind, pure, and higher than the high Imperishable.
Because of the designation [of the Self] through its specific distinctions, the other two are not [the Self];

Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Brahman because of its common designation and because of specific scriptural indications; it is certainly not the gastric fire and so forth.

If it were being remembered, it would be an inference; therefore, the Supreme Lord and Vaiśvānara are not [the gastric fire], for [the latter] is merely the digestive fire, due to [its association with] sound and other such qualities.
If it be argued that [the individual soul is meant] because of its being established within, we say no; for the Supreme is not like that.
Moreover, because of the teaching regarding vision therein, and because [such vision] is impossible [in the case of the individual soul], the Supreme Person is intended.
Now, regarding this, the followers of the Jāsaneya school maintain that it is indeed that same fire;
for the reasons already stated, it is neither the elemental fire nor a deity.
Jaimini is certain that Vaiśvānara here is indeed the Supreme [Self];
moreover, he maintains that there is no contradiction even with the direct [scriptural statements] regarding the Supreme.

Bādari, through remembrance; and Jaimini, through attaining [the state of the Lord].
For thus they demonstrate the supreme Śiva Vaiśvānara;
and in this same way, the noble ones have attained that ancient [state].
The digestive fire, the distinguished Vaiśvānara, and Umāpati are,

There arises a doubt as to whether the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is Brahman or the Pradhāna; what, then, is the initial position? Some maintain that it is the Pradhāna.

for because of its own specific designation, the Supreme Brahman is meant, and not the Pradhāna or other such entities.
For the quality of being that which is to be approached by the liberated belongs to that which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
indeed, no one has ever ascertained that attribute for anything other than that which has that [abode] as its primary referent.
The Supreme is not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, on account of the absence of inference and because of the word "that."
And because of the designation of its distinctions, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme;
likewise, also because of the context, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme.
Likewise, on account of abiding and eating, the one who is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme;

For it is Brahman that is celebrated as the Imperishable (Akṣara) because it sustains the ends of space;

They are liberated.

Because of that imitation, and because it is also remembered in the Smṛti and the Śruti,

By that word, Brahman is known as being within the small [space], divine, and wonderful;

"Just as the *liṅga* is to be maintained by humans, so indeed is it by the gods;

a doubt arises, and the sage Jaimini maintains his view on that matter.

Likewise, there is no entitlement for Śūdras and others;
however, all those who have been purified by the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are indeed entitled.
Furthermore, their lack of respect is indicated by the disrespectful manner in which they are mentioned;

therefore, from words such as "Lord" (pati) and so forth, the eternal Brahman is indicated by its characteristic marks.
Those seeking liberation should always hold within the lotus of their heart and always worship the Lord who is partless,
immutable, and resembles pure crystal.
The supreme Liṅga, which is the cause of all worlds, consists of all worlds,
and exists both within and without; it is the subtle, the great, and the ultimate essence of the jewel.
The immutable Lord is perceived by His devotees without effort;

From that time on, the fourth single syllable became the *bhakta* (the shared portion), consisting of the three morae *a-u-m* followed by a half-mora (*ardhamātrā*). Therein, in the portion resting upon the letter *a*, on the right side of the supreme *liṅga*.
The letter *u* is in the north, and the letter *m* is in its center;
the sound (*nāda*) consisting of half a mora is heard at the top of the *liṅga*.

Among the qualities, he is Rajas; among the forms, he is Brahmā; and among activities, he is the primordial one.

Rudra in the qualities of darkness (tamas), and likewise as the first among the forms and among the activities.
One should contemplate the withdrawal within the three worlds and the principles (tattvas), [placing] Śiva as supreme;
likewise, Vidyā, Kalā, Aghora, and Ghora within the five Brahmans.
Whether in the portion of the *liṅga* above the pedestal or within the three causes, the Jina [is present];
likewise, the human and the divine sovereignty—thus is the world pervaded by the Sāman.
Then Atharvan spoke of the state beyond qualities (*nirguṇya*) of the Self;
thereafter, he [spoke] of Maheśvara, who is Sadāśiva even within the manifested forms.
Even though Śiva, the Supreme Self, is devoid of action,
he performs actions for the sake of favoring living beings, by which means sentient creatures are liberated.
Since speech, along with the mind, has ceased even regarding the worlds,
that which is beyond the world is the world of Soma, which is supramundane.
There, the Lord Soma resides eternally with me;
having attained that which is above the world of Unmanā, one does not return.
And Śānti, and Śāntyatīta, as well as the pervasive Kalā itself.
Likewise, among those five Brahmās, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna are located;
furthermore, the head of the Liṅga is the unsurpassed portion among all the portions.
Therein, within the *liṅgas*, the supreme, partless (*niṣkala*), and absolute (*kevala*) [deity] is to be propitiated;
likewise among the principles (*tattvas*), [the deity resides] in the *bindu*, then in the *nāda*, and beyond that in the *śakti*.
Even beyond reality is that which is the supreme reality, yet from the perspective of ultimate truth it is non-reality;
for within the causal principles, Māyā is the cause of agitation, transcending the triad.
Beyond the infinite Śuddhavidyā is Maheśvara;
beyond him is Sadāśiva, the sovereign lord of all the lords of knowledge.
From the Veda of the body of all mantras, which is endowed with the three powers,
from the five-faced and ten-armed one, who is both manifest and unmanifest.
Therefore, from that supreme Bindu, and from the Ardhendu following it;
from that which follows it, the Nirodhīśa, and from the one called Nāda following that;
Then from Suṣumneśa, who is beyond that, and also from Brahmarandhreśvara;
then from the Śakti who is beyond that, and further still from the Śiva-tattva.
The supreme cause, manifest and itself without cause, the auspicious one;
the sustainer of all causes—that which is the Savior, the imperishable object of meditation.
The space within the heart, situated above the Supreme Self, [is distinct] from the impure human state and other such states arising from Māyā through the power of sovereignty. (p. 52)
And from each subsequent [level], beginning with that which has the impure path as its domain.
Beyond that, from the supreme beyond the Samana level— starting from Śuddhavidyā and so forth—
is the supreme sovereignty, which is beyond mind (unmana), upward-bound, beginningless, limitless,
independent of others, devoid of any superior, and eternal.
Since the Atharvaṇa Śruti is thus superior by virtue of these ten kinds of subjects, therefore the entire universe is pervaded by the Atharvan.
The Ṛgveda further declares: "This form of the world is spoken by me, by which this Self is eternally designated as the reality."
The Yajurveda said: "O Vatsa, I shall now speak even of dreams;
for knowledge, having transformed into the nature of objects of enjoyment, is to be known within me."
And Sāman says: "That which is called deep sleep is everything; everything is spoken of by me.
By my own purpose, this world is overcome by Śiva, who is characterized by tamas."
Atharvan said: "That which is called the fourth (turiya) and even that which transcends the fourth (turīyātīta) are overcome by me;
therefore, I am the Supreme, transcending all paths."
The third, however, consists of the paths (adhvan) and is known as the essence of Śiva-vidyā;
it comprises the three qualities (triguṇa) and is to be purified by those seeking the state of the Lord (pati) through the means of the triple Veda (trayī).
The path that has transcended time is called the Fourth (turya), the supreme state of Nirvāṇa. Beyond even that is the state free from qualities (nirguṇya), which purifies this very path.
Nāda and the End of Sound (nādānta) are the means of valid cognition for these two; they constitute my own nature.
Therefore, my position is that the Supreme Lord is primary by virtue of his autonomy;
for whatever exists as a reality, all of it is so through the conjunction of the predominance or subordination of the *guṇas*.
They declare the meaning of the Praṇava to be both collective and distributive;
therefore, that syllable is indeed the signifier of both the existent and the non-existent.
First, Śiva creates this entire universe with the syllable "Om.
Indeed, Śiva is the Praṇava, and the Praṇava is remembered as Śiva.
Since there is no absolute difference between the signified and the signifier,
this Rudra, who is beyond thought, is signified together with the mind.
They turn back without reaching it; he alone may be designated by the single syllable.
From that single syllable called "A," the Command (ājñā) is said to be Brahman.
From the single syllable known as *U*, Vidya-Viṣṇu-Rudra arises;
from the single syllable known as *M*, Śiva-Rudra is proclaimed.
From the right side of Maheśa was born the one known as Brahmātmā;
from the left side arose Viṣṇu, who is designated as Vidhi.
From the heart of Śiva, Rudra emerged, who is known as Śiva;
Brahmā is the initiator of maintenance, and Viṣṇu is the deluder of maintenance.
Therefore, Rudra is the eternal regulator of their dissolution;
thus, these three are declared to be the triad of causes of the world.
And Śiva is the supreme cause, the cause of the three causes;
yet, failing to understand this truth, those bound by passion harbor mutual enmity.
Between those two, a great liṅga arose there spontaneously;
thus they say "Oṃ Oṃ," as it was declared here by the Atharvaṇa.
Even while the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, along with thousands of other branches, were themselves clearly articulating their meanings from his own mouth; even so—
Like an experience in a dream, that [reality] is determined by those two;
the sign (liṅga) which reveals reality itself has arisen as reality.
From that [consciousness], the state of being a sign (liṅgatva) arises for the sign (liṅga), and the state of being the possessor of the sign (liṅgitā) for the possessor of the sign (liṅgin);
from that, through the particularity of the entire universe, it also arises for one's own self.
The arising and dissolution, as well as the reality of the six paths,
are the Brahman that is utterly devoid of existence— the partless, sovereign Linga.
The eternal Lord of this phenomenal world, which consists of both the individual soul (paśu) and its bonds (pāśa),
who is entirely free from fear, and who is immutable, neither increasing nor decreasing.
External, internal, both external and internal, yet devoid of both external and internal; eternally free from any superior state, it is distinct from the entire world.
Characterless, indefinable, beyond the reach of speech and mind,
having the single flavor of luminosity, peaceful, serene, and eternally risen.
Endowed with such power, it is the abode of all that is auspicious;
thus has the greatness of the Liṅga been revealed in the Vedāntas.
Having understood that, one should hold it in the heart according to the method of equanimity (*sāmarasya*);
he who bestows the unmanifest *liṅga* is indeed the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
In many such sūtras, the retention of that [mantra] has been illustrated.
The Fourth Quarter of the First Chapter.
Having promised to investigate, the definition of Brahman was set forth;
it was then suspected that this definition might also apply to Pradhāna.
This [objection], which was previously refuted on the grounds of being non-verbal,
is now undertaken again for the purpose of refuting it by raising the doubt that it is indeed verbal.
The aphorism beginning with "based on inference" (ānumānika) is the determination of its meaning;
that which has been determined here by means of inference is what has been propounded by the Sāṃkhyas and others.
For some, that which is unmanifest is indeed the Pradhāna; moreover, in the Śruti, that which is well-known in Sāṃkhya as "the Great" (mahat) is also recited here.
If it is argued thus, we say no; for by the word "that" (tat), the body is indeed grasped, since that which was set forth as the metaphor of the chariot is not grasped at all in its unmanifest state.

The body itself is indeed the unmanifest; it cannot be the *pradhāna* or other such principles. Although it does not exist as gross because it is produced from subtle [elements], nevertheless, it is determined by both the Śruti and the Sūtras to be "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
Because it possesses meaning and because it is dependent upon that [Brahman], its status as supreme is recognized;
and because it is declared to be an object of knowledge, it does not become like the Pradhāna.

If it is argued that the Śruti also speaks of the Pradhāna, we say no; for, according to the context, the Wise One (the Self) is meant, not the Pradhāna. Furthermore, there is a question concerning three entities: fire, the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśvara).
(56) For in this very way the introduction [is made], as with the "Great One" (mahat) and likewise;
it is not accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, but is determined to be the embodied self (śārīra).

Because there is no distinction [from the preceding context], the primary sacrifice is not mentioned here, as in the case of the *camasa* cups; however, due to the introductory statement, the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) is indeed used in a restrictive sense.
Even the primordial nature (prakṛti), whose essence is fire and water, is grasped by the word "unborn" (ajā);
for thus it is maintained by some here that the primordial nature is indeed power (śakti).
And because of the teaching of that [triple] conception, it is spoken of here as in the case of honey and so forth;
for there is no contradiction, since by the word "Unborn" (ajā) the primordial nature (prakṛti) is intended as power (śakti).
Because there is an excess of diversity [of entities], it is not included within Sāṃkhya;
therefore, the doctrine of Sāṃkhya is not accepted here as being supported by scripture.
The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and so forth are intended to complete the number [of deities] based on the remainder of the passage;
for thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "According to some, [the number is completed] by means of light (*jyotis*), not by the unreal."
For even there, the attainment of the required number is possible through the vital breaths and so forth;
furthermore, as in the case of the reed-flutes and other instruments, it occurs by way of being the cause.
In that very context, because it is designated as such, the Self alone is intended;
and because of the subsequent summary, Brahman alone is to be known, and nothing else.

Therefore, because of the mention of the world and because of the exclusive mention of Brahman, it is firmly established even by the sūtra "But [the word 'self'] refers to the individual soul and the chief vital breath" (B.S.
1.1.31). Likewise, the sage Jaimini maintains that the purpose of the question and its explanation is something other than [the individual soul].

In this context, it is considered that the mention of "prāṇa" as well as the mention of the "liṅga" (subtle body) within the lotus of the heart [refers to] the Supreme Brahman, because of the connection of the sentences.
That supreme Brahman, which is to be worshipped and must be known by the wise,
should be maintained as the imperishable *liṅga* within the lotus of the heart, on account of the fulfillment of one's solemn vow.
The sage Āśmarathya considers that [the soul] returns there out of reverence; likewise, because of its existence, Auḍulomi will indeed be mentioned next in sequence.

Because of their abiding together, Kāśakṛtsna [maintains] that there is neither difference nor non-difference between Brahman and the individual soul; for those two, there is certainly a state of perfect equilibrium (sāmarasya).
Because both difference and non-difference are accepted, like sparks from a fire,
the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed the direct worshiper, while Brahman alone is the object of worship;
through the state of equilibrium between the subtle body (*liṅga*) and the physical body (*aṅga*), difference and non-difference are established.

For the material cause (upādāna) is indeed the primordial nature (prakṛti), while Brahman alone is the emanated effect; and because it does not contradict the supporting examples, it is accepted here as being like clay and so forth.
From such an instruction, its status as the material cause is investigated;
and both the status of being the material cause and the status of being the agent belong to Brahman, according to the weight of the scriptural statements.
Furthermore, since both are explicitly recorded in scripture,
it was determined by the sūtra "And because [Brahman] is the source" that Brahman is both the material cause and the agent.

The terms *kartṛtva* (agency) and *prakṛtitva* (material causality) are expressed by the word *yoni* (source) in their respective senses; for [the Lord] transforms Himself through His own material nature (*ātma-kṛti*). Thus [it is said]: "Himself by Himself."
Therefore, both the state of being the material cause and the state of being the agent are established for the Supreme;
by this, all [objections] are explained—thus it is stated in the Sūtra.
By these reasons, all the Vedāntas have that Brahman as their ultimate purpose. That Brahman, established in every sūtra, should be held within the heart.
This is the sovereign power, the manifestation, the sign of Brahman in the lotus of the heart.
It should be maintained and worshipped by those seeking liberation through the practice of *sāmarasya* (equilibrium).
Therefore, with every effort, a human being [should perform] all ritual actions.
Having turned [the vessel] around at the appropriate time, one should worship it upon the palm of the hand.
Since devotion has been fashioned like a boat to carry one across [the ocean of existence],
what need has one endowed with devotion for passion (*rajas*) or darkness (*tamas*)?
Whether one is an outcaste, a barbarian, a fool, or even one who has fallen from grace—
if they have attained the state of Śiva, they are worthy of worship by all the gods and demons.
Therefore, one should hold Śiva in the heart with every effort,
because for those who lack devotion, there is no fruit whatsoever anywhere.
Then, having deliberated with the Vedas, the scriptures, and those learned in the Vedas, it was firmly determined:
whether one is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed;
or even a killer of a mother, a killer of a father, a killer of a hero, or a killer of an embryo.
If one worships with devotion the Shiva-linga, which is higher than the highest, even without mantras,
one is liberated from those sins provided there is a mind intent on equanimity.
Therefore, with every effort, even if one has fallen from grace, one should worship Śiva;
provided that he is a devotee, possessing no other [interest], subsisting on alms, and having his senses subdued.
Even after committing a very great sin, if one worships that Linga with devotion by means of the five-syllabled mantra,
one is liberated from that sin.
Those who abstain from food, those who subsist on air, and others who are emaciated by vows— even for them,
there is no attainment of the world of Śiva through these observances alone.
Whoever worships the Liṅga even once with devotion using the five-syllabled mantra alone shall go to the abode of Śiva by virtue of bearing the Śiva-liṅga.
Therefore, all austerities and sacrifices, even those with the giving away of one's entire possessions as the sacrificial fee, [are not equal to this].
These [other merits] are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
Whether one is non-Rudra or Rudra, one should worship the Śiva-liṅga.
Whether a man has fallen even once, or is deluded, or is becoming deluded,
he should constantly [recite] either the six-syllable mantra or likewise the five-syllable mantra.
Those who worship Mahādeva once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or at all times, should be known as lords of the Gaṇas.
He by whom the Liṅga of the Lord was not worshipped while born as a self-harming being,
remains wandering for a very long time in this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Having obtained this human birth which is so difficult to attain, he who does not wear that emblem makes his life fruitless, since it will not lead him to liberation.
The wise should always bear the Śiva-liṅga upon the region of the heart;
for having attained this rare human birth, one who bears the liṅga within the heart has achieved his purpose.
The birth of those alone is fruitful, and that best of men has achieved his purpose,
who are born from the Liṅga and are solely devoted to the Śivaliṅga.
Those devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga do not partake in suffering;
those who desire great enjoyments and sovereignty even in the abode of the gods always worship the wonderful liṅga residing within the heart.
Good fortune, a radiant form, truthfulness, majesty, valor,
and fame in the world shall accrue to one who worships the Liṅga.
Therefore, having renounced everything, one whose mind is intent solely on Śiva [should proceed].
If one desires one's own welfare, one should perform the rite of *sāmarasya* (union). Herein is a summary of the authoritative sources found in the Purāṇas and the Āgamas.
Having searched through these writings on a single subject,
one should respectfully disregard repetitions for the sake of strengthening the intellect.
If it is asked, "What is to be accomplished by describing the purport of the Sūtra through these infallible words while demonstrating its non-contradictory nature?
listen: The description of the purport of the Sūtra must be undertaken by means of these unerring statements. If you ask what is to be achieved [by this], listen.
In summary, these statements establish the uniformity of the Vyāsa-sūtras with the categories of reality proclaimed in the Vīraśaiva Āgamas.
Those very categories of meaning that exist in the Āgamas will be explained in the Vyāsa-sūtra by means of different words and through various modes of designation.

Through the *Śāstrayonitva-sūtra*, the status of the scriptures as the source [of knowledge] is heard; thus say the followers of the Āgamas: "The Linga of the Guru should be upon the tip of the tongue."
Śiva is the direct instructor of all sciences,
since he is that Person in the eye [referred to] by the Jyotiścaraṇa-sūtra.

That which is called the Supreme Brahman, the followers of the Agamas have sung of as being the very Śivaliṅga, because it possesses the nature of a liṅga in both its aspect as vision and its physical form.
For this very reason, the nature of Brahman is heard in scripture as being "prāṇa" among the vital breaths;
likewise, the *prāṇaliṅga* is proclaimed in the Āgamas and within [the scriptures].
That very Brahman which was proclaimed in the section known as the Dahara-adhikaraṇa is indeed declared in the scriptures of Āgama to be the Mahāliṅga.
In the section known as Ānanda, that which is proclaimed as Brahman is said by those expert in the meaning of the Āgamas to be the Bhāvaliṅga.
The threefold offering that was described according to the distinctions of the offering of one's being and so forth—
that very same subject is now investigated in this section concerning the offering of the mind.
Having raised the objection that there might be a distinction in the nature of the *chandas* (Vedic meters), it was then examined [in the following manner]:
"Because it impels," and so forth; this is found in all the commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and in the *Vārtika*.

Indeed, the very same meaning that is expressed by the term *sthāna* and so forth in the Sūtras is everywhere proclaimed in the Āgamas by the word *sthala*. In this manner, the identity of form can be stated for every single Sūtra.
Fearing excessive prolixity, I shall begin with the subject at hand. Regarding what is called "difference-and-non-difference," let it be understood as follows:
by some, superimposition (adhyāsa) has been indicated in the opening of this treatise and established therein.
In the opening verse, both the subject matter and the purpose must be indicated;
the subject matter consists of the identity of the essential nature of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.
If it is argued that the meaning of the Sūtra is simply that such knowledge depends upon practice,
then— given the non-existence of the identity between the nature of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—
it would not be logical for that [identity] to be its object; let this be determined from the perspective of reality.
Furthermore, the identity of the essential nature of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is not stated anywhere in the Sūtras;
however, in the Sūtra "A part, on account of the scriptural statement" (Brahmasūtra 2.3.43), the status of the individual soul as a part (aṃśa) of Brahman is indeed taught.
