The difference between the divided [parts] and their state of being merged is said to be like that of sparks from a fire;
for indeed, the identity of nature between the fire and its sparks is not observed.
By which the identity of the individual soul with Brahman may be realized once again.
It is not logical for both difference and non-difference to reside in one and the same thing, because they are mutually contradictory; therefore, this must be explained by the wise.
The false distinction is produced by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) characterized by ignorance;
for it is like the case of both [the snake and the coil], as in the example of the snake and its coils.
Or rather, like light and its substratum, because of their being non-different from You, as previously stated;
likewise, the granting of permission and the avoidance [of faults] are due to the connection with the body.
"Just as light and so forth"—thus it is possible because of that;
likewise, because of logical consistency, there is the instruction "like a lamp" immediately following that.
For it is thus shown: furthermore, because difference and distinction are established both by means of valid cognition and because they are observed in illustrative examples.
One should understand that there is a state of mutual non-contradiction among them;
and so it will be stated by them [the Sūtrakāras] in the *Sūtra* beginning with "The enjoyer and so forth" (*bhoktrādi*).
Having clearly perceived the absence of contradiction, the Sūtra has thus been explained;
for if it were otherwise, the doctrine of Brahman as the cause would be undermined.
Even if scripture is not sublated by the power of right reasoning,
it must itself be the authority regarding its own subject matter.
Nevertheless, when its own object is sublated by another means of valid cognition,
it would itself be set aside by that other [means], just as in the case of hearing the injunction regarding the *kṛṣṇala* grains.

Just as mantra and arthavāda do not find a firm footing outside their own respective domains, so too it is said that reasoning has its standing only within its own sphere and is likewise unfounded elsewhere.
Furthermore, the weakness of reasoning is observed in the case of dharma and adharma.
If this is your view, you should know that it is improper for the Śruti to communicate an object already established by another means of valid cognition.
What object established by another means of knowledge is here being taught by the scripture?
For this distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is well known in the world:
the conscious embodied self is the enjoyer, while these objects such as sound and the rest are the things to be enjoyed.
Just as Devadatta is the enjoyer and those [objects] such as the sacrificial oblations are the objects of enjoyment,
so too would the distinction between enjoyer and object of enjoyment be absent in every instance.

If the enjoyer were to become the state of the enjoyed, or the enjoyed were to become the state of the enjoyer— since they are non-different from Brahman, the supreme cause— then such mutual transformation would necessarily follow;
yet this is not tenable if [the distinction] is not sublated.
For this very reason, it is not logical for one who says that the well-known distinction [between cause and effect] does not exist,
and thus there is no certainty regarding Brahman being the cause.
One might say "it is like the world" in response to that foolish person;
however, this division is indeed logically consistent within our own position.

Thus, because it is observed in the world that waves and so forth arise from the ocean which is of the nature of water, their distinction is logically possible even though they are non-different from it; yet this is not the case for things like jars, which are non-different from the nature of earth.
(64) It is held that among many things such as foam and the like, there is mutual identity;
however, this is not possible in the case of waves, ripples, and so forth, because they lack such mutual identity.
The non-difference of the noble-souled ocean from its rivers is not established.
In this system as well, the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is thus established;
for it is not possible to prove that anything other than Brahman—which is of the nature of pure Being—exists.
But surely this is merely a verbal justification for the absence of contradiction;
for that non-difference [of cause and effect] was established in the Sūtra by the words "from the mention of 'originating material' (ārambhaṇa)," and so forth.
Because the scripture beginning with "a mere matter of words" (vācārambhaṇam) establishes that everything in every way is so,
and because it is proven that the manifold of difference is sublated.
Moreover, by this Sūtra, or by the Śruti consisting of speech and so forth,
the sublation of the entire phenomenal world is not established.

The manifoldness of difference is not established by the means of valid cognition known as direct perception; therefore, it cannot be sublated by scripture. Rather, it is stated that [non-duality] is what is logically consistent.
The scripture itself has another purpose due to its contradiction with direct perception and other means of knowledge;
for as it was established in the previous system (Mīmāṃsā), one should cook the *kṛṣṇala* grain because of the injunction.
When the literal sense of "gold māṣa" is sublated by direct perception regarding the act of cooking,
the word is accepted as having a secondary figurative meaning (lakṣaṇā) intended solely for the purpose of indicating "heating."

In the injunction "one should sacrifice with soma," the meaning accepted is that one should bring about [the result] by means of a sacrifice; for, when both "with soma" and "by means of a sacrifice" are construed in grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya), there is a connection between the soma and the sacrifice.
Just as difference [is understood] through secondary implication (lakṣaṇā) by sublation of the non-difference perceived [by the senses],
so too, if there were a sublation of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca).
In that case, since the nature of the Veda, the recollection for the sake of others,
and likewise the knowledge of the meaning of sentences are all included within the phenomenal world (prapañca), [they too would be unreal].
If even those [objections] are sublated, how can the phenomenal world (prapañca) not be sublated?
And how is it that my tongue is not barren like a woman unable to conceive?
And even when conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is sublated, its own essential nature (svarūpaka) indeed persists;
therefore, it can certainly be said that the effect is established.
The non-existence [of the world] occurs only through the sublation of its counter-correlate by means of mere discourse;
however, the true nature of the phenomenal world is certainly not sublated by scripture.
For what indeed could constitute a contradiction?
It would be the sublation of its own nature; however, the truth of that [nature] consists in its being unsublated.
If conceptual proliferation were accepted, there would be no sublation of its reality;
therefore, this Sūtra does not establish a sublation of the Śruti.
However, since there is indeed non-difference, one should not consider that there is a contradiction between difference and its designation; likewise, this is seen elsewhere as well.
And because of the designation as something else, because of the failure to act for its own welfare, and so forth, there is the consequence of defects; likewise, [the text] says "That thou art."
Because of the scriptural declarations of the complete non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman,
is creation the work of the individual soul, or is it the work of Brahman alone?
(66) "The individual soul (jīva) would create its own welfare and not its misfortune, such as hell,
and so forth"— having raised such an objection, one should look further to the Sūtra on the designation of difference (*bhedanirdeśa*).
"Is the individual soul (jīva) not the agent? But rather, Brahman alone is the supreme agent. Even though it is established within that soul, it indeed creates," having thus declared.
Or how could there be both deficiency and superiority in the description of difference?
And how could the Lord of All, being directly omniscient in every respect,
create sorrow and the like in living beings while perceiving them as his own self?

Anticipating the objection that sorrow and the like would follow as being experienced as residing in the self, it is stated that such a connection is untenable, just as in the case of a stone and so forth.
And by this [reasoning], when a distinction is intended between sun-crystals, lapis lazuli,
and other stones on the basis of their common nature as "stone-ness," [the following occurs].
Due to the difference between individuals, there is a distinction of inferior, middling, and superior forms;
likewise, there is a diversity of intrinsic natures and a diversity of bodies.
And thus, even for the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para), a distinction between their manifestations is established;
thereby, inferiority, superiority, and the diversity of their functions become logically possible.
The universal "stoneness" is undivided, whereas the individuals are indeed distinct;
thus, both difference and non-difference cannot coexist in a single locus.
Furthermore, there is the absence of that difference whose counter-positive is delimited by universals such as "stoneness," and also the difference whose nature is the absence [of identity],
which possesses a counter-positive delimited by "lapis lazuli-ness" (*vaiḍūryatva*) and so forth.
Because the distinction among individuals and the demonstration of that fear are established,
it is not possible to suspect this in the case of both the diamond and the lapis lazuli.

The application of linguistic conventions such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is acceptable here, because it is desired [by us] that these [conventions] involve the mention of non-difference from the universal.

Precisely because there is an absence of non-difference in their specific qualities, even Īśvara does not possess non-difference from the individual soul (jīva) in his nature as the Self; thus, the vision of such non-difference is enjoined once again.
At the point of explanation, I have accepted the term "self";
however, having raised this objection, the refutation is also demonstrated in detail.
Therefore, since these two—difference and non-difference—are established, we shall desist from further discussion.

Thus ends the first instruction in the *Kriyāsāra*, a compendium of the essence of the Vedas and Agamas, composed by Nīlakaṇṭha, who is proficient in the one hundred and one topics of the secret doctrine of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita school.

Now begins the second instruction. In this first instruction, [the teaching is given] sequentially regarding Brahman— the omniscient and omnipotent material cause and efficient cause of the phenomenal world.
The first [chapter] is the demonstration of the concordance of all Vedānta statements;
the second is the absence of sublation by contradiction with Smṛti and other authorities.
Instruction is demonstrated through many logical arguments;
therein, the Vedānta texts show that Brahman is the cause of the worlds.
The followers of Sāṃkhya call it *pradhāna* (primordial matter), while others call it *upādāna* (material cause);
therefore, due to this contradiction, one of the two must necessarily be refuted.
In that regard, scripture has its scope with respect to duties and so forth that are to be performed.
In that case, since the Śruti has scope regarding matters such as the duties to be performed,
whereas the Smṛti lacks such scope, it is logical that the Smṛti is sublated by the Śruti.

Perceiving through direct seer-vision (*ārṣa-pratyakṣa*) that the primary matter (*pradhāna*) is the cause of the perceptible world, the Sage composed the Smṛti; therefore, it has its root in direct perception.
Therefore, it is indeed logical that the Smṛti is sublated by that Śruti;
however, there is no such sublation of Śruti by Smṛti, because other [conflicting] Smṛtis would otherwise have no scope.
If it is argued that, due to the occurrence of various faults, one may speak of multiple causes in accordance with various Smṛtis, [we reply: this is certainly not possible.
Since various conceptual constructions cannot arise arbitrarily regarding an object,
the Śaiva doctrines are therefore established by means of the authorities proclaimed in the Vedas.

And when a prohibition is observed in some instances, as from such scriptural statements as "the nectar [is] first," there would indeed be a sublation of those [Smṛti rules], but not a sublation of the Śruti by them.
Now, if the authority of the Śaiva doctrines is indeed accepted,
[what becomes of] the rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma and others well-known from the earlier section [of the Veda]?
Due to the mutual contradiction between the doctrines of the Vairas and the Śaivas,
the same applies to the *agniṣṭoma* and other mantras, as well as their respective auxiliaries.
O Hero, among all the portions of the Vedas, there are certain sections pertaining to Śaiva rites which consist of the primordial form of nectar.
Furthermore, due to mutual contradictions and because they follow many different Vedas,
there is indeed a discrepancy regarding the very mantras employed in Vīraśaivism.

If it is argued that [the Upanishads] must be understood as having another purpose, listen: [it is because] they serve as injunctions for the performance of the duties (dharma) taught in the earlier section (pūrvakāṇḍa). (p. 69)
By such scriptural passages as "having abandoned everything else," it is otherwise [stated].

Or how is it established by you that [the Upanishads] possess superiority over the duties taught in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), given that they are equally "appropriated" (upātta) [as scripture]? Indeed, their superiority must be asserted.

Because it has been stated that between these two— the section on Brahman and the section on ritual action— there exists a relationship of principal and subordinate, like that between glass-stone and a jewel, and because of the doctrine regarding the superior strength of knowledge.
Since it is established by such statements as "Not by action, nor by progeny,
nor by wealth," that the bond is destroyed solely by knowledge,
the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is not rendered useless; this is demonstrated through the following analogy.
If it were inferred that mere scripture is useless, then its being rooted in the Veda could not be asserted;
thus, the established order of the argument would be violated.
We do not claim that any portion of the Veda possesses authority as pure consciousness;
rather, we assert the superiority of the section on knowledge over the section on ritual action.
In that regard, an illustration for the Vīraśaivas is stated there,
concerning the various [jewels] situated in the jewel-market in their respective order.
Furthermore, the buyer should demonstrate the value of items such as glass, pearls, and emeralds in accordance with their respective market prices.
Apprehenders grasp [an object] solely according to their own capacity;
it is not at all intended for the purpose of refuting another.
Thus, when the authority of the Veda is established in a general sense, it then functions among those who follow the Veda according to their own respective qualifications.
(70) When one has ascended by means of the steps of the gradual path— whether by three or two stages— there is certainly no tearing away of the steps through such a leap.
In that same way, all [scriptures] possess authority here;
therefore, a Śaiva may also diligently perform all rites in certain instances.
If one should act upon the authoritative means of knowledge, then let it not be denied;
for in this world, there are kings and wealthy men who possess abundant jewels among the virtuous.
One wears a small purchased jewel; it is not thereby rendered faulty.
Likewise, the Vedas are of such a measure—let this suffice, for what need is there for further elaboration?
Here, my own method according to the Siddhānta school will be shown:
[the method] for all Vedānta statements regarding the Omniscient and Omnipotent One.
In the *Liṅga*, concerning the Supreme Lord— who is both the material cause and the efficient cause of the universe—
it is stated in the primordial teaching by virtue of the power of the signified and the signifier.
Since the identity of the mark and its constituent parts is observed here when the concordance has been shown,
that [opposing view] is subject to the defect of being set aside by contradiction with Smṛti and by the fault of having no scope.
The second chapter is intended to avoid that contradiction,
for the Vedas indeed declare that the Supreme is the material cause of the world.
Since it is stated that "smṛti is primary," there is a doubt as to which of those two should be sublated when they are in conflict.
In that regard, with respect to the dharma and so forth to be practiced, the Śruti is considered to have scope [for other purposes],
whereas the Smṛti would be without scope [elsewhere] and thus serves as its definitive expounder.
Therefore, the sage declared that the sublation of the Śruti by the Smṛti is logical.
(71) Having ascertained through yogic perception that "that alone is the cause of the world," he subsequently composed the *Smṛti*.
If it is argued that "in this case, the authority of Smṛti is stronger because it is rooted in direct perception," we say no; for it is not tenable that the Pradhāna should be the cause.
Because various causes are postulated in accordance with various traditions,
because conceptual construction is untenable, and because of the defects inherent in [the notion of] a real entity.

Furthermore, because [the Purāṇas] possess qualities such as being composed by great sages (maharṣi), and because they are mutually contradictory, they lack authority due to their human origin; this, however, does not apply to the Veda (śruti).
In that case, it is stated that the primary statement has its basis in direct perception (pratyakṣa),
because of the instruction [of the Sūtra] that "the others are not perceived."
How much less so by Kaṇāda and others who were endowed with the vision of the Ṛṣis?
For that [Pradhāna] is not perceived, because there is no traditional authority (smṛti) regarding it as a constituent part of Pradhāna.
This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is the nature of the Śivaliṅga;
yet, due to the weight of their bonds, the bound souls (paśus) do not recognize it as such.
Not knowing that supreme state which is beyond conceptual construction, the great seers speak of that one eternal Brahman alone as manifold.
Furthermore, some say that Mahādeva is the Lord who is both the form of the lower Brahman and the essence of the supreme Brahman, without beginning or end.
The lower Brahman is designated as consisting of the elements, the senses, the internal organs, primordial matter (pradhāna), and objects; the higher Brahman consists of consciousness (cidātmaka).
Because of its vastness and because it is Brahman, it is called "Brahmāṇī," the supreme and most excellent;
by means of this form of Brahman, [it belongs] to the Lord, the Sovereign of Brahman.
Some declare that the Lord has both knowledge and ignorance as his essential nature;
they say that "knowledge" (vidyā) is consciousness, while "ignorance" (avidyā) is unconsciousness.
This entire universe consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge;
there is no doubt that it is the form of the all-pervading Guru of the universe, since the universe is under his control.
The wise know the form of Śiva to be error, knowledge, and that which is beyond;
or else, the intellect regarding objects is said to be manifold error.
If the perfection of the form of the Self is proclaimed as knowledge,
then that reality which is free from conceptual construction is designated as the Supreme.
In this regard, they say that this form of Śaṅkara is presided over by His command;
therefore, they call Him "the eternally existent" (sada) and also "the Lord of the Assembly" (sadasaspati).
The word *sat* is used by the virtuous (*sadbhiḥ*) only for that which is true and good;
however, the word *asat* is spoken by those who proclaim the Vedas for its opposite.
The entire universe, both real and unreal, is the body of the Supreme Lord;
that which is called "existent" and that which is described as "non-existent."
Because he has fallen upon those two, Śiva is called the Lord of the Assembly (Sadasaspati);
they say he consists of both the perishable and the imperishable, existing as the succession of the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings, while the unchanging is called the immutable (akṣara). Both of these are forms of the Supreme Lord, since they are under His control.
Of these two, Śiva is the supreme, the tranquil one, remembered as being beyond both the perishable and the imperishable;
he is both the totality and the individual form, and the cause of both the totality and the individual.
Some sages declare Śiva to be the supreme cause;
they know the unmanifest as the collective totality (samaṣṭi) and likewise the manifest as the individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi).
Those two forms of the Supreme Lord follow His will;
because they exist as its cause, the Śivaliṅga is higher than the highest.
Those who know the meaning of causality declare that the Lord is both the collective and individual cause;
by some, He is described as having the nature of both the genus and the individual.
That which persists throughout the individual instances (piṇḍa) is called the "universal" (jāti). An individual instance, whose form is distinct from others, is the substratum of that universal.
Since both individuals and classes were governed by His command,
Mahādeva is therefore remembered as having the form of both class and individual.
Śiva is said to be the self consisting of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla;
they call Pradhāna "Prakṛti" and likewise Puruṣa "Kṣetrajña."
The wise declare that there are twenty-three principles;
time is the sole cause of the transformation of the manifest world and its effects.
Of these, Śiva is the Lord, the Ordainer, the impeller and the withdrawer;
they call him the sole cause of manifestation and concealment, the self-ruling, unborn one.

Therefore, the cause possessing the nature of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Vyakta, and Kāla is the sovereign lord (adhipati) of those [categories]; he is the creator, the enjoyer, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
p.
74) Some declare that the Lord is of the nature of Virāj and Hiraṇyagarbha;
Hiraṇyagarbha is the cause of the worlds, while Virāj is the Lord of the universe.
Śiva is described by the poets as both the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) and the Supreme (Para);
others declare him to be the Self of the Prājña, Taijasa, and Viśva states; and still others say he is the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
Others declare that the agent, the action, the effect, the cause, and the supreme cause [constitute reality],
while still others describe it as consisting of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Others call it the fourth (turīya), and some even call it that which transcends the fourth (turīyātīta).
Some declare him to be a transmigrator, while others say he is not a transmigrator;
some declare him to be independent, while others know him to be dependent.
Some call it terrible, while others know it as gentle;
some say it is devoid of qualities, while others know it as possessing qualities.
Some say he possesses passion, while others say he is free from passion;
some say he is inactive, while other people say he is active.
Some have declared it to be without faculties, while others have declared it to possess faculties;
some have declared it to be eternal, and others have declared it to be non-eternal.
Some indeed say it is formless, while others know it as possessing form;
some call it visible, and others call it invisible.
Some say it is expressible; others say it is inexpressible.
Some say it consists of sound; others say it transcends sound.
Some say it consists of reflection; others say it is devoid of reflection. Others say its nature is knowledge, while still others call it consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Some say it is knowable, while others say it is unknowable;
some call it one, and others call it many.
When the Supreme Lord is thus conceptualized,
sages do not perceive His true nature, due to the cause of their various conflicting notions.
But those who have surrendered to the Supreme Lord by means of their entire being,
they recognize Śiva, the supreme cause, without effort.
As long as one does not behold the Lord, the ancient Seer, the ruler of the universe,
so long does one remain bound by the noose in this cycle of existence, wandering through suffering like the rim of a wheel.

When he perceives the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person whose source is Brahman— then the wise man, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality.
For Śiva, there is no bondage consisting of the atomic (āṇava), nor that of karma, nor that of māyā,
nor that which is natural (prākṛta), nor that which is intellectual (bauddha), nor likewise that which consists of egoism (ahaṃkāra).
He has no mental bondage, nor any belonging to the mind-derivatives, nor one consisting of the sense-faculties;
he has no bondage to the subtle elements, nor any bondage whatsoever to the gross elements.
Neither time nor its divisions, nor knowledge, nor destiny;
neither passion nor hatred exists in Śambhu of immeasurable splendor. Nor does he have any attachment to things that are either skillful or unskillful.
(76) His actions and their maturation, as well as the resulting pleasure and pain,
do not connect him with the underlying intentions (*āśaya*), nor does he have any connection with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of those actions.
With respect to enjoyments and the latent impressions of enjoyment pertaining to the three periods of time,
he has no instrument, no agent, no beginning, no end, and likewise no interval.
There is neither action nor instrumentality, nor that which is not to be done, nor that which is indeed to be done.
For him there is neither kinsman nor stranger, neither restrainer nor instigator;
he has no master, no teacher, no protector, and none who is superior or even equal to him.
For him there is neither birth nor death; nothing is desired, nor is anything undesired.
There is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither liberation nor bondage.
Whatever is not auspicious does not exist for him at any time,
for he possesses every single auspicious quality, since he is Śiva, the Supreme Self.
That Śiva, presiding over all this by means of his own powers, remains unswerving from his own nature; therefore, he is remembered as Sthāṇu (the Immovable).
Since this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is presided over by Śiva,
and since Śarva abides as the form of all things— knowing this thus, one is not deluded.
All is Rudra; salutations to him! He is the Supreme Puruṣa, the Great One, the golden-armed Blessed Lord, the Lord of gold, the Sovereign.
Abika, Pati, Īśāna, Pinākin, Vṛṣavāhana, Ekarudra, Paraṃbrahma, Puruṣa, and Kṛṣṇapiṅgala.
This [Lord] should be meditated upon within the heart, inside the small cavity (dahara), as being the size of a hair-tip;
he has golden hair, lotus-eyes, and is both reddish and copper-colored.
That god who moves about, blue-necked and golden-hued—him [I praise].
He is gentle, the sacrificial oblation, as well as the mixture, the imperishable, the immortal, and the inexhaustible;
he is that supreme, extraordinary Person, the Blessed One, the end-maker of the end-maker.
He is volition, yet liberated from volition; he is beyond all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) and higher than the highest.
In this world, his knowledge and sovereignty are seen to be unsurpassed.
The wise declare that Śiva exists as the one who transcends all;
he establishes the expansion of the scriptures for the Brahmins produced at each dissolution.
He alone is the original instructor for those who exist within the limitations of time;
he is the teacher even of those gurus who are themselves bound by the constraints of time.
The Lord of all is indeed the master of all, free from the limitation of time;
His power is pure, innate, and transcends everything.
Knowledge that is unimpeded and eternal, a body that is utterly stainless,
sovereignty without rival, bliss, and ultimate power.

Splendor, majesty, heroism, as well as forbearance and compassion—these belong to him who is complete through the acts of creation and the rest; for the Self, there is no further purpose to be served.
The benefit of this meritorious action is solely the favoring of others;
the syllable *praṇava* is the designator of that Śiva, the Supreme Self.
The *praṇava* is remembered as the supreme among words such as Śiva and Rudra;
through the contemplation of Śambhu—who is expressed by the *praṇava*—and even through its recitation, [liberation is attained].
That perfection which is to be attained is indeed supreme; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures declare that the single-syllable *liṅga* is [the means].
Regarding the identity of the signified and the signifier, those renowned ones have declared that its four measures are proclaimed at the summit of the Veda.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and also the resonance (*nāda*):
they say that the letter *a* is the Ṛgveda, and the letter *u* is called the Yajurveda.
The letter *ma* is the Sāmaveda, as heard in the Atharva-śruti;
the letter *a*, however, is the Great Seed, the Passion (*rajas*), and the four-faced Creator.
The syllable *ukāra* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the womb, the principle (*tattva*), and the protector Hari;
the syllable *makāra* is the person (*puruṣa*), the seed, darkness (*tamas*), and the destroyer Hara.
The Nāda is the Supreme Person, the Lord, devoid of qualities, actionless, and auspicious;
thus, by means of these three measures, everything is threefold.
Having denoted the Self that is Śiva, it awakens [the consciousness] by means of the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*). For there is nothing higher than Him, nothing more subtle, and no one greater than He.
Like an immovable tree standing in heaven, by that One Puruṣa all this is pervaded.
His power is innate, to be known as distinct from the universe;
it shines in both singular and manifold forms, like the radiance of the sun.
His powers are infinite—will, knowledge, action, and so forth; and just as sparks arise from a fire, so do [the individual souls] emerge from Him.
Śiva, Īśvara, and others, as well as the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras and so forth,
became various Puruṣas, and there was also Prakṛti, who is higher than the highest.
The principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), as well as the forms such as the Unmanifest (aja) and others,
and whatever else there may be— all that is declared to be her effect.
That power is all-pervading, subtle, and consists of the nature of awakening and bliss;
the Lord Śiva, adorned with the cool-rayed moon, is said to be the possessor of that power.
Śiva is the object of knowledge, and Śivā is knowledge, as well as wisdom, revelation, and tradition;
she is fortitude, stability, and steadfastness, as well as the powers of knowledge, will, and action.
The Command (ājñā) is indeed the Supreme Brahman, and there are two sciences, the higher and the lower;
for pure knowledge and the pure power are everything, since they are produced by Śakti.
Neither illusion, nor primordial nature, nor the individual soul, nor modification, nor transformation;
neither being nor non-being—whatever exists, all this is pervaded by that.
That Goddess, through her illusory power (māyā), having deluded everything from Brahmā downwards, including all that is moving and unmoving, effortlessly liberates them even as a mere sport.
The Lord of All, having pervaded the universe, abides together with this twenty-seventh form; therefore, liberation proceeds from this.
In the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Āgamas everywhere,
various positions have been described through reasoning and the words of the Veda.
Therefore, relying on the path of the established doctrine, the proponents of Brahman should diligently seek the unity of purpose among the aphorisms and the Upanishads.
When the Veda’s summit has set forth for the sake of the identity of the sign (liṅga) and the body (aṅga),
the connection with Brahman as the sign is indeed certain and constant everywhere.
But if the Sāṅkhya tradition is invalid,
then the validity of the Yoga tradition must be accepted as superior, according to the injunction that it is to be distinguished [as the higher].
Because that [text] is seen to bear the mark of the Veda by the statement "That is Yoga," and because the status of Pradhāna as the cause is established by the Yoga-smṛti.
If it is argued that the proponents of Brahman as the cause [assert] a connection between the mark and the subject through identity, [we reply:
because they are human compositions, they are tainted by the flaw of error.
It is certain that the Smṛti is sublated by the Veda, which is of non-human origin;
however, regarding its portion concerning meditation and the like, that Smṛti possesses authority due to the weight of logical reasoning.
Hearing, reflection, and meditation— these are taught everywhere with one voice throughout the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama as this very yoga.
Yoga is indeed the connection between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
by the expression "meditation-yoga" (dhyānayoga), those established in yoga are illustrated.
The individual soul is the body and the Supreme is the subtle mark; the auspicious state of their essential identity is called "Yoga" by the virtuous who know the true meaning of the Śiva-tattva.
Having meditated upon the Lord of the Universe, who is the very nature of the Knower of All (Jātavedas) and is the size of a single hair-tip,
in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus, he should be held fast by those seeking liberation.
The all-knowing, the creator of all, the wondrous support of everything—
the Liṅga enveloped by the Praṇava, the meaning of the Praṇava, higher than the highest.
The direct cause of the creation, maintenance, and end of the entire world—
the auspicious one, accompanied by Umā, blue-throated, and three-eyed.
One should hold the tranquil Lord Īśāna within the lotus of the heart.
Brahman, which is existence-consciousness-bliss and completely full in every respect,
is not seen anywhere because it is beyond the range of the senses.
That is seen within this body; therefore, it is the city of Brahman (brahmapura).
Within that, however, is the small lotus-like heart-lotus.
The wise have declared that the small abode known as the lotus exists;
Brahman resides within it, and for that reason it is celebrated as the "abode."
That abode exists within the body; therefore, the body is called a "city" (pura).
For the subtle body (liṅga) resides in this mansion known as the lotus.
Because its form is the measure of the void, it is called "Space" (ākāśa);
it is an inexhaustible and wonderful treasury of the jewels of auspicious qualities.
Although the Self, O Śaṅkara, exists everywhere within the body,
its manifestation is exceedingly intense in the heart and not so elsewhere.
Indeed, the self is designated by the word "I"; there is no dispute on this point for anyone.
For it is observed that every person in the world employs the word "I."
For I indeed enter the heart, and therefore I abide there;
because within his heart, an exceedingly brilliant light exists eternally.
It is not so elsewhere; therefore, the heart is indeed preeminent. For this reason, the primordial, ancient *liṅga* should be held within the lotus of the heart.
This one who has transcended the castes and stages of life is the direct vessel for liberation alone;
he is the primordial, ancient emblem. This one who has transcended the castes and stages of life is the direct vessel for liberation alone.
For this very yoga is accepted here as the meaning of all the scriptures;
however, the authority of the Yoga-smṛti applies only to that portion [of the teachings], and not to anything else.
As for the contradiction that was established by means of the Sāṅkhya-reasoning:
"Whatever is entirely dissimilar [to something else], they know that it does not have that as its material cause."
Just as all things such as bracelets and the like do not have earth as their material cause,
so too this entire world under dispute does not have Brahman as its material cause.
Since scripture is subject to the three measures [of perception, inference, and verbal testimony] and is thus weaker than logic,
the world cannot have Brahman as its cause, because it is sublated by that logic.
The world's consciousness is established by the statement "and [it is] consciousness," while Brahman's consciousness is established by the statement "He who is omniscient.
How then is it not the case that Brahman, being distinct from the world, lacks a cause?
From this statement "the waters spoke," because consciousness is ascertained,
the distinction between the enjoyers and the objects of enjoyment is observed.
Because statements such as "for dogs" and so forth have the underlying reality (adhiṣṭhāna) as their purport, sublation is firmly established; therefore, the world does not have Brahman as its cause.
This being the case, that which was stated [previously] would be false;
for the origin of sentient beings from the insentient is heard in the Śruti.
Whether conscious or unconscious, [the origin] is intended by both the Śruti and the Sūtra;
just as hair and scorpions arise from a person and a cow-dung respectively.
For if it were non-existent in its entirety beforehand, then the effect would be a non-existent thing;
for while there is a negation in terms of the nature of the effect, there is none in terms of the nature of the cause.
Therefore, because of this reason, there is no doctrine of non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) regarding existing things;
thus, this same fault will be equal even in the opponent's position.
For, from the Pradhāna which lacks sound, there is the determination of an effect possessing sound;
however, this is not [the case] because of the existence of examples, such as trees and so forth that are [merely] heard.
Likewise, due to the defect in its own position, there is no room for the Sāṅkhya;
for when a defect is equal for both sides, or even the rebuttal is equal, [the argument fails].
One person alone should not be subjected to interrogation when investigating such a matter;
for an objection raised through mere logic does not find favor regarding the meaning declared by the Śruti.
Since reasonings are unstable and dry, they may turn out otherwise;
some have been set forth here by certain experts, while others have been formulated by different ones.
An object that has already been inferred by one person is rendered even more clearly manifest when it is further inferred by other, more diligent inferents who are skilled in the art of reasoning.
Other more diligent [scholars] establish [the truth] in a different way;
for the instability of reasoning is indeed countered by reasoning itself.
Some lines of reasoning were to be established, and some lines of reasoning were already established;
yet, in the establishment of all these reasonings, not even a trace of fault occurred.

If it is argued that this lack of foundation for reasoning would not be established if reasoning were the means of definitive conclusion—just as in the case of eating and so forth, where [action] is rooted in reasoning—we say: no, indeed.
The collection of worldly reasoning,
though logical regarding its cause, is nevertheless subject to the aforementioned fault due to the consequence of non-liberation.
For that reason, all the remaining types of appropriation have been explained.
Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no distinction [between the soul and the body] because the enjoyer reaches [the body], then this would certainly be the case in the world as well.
p.
84) Just as in the world, the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the act of enjoyment exist through Brahman as their self;
so too, even though there is non-difference, a supreme distinction is determined by way of their own essential natures.
Therefore, because of the non-difference from the cause, the effect is also determined;
that certainty is always established by the statement [in scripture] regarding its being "originated therefrom," such as in the words "consisting thereof" (*tadārambhaṇa*).

If it is argued that he is not [the Self] because he is perceived in existence, because he exists, and because there is a designation of his non-existence in the subsequent state, we say no; for he is determined to be so on account of the remainder of the sentence.
That sentence, along with its meaning, culminates in another dharma;
this occurs here through reasoning and other words, just as it is in the case of the *vapā*.
For that [Brahman] is ascertained by the Sūtra itself through the designation of the other;
because of the mention of distinction, Brahman is the creator, and not anything else.
Furthermore, its impossibility is seen from the analogy of clay and so forth;
therefore, by means of the concluding aphorism, the transformation of Brahman [is refuted].
It is certain that the intellect (buddhi) is accepted as being like milk in relation to the phenomenal world (prapañca);
this very point has been established by the *Kṛtsnaprasaktisūtra*.
For instance, would transformation occur in its entirety or by means of a part?
If transformation occurred in its entirety, the non-existence of Brahman would follow as a consequence.
If transformation occurs through a part, Brahman would possess parts;
consequently, the scripture stating that it is "actionless" and "partless" would be contradicted.
If it were so, through the abandonment of its prior form and the emergence of another form, Brahman would become insentient; it could not, however, remain non-insentient.
(85) Since scripture is the very root of [our knowledge], when Brahman undergoes transformation into the form of the world,
it is proclaimed that the non-inert Brahman remains indeed distinct [from the world].
Having spoken of the creation of fire, water, and food, that very deity reflected with the words,
"Come now," [realizing] that [the world] was without the triad of fire, water, and food.
Because it has been stated that the deity is the seer, and because of the verbal testimony,
the existence of the deity must be accepted as distinct, in accordance with the scriptural word.
Where the purpose is not established by reasoning but is enjoined by scripture,
that [purpose] is accepted because scripture is rooted in the Word, as in the case of the gods and so forth.
For in this way, transformation in the self is established by the Sūtra;
thus, by means of the fault in his own position, that very [point] is firmly reinforced.
In this context, the transformation belongs to the gods due to their possession of power, but not according to the Śruti;
therefore, the Sūtra "sarvopeta" (endowed with all [powers]) has been shown to refer to Brahman.
[Objection: Even so, since the gods possess instruments (karaṇa), they cannot be the creators of Brahmā; [Response: That has already been stated.
If it is argued that [the Self] is not [the agent] because it is devoid of instruments (*vikaraṇatvāt*), that has already been refuted immediately following this very point;
and if it is further argued that it is not so because Brahman lacks purposefulness (*prayojanavattva*).
By the sūtra beginning with "because it is like the world," it is shown that just as it is for kings, so it is for you;
thus, both partiality and cruelty are not at all applicable to Brahman.
Therefore, if it is asked how that [creation] can belong to Brahman,
the answer is shown later by the sūtra beginning with "vaiṣamya" (inequality).
86) Therefore, even in the case of a doubtful defect, [the status of] Brahman is not [established];
this is supported by the Sūtra and also by the Sūtra beginning with "upapadyate" (it is logical).
And because it is the witness of the manifestation of all phenomena,
that Brahman is one, eternal, supreme, and characterized by power.
It has been demonstrated that both the substrate (upādāna) and the efficient cause (nimitta) are Brahman alone;
this is what was determined by the wise through such statements as "the Self is the mark" (ātma-liṅga).
That very subject has been investigated here with the support of Śruti and Smṛti;
now, the path of our own established doctrine (siddhānta) is being clearly demonstrated.
That which was stated regarding the aspect of transformation has been explained by me in detail further on;
as well as the objections raised by the proponents of Brahman as the cause, such as the Sāṅkhyas and others.
That has already been refuted previously; now, however, the defects in those [theories] are being set forth so that the activity of discerning people may not occur therein.
For thus the Sāṅkhyas believe: whatever transformations are observed to be permeated by something, they have that as their material cause, just as pots and the like are permeated by clay.
Just as those [beings] have earth as their material cause, so too this entire world,
being endowed with pleasure, pain, and so forth, must have a material cause of that same nature.
Whatever is of the nature of pleasure and so forth, being general in character, must consist of the three guṇas;
for those entities which are indeed limited are necessarily preceded by a combination [of causes].
Just as sprouts and the like [arise from seeds], so too is this limited world;
it is preceded by the conjunction of these three: sattva, rajas, and tamas.
The *pradhāna* is inferred by way of the relation of cause and effect;
Brahman is not the cause of the world, because consciousness does not persist in that which is insentient.
Pradhāna is not the cause of the world because its arrangement is impossible;
the arrangement of palaces and beds is produced by an intelligent artisan.
This world cannot be constructed by insentient stones;
it is an external body and the locus for the various experiences of karma.
It was fashioned by esteemed artisans, or else conceived in the mind as something distinct,
created by the Lord who is omniscient and possesses inconceivable power and majesty.
It is not by means of the insentient *pradhāna* [that this occurs], for such a thing is nowhere observed;
rather, it is the word itself that brings together [the meanings] when the syntactic connection would otherwise be untenable.
Furthermore, those entities such as jars and the like are not indeed [mere] conceptual constructions;
for they are observed to be associated with pleasure and pain, since pleasure and so forth are internal [to the subject].
Furthermore, because external objects such as jars are observed to be causes of pleasure,
their being preceded by conjunction is inferred from their finitude.
That [reason] is inconclusive because even for limited things such as living beings,
there is an absence of being preceded by a conjunction, due to their [independent] activity.
For the activity of the primary matter (pradhāna), which is insentient and yet presided over by a sentient being,
is not tenable, since such a thing is not observed in the world.
The movement of a chariot is seen to be directed by consciousness, never by itself;
since he has accepted a state of indifference, the Puruṣa is not the instigator of action.
Even insentient milk proceeds toward the growth of its calf;
and if the water of a river flows by itself for the benefit of the world.

It is not so, because even there dependence exists, as shown by the scripture beginning with "He who dwells in water"; for there is no infinite regress, since [the Self] is established as distinct from that.
What is called "pradhāna" by the Sāṅkhyas is the state of equilibrium among sattva and the other guṇas;
apart from that, there is no other initiator of the activity of pradhāna.
Whatever may be the cause of engagement or withdrawal, the Puruṣa remains indifferent;
he is neither the initiator nor the desister.
Consequently, because it would be independent of that [cause], creation would occur at all times;
dissolution would never occur, and thus the Pradhāna would not be considered the cause.
Just as grass and water that have been consumed turn back into milk of their own accord,
so too does primordial matter (pradhāna) spontaneously assume the form of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest.
In this view, grass and the like do not themselves become milk;
however, in the world, they do so through other factors such as oxen and the like.
Even grass and such things, when consumed, turn into milk; how much more so [the case of the cow]?
Or rather, it may be that this process occurs only through what has been consumed by the cow herself.
It is not appropriate for it to be so here either, because there is no purpose;
for even if one accepts the occurrence [of activity], it cannot exist without a purpose.
Activity proceeds for the sake of the Puruṣa, because otherwise there would be a violation of the fundamental proposition;
therefore, it is not logical to state that the Pradhāna itself has a purpose.
If, on the other hand, because that [Prakṛti] is insentient,
there should arise for the Puruṣa either enjoyment, or liberation, or both— this is the doubt.
The occurrence of experience rests upon the Puruṣa, who possesses various extraordinary powers of receptivity.
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of no liberation, nor indeed any final release;
for since final release is already established, the Puruṣa is eternally liberated.

It is not the case that there is no fear because of the absence of contradiction with the purpose; nor is it the case that there is no fear by way of alternation, because the objects to be enjoyed are infinite and enjoyment can never reach completion.
In this way, the attainment of liberation does not result from the cessation of longing;
for activity is indeed the nature of that longing which belongs to the conscious being.
If [the Pradhāna] were capable [of action], there would be no activity;
moreover, it would possess the power of vision while being devoid of the power of activity.
Just as a magnet, though itself inactive, impels a man who is lame and devoid of the power of sight but possessed of the capacity for action by presiding over him, so too does the Self.
Just as iron, though itself devoid of motion, becomes the mover [of the magnet],
so too the Puruṣa, endowed with the power of vision, causes [Prakṛti] to act.
If it is argued that the *pradhāna* is endowed with the power of activity, this is not so; for there would be no liberation from defects, and it would contradict what has been accepted [by you].
The activity of the independent Pradhāna is described;
but how, then, can there be activity on the part of the Puruṣa, given his lack of agency?
If the person were one to whom no excellence could be imparted, then how could he be an instigator?
For if he were to set a blind man in motion by means of his vocal activity, he himself would be lame.
If the beloved is present, there is no activity on the part of the man; rather,
it is iron that acts as the instigator, whether by mere proximity or by being polished.
A person cannot be the instigator merely by virtue of being present;
for since his presence here is eternal, activity would result in the occurrence of attachment at all times.
Therefore, it cannot be said that [the process] is like a man [pushing] a stone;
and because the status of being a subordinate factor (aṅgin) is untenable, there is no activity originating from the Pradhāna.
Since sattva and the other [guṇas] remain in a state of equilibrium during the supreme dissolution,
they cannot function as mutual constituents (aṅgin) due to the absence of any cause for disequilibrium.
If inequality were described as occurring without a cause, then activity would occur at all times; however, it is not observed that such is the case.
The fault just mentioned would apply;
however, we do not infer it to be so, provided those qualities are independent by nature and immutable.
And their intrinsic nature is such that it conforms to the production of effects;
for the activity of the qualities is unstable, and from that, indeed, inequality arises.
If it is explained that the manifestation of the world occurs through the command of Pradhāna,
or by the conjunction of its powers, or by its own inherent nature;
Furthermore, those defects such as impossibility and so forth do not remain in that state;
for one who measures this power of consciousness is turned back because of his status as a disputant.
Furthermore, in the context of the discourse on Brahman, this [position] would not withstand logical scrutiny;
let there be causes for the inequality of the qualities (guṇas) at your dissolution.
O Lord,
because there is no external cause for it, may Your qualities never again experience such partiality;
indeed, they should never at any time partake in inequality.
If it is argued that [the distinction between the primary and the subordinate] arises precisely from the absence of specific characteristics among the signs,
then the impossibility of establishing the status of being the "principal" remains exactly as it was before.
Furthermore, there is mutual contradiction in this Sāṅkhya tenet:
in some places it is said that only seven organs depart [at death], while in others, eleven.
In some places they say that the five subtle elements (tanmātras) arise from the Great One (mahat);
likewise, in other places, the three internal organs arise from the ego (ahaṅkāra).
In some places they say "one," and thus again in many ways;
both by the Śruti which expresses the absence of instruments, and also by the Smṛti, they contradict one another.
Because it is contradictory, this doctrine of Kapila is inconsistent;
thus, the causality of the *pradhāna* has been refuted.
Now, the causality of atoms is refuted:
"An atom is motionless in four ways at the beginning [of creation] and during the supreme dissolution."
Just as the yogis possess a measure known as sphericality (pārimāṇḍalya),
so too do the atoms remain possessed of their own respective tangibles.
Subsequently, at that time of creation, by the desire to create of the Supreme Lord,
and from the mutual conjunction of the atoms of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, [the gross elements were produced].
The initial action occurs within atoms, and by that action the atom becomes minute;
then it joins with another atom, and beyond that, with two and two more.
From two atoms joined together, each dyad (dvyaṇuka) would arise; however,
it could not arise from a single [atom], as is observed in the case of threads.
But since the state of being the originator of a cloth exists likewise in its root cause,
there two atoms are the inherent cause (samavāyi-kāraṇa).
Their conjunction would be the efficient cause, while [the atoms] themselves would be the inherent cause by virtue of their designation;
the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth would be the instrumental cause, and these [causes] reside in the atoms.
From those [atoms], qualities such as touch arise in the dyad (dvyaṇuka) as belonging to the same class;
for qualities such as touch are produced from the qualities of the cause.
According to the principle that qualities initiate effects [in their own substratum], then, by means of three dyads assisted by conjunction,
one single dyad [is produced] from them.

"Greatness is begun [therein]"; furthermore, the qualities residing in the dyad (dvyaṇuka) are traditionally held to be the initiators (ārambhaka) of the primary qualities, such as touch, in the triad (tryaṇuka).
And from triads [of atoms] comes the larger, and from those the largest; thus in sequence:
the wind is large, fire is large, water is large, and the earth is large.
Beings arise from Brahman, yet it is not said that there is an origination of the world;
rather, this quality of consciousness serves as the cause for another instance of consciousness.
In this regard, whatever objection is raised by the Vaiśeṣikas concerning Brahman’s status as the cause is thoroughly examined by means of this very sūtra.
This is not a universal rule accepted by the wise everywhere;
for the reason that qualities in an effect produce another quality of the same kind.
(93) Since they begin [the process] with the conviction that it is under their control, [they assume] such a thing as sphericality (pārimāṇḍalya) in atoms,
and likewise in the dyad (dvyaṇuka).
Because its commencement is not admitted and because its atomicity and so forth are observed,
just as both atomicity and shortness reside in their causes.

Since minuteness and shortness exist in the dyad (dvyaṇuka) along with their homogeneous causes, and since largeness and length are likewise observed in the dyad; [therefore, these qualities must have causes].
And thus, it is an established principle that qualities residing in the cause produce qualities of their own kind in the effect.
In this way, it is not possible for consciousness, even if it possesses the quality of Brahman,
to suddenly become the cause of another consciousness within the body.
There is no inconsistency whatsoever in Brahman being the cause of the phenomenal world;
however, specific qualities do not have qualities of their own kind as their cause.
Let it not be said that measurement and so forth are general qualities;
for "generality" and "particularity" regarding qualities exist merely by way of verbal designation.
Now, the causality of atoms is refuted;
for it is untenable that these atoms remain motionless during the dissolution of the world.
And for the production of conjunction, there is no initial action that serves as its cause;
nor is there any other [cause], because at that time there is an absence of any such cause.
Likewise, what is the cause for the state of action at the end? Is it something directly perceived, such as impact, effort, and so forth, or is it called "unseen" (adṛṣṭa)?
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because due to the absence of a body, dissolution and so forth would be impossible;
furthermore, since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is insentient, it cannot by itself produce karma.
Since the person, though born with consciousness, would be as if insentient,
and because the knowledge of the Lord is eternal, the production of karma would occur at all times.
Likewise, since the self here can exist even without a conjunction [with a body],
and because there is no adventitious cause for anyone whatsoever, [the self is eternal].
If the first [action] did not exist in the atoms, conjunction—which is dependent upon it—would not occur;
and in the absence of conjunction, the state of being a dyad (dvyaṇuka) would not be established.
Therefore, it is not tenable to speak of a cause for the atom;
for in the theory that atoms are the cause, there is no effect such as the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth.
For they describe the connection between the two atoms as being distinct from the atoms themselves and characterized by the relation called inherence (samavāya).
That description is not tenable, because even on the basis of similarity, there would be an infinite regress;
for just as an effect is entirely distinct from its inherent causes, [so too must the cause be distinct from its own causes].
The wise, however, describe a relation by means of another relation;
and thus, because inherence itself possesses the quality of being inherent.
Therefore, because they are absolutely distinct, it must be related to something else;
and likewise that [other] must be related to yet another, resulting in an infinite regress.
It is an error to think that inherence (samavāya), whose very nature is to be a relation,
becomes related without depending on another relation.
Nevertheless, since even a relation must be postulated for this absolute difference,
conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would be subject to alteration because it does not depend on inherence (*samavāya*).
Nor can it be [a quality], because it does not depend on conjunction and so forth as a quality does;
for the distinction between quality and substance is merely conventional.
Are they of the nature of activity, or of the nature of cessation? Or are atoms of the nature of fear, [fearing] that they might be destroyed?
The first position cannot withstand scrutiny because, due to the necessity of activity being eternal, the absence of dissolution would follow;
nor does the second hold, because of the cessation [of activity].
Furthermore, because it would entail the consequence of the non-existence of creation, even a third [nature] is not tenable;
nor is it possible, due to the contradiction between two natures therein.
Nor does even a fourth position find favor in the hearts of the wise,
namely that activity occurs due to a cause despite [the soul] possessing the nature of both [agency and non-agency].
Because of the constant proximity of the cause, such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), activity would always be perpetually engaged; therefore, atoms cannot be the cause.
That substance which is being divided is further possessed of parts;
beyond which [division], atoms (paramāṇu) would no longer be capable of being divided.
Those possessing form are of four kinds; they are the eternal originators of the fourfold network of primary elements and their derivatives.
The doctrine of the Vaiśeṣikas is charming only at first sight:
it asserts both the atomicity and the eternity of atoms that possess color and other qualities.
Just as it is observed in the world that whatever possesses form is subject to reversal, so too,
in relation to its own cause, that [entity] is impermanent and indeed gross.
Just as cloth and the like, so too are material atoms coarse and impermanent; indeed, they must perish when their substance is destroyed.
Since the parts and so forth of a cause do not exist here, nor its disintegration,
do not say that there is the destruction of atoms.
The definition of the distinction between qualities and substances is merely conventional,
even in the case of ultimate atoms, despite the absence of the destruction of parts and the like.
The destruction of color-form and other qualities, when combined, occurs through contact with fire;
therefore, the destruction of atoms follows, and thus their impermanence is established.
Earth is gross and possesses the qualities of smell, form, taste, and touch;
water is said to be subtle and possesses the qualities of taste, form, and touch.
Fire is seen to have the quality of form and touch, being more subtle [than earth];
wind has the most subtle touch; these, indeed, are the other elements.
They are endowed with qualities both accumulated and likewise diminished,
and they possess a gradation of grossness and subtlety.
In the same way, the higher atoms here are likewise joined with diminished qualities;
thus the logicians (tārkikas) should conceive them as being endowed with diminished qualities.
Nor indeed must a fault arising from either case be avoided through arguments,
provided that the qualities are conceived as being both increased and decreased accordingly.
Furthermore, in the case of liberation, there would follow both an increase in form and an increase in afflictions;
likewise, this would occur even without any increase or decrease in the physical body.
For there is neither an accumulation nor indeed a diminution of qualities.
Likewise, because it is always observed by wise men in the world regarding bodies—
whether there is an increase in their form or even a decrease thereof.
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of [the atom] being non-atomic;
therefore, this is not the case, provided that neither decrease nor increase in its qualities is postulated.
Then, in water, all four qualities are perceived;
in fire, likewise, fragrance and taste; and in air, fragrance, form, and taste.
If, moreover, all [the elements] possessed each a single quality in the air,
then there would be no touch in fire, nor indeed color or taste in water.

If [the earth] were merely atoms, then color, taste, and touch would not exist in the earth; yet they are certainly perceived. Therefore, the theory that atoms are the cause [of gross objects] is not tenable.
And there is absolute disregard [for the world], because of not accepting [the existence of] dull-witted persons and the like.
Having refuted both the Sāṅkhya and Nyāya systems with many arguments,
may even the contradiction regarding the conduct of the Guṇas not spread further.
If there is no fault to be heard regarding the teacher, the *liṅga*, and so forth,
yet one says, "I shall instruct him because I have heard [of his faults]," that is called the conduct of a group (*gaṇācāra*).
Whatever has been imagined as a refutation by the Sāṅkhyas or even by logicians,
that I have neither remembered nor considered with my mind.
However, their preferred position has been refuted by me through logical arguments.
In the same way, such a person is seen among those who follow the Dharma as one who corrupts the Dharma;
without hearing of his corruption, one should expel him from that place.
Just as one might separate rice grains mixed with sand and carry them away,
so did he set aside the stones of ill-spoken arguments regarding the doctrines favored by the Buddhists and others.
I grasp consciousness as a jewel, abandoning its momentariness therein—
just as one who knows how to destroy defects by means of reasoning takes up a gem that has been polished on a whetstone.
Now, the threefold doctrine of the Buddhists is being refuted:
some assert the existence of all things, while others maintain that there is only consciousness.
Some proponents of emptiness alone refute the existence of all things;
therein, their method regarding the fourfold [elements] beginning with earth is as follows.
Those atoms, whose natures are respectively sound, moisture, heat, and aridity, aggregate into the state of earth and so forth; therefore, they appear as such.
Through the distinctions of feeling, form, consciousness, perception, and mental formations,
there are likewise the five aggregates within oneself in every respect.
They are aggregated there by virtue of being the basis for conventional usage;
thus they have wandered [in error], thinking that the aggregate of form consists of the sense-faculties together with their objects.
That which is called the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) consists of the very forms of apprehension;
it has objects such as form as its domain and arises from the sense faculties and so forth.
That which extends like a staff is declared to be the aggregate called sensation;
it consists of the experience of pleasure as well as the experience of pain.
That should be understood as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which consists of distinct mental representations;
while the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is said to be conceptual cognition (*savikalpa-pratyaya*).
The afflictions (kleśas) are thus passion (rāga) and so forth, as well as intoxication (mada), pride (māna), and the like;
likewise, the secondary afflictions (upakleśas) and both dharma and adharma are proclaimed.
The five aggregates and their collection are what is referred to therein as "this" and "I.
This origination is of two kinds: that which is caused by both [ignorance and craving].
And that material aggregate has atoms as its cause and the aggregates as its cause;
therefore, from those aggregates, form arises, and thus it occurs in both cases sequentially.
If that which is intended is not attained, it is said that there would be "non-attainment" (aprāpti);
the attainment of that [intended object] is called "conjunction" (saṅgati).
The aggregate is inherently devoid of a self because its constituent parts are insentient,
and because the manifestation of consciousness is dependent upon the accomplishment of the collection.
Because there is no other conscious agent here to bring [things] together,
and because you yourself have established the momentariness of everything.
No conscious agent who is permanent is accepted;
nevertheless, because ignorance is the primary cause of their mutual [interaction].
The course of worldly existence is thus consistent, and those factors beginning with ignorance are as follows:
100) namely, ignorance, mental formations, consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth.
There may be six years; [then come] contact and, after that, sensation.
One should know that craving is grasping, and likewise birth;
there shall be old age and death, as well as sorrow and lamentation.
Furthermore, suffering and mental distress—these and others of a similar nature—are mutually caused; this has been accepted by them as their established position.
Ignorance is said to be delusion, preceded by passion for cyclic existence;
consciousness is described as the cognition of objects as real entities.
There are four designations for the aggregates of clinging;
by means of these aggregates, the embryo and subsequent stages of the body are brought forth.
It has been described that the state of the embryo, such as the bubble-like stage (*budbuda*), possesses a similarity [to the preceding stages];
that is called the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and those are the six faculties (*indriya*).
The conjunction of name-and-form and the sense-faculties is called contact (*sparśa*).
Feeling (*vedanā*), consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth, is what is to be grasped by me; such is this [teaching].
From craving comes attachment; from that, the wise know, arise merit and demerit through the production of vocal and bodily activity—this is clear.
The manifestation [of the aggregates] is birth, and their maturation is aging;
the destruction of those very aggregates once born, they know as death.
The internal burning felt by one who is dying is called sorrow (śoka);
the lamentation arising from that is designated as wailing (parivedanā).
When the experience of what is to be accomplished by the five sensory consciousnesses is remembered, that is mental suffering; it is called *durmanastā*.
Just as from a seed there arises a sprout, and from the sprout a leaf,
from the leaf a stalk, from that a stem, and after that a bud; so it is.
From the embryo comes the sprout, from that the flower, and from the flower the fruit;
such is the sequence, even though seeds and the like are insentient and lack consciousness.
Just as there is a relationship of mutual dependence between two distinct presiding agents,
so too is the relationship of cause and effect observed here in this case as well.
Ignorance and the rest are declared to be known as the causes of birth and so forth;
and birth and the rest are to be understood as having ignorance as their cause.
And here they are seen revolving like a water-wheel;
if it is argued that this "assemblage" is implied by the sense [of the context], it is not so.
Since they are merely produced, then a composite would be logical for you,
provided that a cause for the composite were perceived by you.
Even though ignorance and the rest are mutually conditioned, nevertheless, at that time,
each preceding one would be the cause for the arising of each subsequent one.
The state of being a cause for an aggregate is not possible in any case whatsoever;
rather, by implication, it follows that the aggregate is preceded by ignorance.
Just as the *vighā* and other such beings, failing to find their own existence apart from a community, are said to depend upon a collection of five; so it is here.
Therefore, let some cause for that aggregation be stated;
for your cause is not established by itself merely through dependence.
If it is argued that ignorance is the cause of the aggregate (saṃghāta), we say no;
for how could that very [ignorance], having itself obtained its own self by depending upon that [aggregate], [be its cause]?
Furthermore, they would indeed be the cause for that very same beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
It is asserted that aggregates arise only in continuous succession;
nevertheless, from one such aggregate, another aggregate comes into being.
It may be similar either by necessity or by non-necessity;
as for whether it is contradictory or similar, listen first to what will be said regarding the former case.
A human being never attains the state of a Veda-possessor (or similar status) at any time;
rather, in the second moment, having become an elephant, that man may then become a god.
Because of the absence of a director and because of the non-existence of a permanent action.

Having accepted that knowledge and the rest serve as instrumental causes for its production, it was stated that the formation of the aggregate [of the body] does not occur; thus, their status as causes of production must be asserted [as being merely instrumental].
Now we shall explain why it is not so for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness:
the preceding moment, as it ceases, gives rise to the succeeding moment.
By one who accepts this [relation] between two successive moments,
the absence of cause and effect cannot be stated anywhere.
Furthermore, for a preceding moment that has already ceased or is in the process of ceasing,
there can be no causality toward a subsequent moment because it is seized by such a state of existence.
For it is observed that earth, color, and so forth, which possess duration, serve as causes for their effects;

however, the causality of an effect is not seen in that which has been swallowed by non-existence. Furthermore, in the doctrine known as momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga), the preceding moment is certainly not the cause.
And because it is swallowed up by cessation, the subsequent one is so described.

103) Now, if one were to say that the production of the fruit occurs while the cause still exists, there would be a contradiction of one's own thesis, as well as [a contradiction] with the principle of "in dependence upon four causes."
The thesis that mental factors arise from the mind would be abandoned;
for "mind" is defined as consciousness, while "mental factors" are pleasure and the rest.
The cognition of blue has the appearance of blue because it is perceived as having blue as its object;
its possession of the form of blue and so forth arises from that immediately preceding [condition].
Prior to the cognition of an object, the mind possesses the nature of pure awareness;
however, through contact with an object, the perception of form is said to arise for the seer.
Furthermore, from the world, there is clarity of meaning due to cooperative conditions;
moreover, it is said that there are four causes for mental factors (caittas).
Otherwise, the thesis would be contradicted solely by the absence of a cause;
or else, it would persist until the production of the subsequent moment.
If the preceding moment were simultaneous with its cause and effect,
then the thesis that all things are momentary would not be tenable.
The nihilists, moreover, conceive of things through various distinctions:
the intellect (*buddhi*), the object of cognition (*bodhya*), and the acts of cognition (*bodha*); yet they hold that which is distinct from these three to be the praised [ultimate reality].
And that which is momentary— these three are known respectively as cessation through deliberation,
cessation not through deliberation, and space, according to their distinctions.
It is heard in scripture that it is a mere absence of an entity and is indefinable;
whereas the destruction of entities through analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is preceded by the intellect.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) would be the opposite [of that];
likewise, space (*ākāśa*) is said to be merely the absence of obstruction.
Now, he refutes both of those [positions] regarding its cessation as well.
Analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, the two types of non-attainment, the flavor, and existence—
because these are excluded, those two [cessations] would indeed have the continuum as their object.
Are these two [the self and the world] objects of the individual entity (*bhāva*) and not objects of the continuum (*santāna*)?
For even regarding all continua, it is said that [the analysis applies] again to the members of the continuum (*santānin*).
For, in that very way, because the continuum [of consciousness] exists through the relation of cause and effect,
those two [past and future] would not exist as objects of existence, since there is no interruption or absence [of the continuum].
For what [continuity] could there be for entities that are without succession and devoid of any designation,
if not through the power of recognition across all their various states?
Therefore, that which is imagined by others—that [the negation] exists through the destruction of the positive concomitant—is not tenable;
let it be understood that there is a contradiction between two [opposites].
And that cessation of knowledge which occurs through analytical cessation is included within [the category of] correct knowledge, together with its attendant factors.
Furthermore, in the first case, there would be the loss [of the self] by itself, as it would be without cause;
in the latter case, the instruction of knowledge would be useless; and in both cases, [the same fault applies].
However, due to this defect, all of that [view] is inconsistent;
and because there is no distinction [in space], it would follow that space itself is non-existent.
Since there is no distinction, its existence is established for now by the authority of the Veda.
Based on the statement, "And it is omnipresent and eternal like space," [the existence of] the entity in space is established for those people who hold conflicting views.
Furthermore, it must be stated that odor and the other [qualities] are inferable from words,
because they are seen everywhere to have earth and the other [elements] as their substrata.
Moreover, for one who maintains that space is merely the absence of obstruction,
when a single *tārkṣya* bird flies through it, there would still be the presence of other beings due to the absence of obstruction elsewhere.
If it were to fall there upon the Tārkṣya who desires to seize it,
or by whatever else the state of being obstructed might be distinguished, then [the argument would hold].
Space would be a real, existent entity, and not merely a non-existence.
Therefore, the doctrine of the Nihilists is not consistent with mindfulness;
for the Nihilists would assert the momentariness of all things.
One might even personally accept the momentariness of the perceiver;
however, the meaning of the statement "and it would not be so because of recollection" is now investigated.
