If recollection were of that which has not arisen from experience, it would be a mere memory; and if that [recollection] occurs in this way, it must have a single agent identical to that of the experience.
Indeed, a memory of an object experienced by one person cannot possibly belong to another;
likewise, it is evident that perception and memory must have a single agent.
Recognition is well known through direct perception to everyone in the world, as in "I have seen that very same person"; if the agent of these two [perceptions] were different, this would not be so.
If that were so, no one would ever perceive it;
for since what exists is never seen, this doctrine is nihilistic.
For those who do not accept that the cause is stable during the production of an effect,
it is shown that the arising of an effect occurs even from its prior non-existence.
(106) Indeed,
the arising of an entity cannot occur without having first destroyed its non-existence;
likewise, that sprout does not manifest from a seed that has already perished.

If they understand that a jar could arise from every [cause]— since it would be indistinguishable from a stationary lump of clay that has already perished— then everything would indeed arise from everything.
In this regard, it is said: "From non-existence (abhāva) there arises existence (bhāva);
just as the production of existence [arises] from existence, so too do existents [arise] specifically from existents."
The postulation of a specific cause for that [effect] would be rendered useless,
as it is the case with seeds and the like once they have perished, or likewise with clods of earth that have been destroyed.
Furthermore, there is no distinction between things such as a rabbit’s horn and other non-existent entities from the perspective of their non-existence;
for if a sprout arises from a seed, why would it not likewise arise from a rabbit’s horn?
Just as the non-existence of blue and other qualities is distinguished from that of the lotus and other things, so too,
because it possesses specific characteristics, non-existence itself is said to have the nature of existence.
If, O King, an entity were to arise from non-existence like a blue lotus and the like,
then the effect would necessarily be endowed with non-existence, just as [products] are endowed with clay.

For things such as bowls and the like are indeed seen; as for what you said—that nothing is seen—and that which was stated, namely, that there is no manifestation here without something being destroyed.
Furthermore, that which was wrongly stated regarding gold is likewise seen again in the case of those very gold pieces that are recognized by their owners.
It acts as the cause at the very beginning and likewise in the case of the sprout and so forth;
however, the seeds and other such things are not the material causes (*upādāna*), for they do not persist as an underlying continuous part.
Therefore, this arising of an entity from non-existence is untenable.
Even if the arising of an entity from non-existence were admitted, in that case,
there would be a state of ultimate indifference for men, characterized by a lack of effort.
Because non-existence is easily attained, the desired fruit would be accomplished; it would always belong to the farmer who exerts no effort regarding his fields and labors.
If the abundance of crops were already perfected, no one would strive for anything;
therefore, your view regarding heaven and liberation is not tenable.
Now the Buddhist proponent of consciousness (vijñānavādin) objects:
"In some cases, external objects among those things to be investigated [do exist]."
Having merely indicated the conclusion [of the previous section],
this process concerning external objects was indeed composed by him again, solely out of deference to that [conclusion].

The Sugatas, who teach that consciousness is the aggregate [of the person], have declared that it is not [the self] because of its impermanence. And regarding that doctrine of consciousness, for one who has ascended by means of the intellect,
the very form [of the cognition] is here the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it is also the result (*phala*).
And thus, even though external objects exist, all worldly transaction is indeed possible only through their ascension into the intellect.

Since conventional transactions such as pride and the like would be impossible [if there were no external objects], how is it that it has been stated that "conventional transaction exists internally, but the object is not external"?
When the external object is being apprehended, is it the atoms, or pillars and the like, or their aggregates? First of all, it is not the atoms.
For those pillars and so forth become objects of determination [only] when they are manifested as atoms, because otherwise no cognition would arise.
The pillars and other such objects are not aggregates of those [atoms], but rather they arise from the atoms themselves;
for their distinctness from both [the atoms and the aggregates] is difficult to establish.
And one who has realized the self and so forth through mere direct experience,
regarding that which is the object of common knowledge of the self and its various objects;
This is partiality; "this is a pillar," "this is a wall"—in this manner, there is much knowledge of jars, cloth, and so forth.
A distinction is not possible without something residing within cognition;
thus, the conformity of cognition to its object must indeed be asserted once again.
Furthermore, when that [object] has been made an object by cognition,
the conceptualization of an external object is groundless, because it is not obstructed by anything other than earth.
That [world] should be viewed as being like a dream and so forth; just as for a person in a dream, there are illusions, mirages, water, cities of the Gandharvas, and the like.
Just as the state of being grasped and grasper occurs even without a sentence-meaning,
so too are waking cognitions [unreal], because there is no difference in their nature as cognitions.
Or how, even when an external object exists, is there a diversity of cognitions?
[The author] says: "And that [diversity] arises, moreover, from the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)."
In this beginningless saṃsāra, according to the illustration of the seed and the sprout,
cognitions and latent predispositions serve as mutual causes for one another.
Because of its variety, it would not be contradictory; that [variety] exists precisely in the absence of external objects.
Since [the opponent] has argued that there is no non-existence because of perception, it is stated:
"Indeed, there is no non-existence of the external; why? Because of perception."
In each and every cognition, an external object is indeed perceived;
and for that which is being perceived, its absence cannot truly be established.
For just as some person, while eating and experiencing satisfaction,
might say of himself, "I am not eating," or "I am not satisfied."
In the same way, a person who has apprehended external objects through the connection with the sense organs should neither say "it does not exist," nor should he say "I do not perceive it."
One might ask: "How can this statement of his be accepted?
[To this we reply: "I do not speak thus; for I do not perceive any such object here."
But lest I perceive a void devoid of attainment,
the absence of attainment must indeed be accepted by force.
No one perceives a pillar as being merely an attainment, nor a wall as being merely an attainment;
thus, they do not perceive pillars, walls, and so forth as such.
When objects are not perceived as attainments, all living beings perceive them [as they truly are].
For this reason as well, it must be stated thus: "The object perceived is indeed other [than the perception];
it is distinct from the perception"—such indeed is the established position.
Thus they explain it, and they also [assert] an external object with effort: that which is an internal form of the cognizable appears as if it were external.
Thus, they [perceive] that consciousness, which is renowned externally throughout all worlds.
Having obtained [the cognition] as it appears, those desiring to counter-argue speak of it as being "outside" and employ the word *vāk* (speech/sound) with reference to the external object.
Otherwise, how could they fearlessly say that "it appears like something external"? For this is not the same as saying, "a barren woman's son appears."
Therefore, it appears as an external object according to one's own experience;
yet, has not the impossibility of an external object also been stated by them?
This is not an act of determination,
for it has been accepted as "good" only because both possibility and impossibility are subject to the means of valid cognition.
Both of these [arguments] proceed by taking recourse solely to activity and non-activity,
and not by taking recourse solely to existence and non-existence.
Neither engagement nor non-engagement is appropriate for a means of valid cognition;
it is not found among any of the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest.
That which is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition is indeed impossible; it is simply not possible for such a thing to exist there.

For since an external object is indeed apprehended by all means of valid cognition through conceptual constructions such as exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth, how could one possibly maintain that it does not exist?
The destruction of the object does not occur through the attainment [of cognition] due to its conformity with the object;

for if the object were not apprehended, then the conformity consisting in the cognition being "colored" by the form of the object could not be perceived, since the external object has already been attained.
Cognitions even in the waking state may be possible without an external object, just like cognitions in a dream;
this is what I am now explaining.
"Just as perceptions in a dream, so too perceptions in the waking state would be possible even without an external object";
this is what is being answered by me.
For waking cognitions do not indeed exist like dream-cognitions;
because of this difference in nature, and because that difference consists in being sublated and not being sublated.
"One who has awakened might say that the object obtained in a dream was sublated;
for that assembly of great people was perceived as being composed of falsehood."

"Perhaps my mind is weary with sleep; therefore, this is an illusion"—in this way, sublation is observed even in the case of illusions and the like. However, an object obtained during the waking state is never thus sublated across any states.
The non-sublated nature of that waking cognition must be accepted;
therefore, this dream cognition is false because it is sublated.

Furthermore, if the waking cognition were sublated, there would indeed be no sublater of dream cognitions; for that which is itself sublatable cannot be a sublater. Therefore, the dream cognition is not false, and thus the argument "like a dream" [is invalid].
The example is devoid of the property to be proven; its sublation is characterized by the sublation [of the thesis].
There is no dissimilarity, for the cognition of one who is awake is not like that of a dream.
The certainty is that there must be a determination [of an object] despite the absence of an external object;
for it has also been said: "The wonderful diversity of cognitions occurs even without an object."
I reply that it is because of the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, even the existence of latent impressions is not possible in your position, as they are not perceived.
Furthermore, for the purpose of perceiving objects, those [consciousnesses] arise with respect to external objects;
they are designated by you as "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) and so forth, corresponding to each respective object.
When objects are not being obtained, what indeed is the cause for that?
Even if beginningless, a succession of the blind is difficult to sustain according to logic;
for latent impressions (*vāsanās*) are indeed specific residual traces (*saṃskāras*) that require a substratum.
Since things are understood in the world even without [logical] means,
there is no basis for a proof for you that exists according to valid cognition.
Therefore, because it is unperceived and because of its momentariness,
that which is imagined by others to be the *ālayavijñāna*—
on account of its being the substratum for latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and its acceptance as momentary— is certainly not [the ālayavijñāna].
Being itself unstable in form like the evolving cognition,
it cannot for that reason serve as the substratum for the latent impressions (vāsanā).
Indeed, when that single entity connected with the three times is not clearly present,
the latent impression (vāsanā) is dependent upon place, time, causes, and so forth.
Since memory depends upon that [consciousness], worldly activity— which is preceded by the recognition of objects— is possible only if the mental continuum is stable.
The thesis of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) certainly falls into ruin,
even in the doctrine of consciousness (vijñānavāda), because of the apprehension of momentariness itself.
And if that refutation which was formulated against the proponents of external objects on the grounds of momentariness applies equally to the production of a subsequent [moment], then...
p.
113) Furthermore, in this context, one should keep in mind the passage beginning with "due to the cessation of the preceding moment" and so forth; by means of this, these two positions are refuted.
Both the doctrine of external objects and the position of the Vijñānavādin are untenable in every respect, because [the required characteristics] cannot coexist within a single entity.
Now, however, he casts far away the doctrine of the Kṣapaṇakas:
"Their categories are seven; these are the living being (jīva), the non-living (ajīva), and the three [types of] influx (āsrava)."

Restraint (saṃvara), destruction (nirjarā), and liberation (mokṣa)—in brief, these are two categories of principles. It is stated that the souls (jīva) and non-souls (ajīva) are included within those [two].
They also describe this further elaboration of those two:
there are five astikāyas, the first of which is declared to be the jīvāstikāya.
From that [arise] the body of the person (pudgala) and the body of matter (kāya); from that, the body of phenomena (dharmāstikāya);
and then the body of space (ākāśāstikāya).
These have been conceptualized in many ways through their internal subdivisions.
The soul is of the nature of consciousness, while the aggregate of insentient matter is non-living;
the activity of the senses is influx (*āsrava*), whereas this [restraint] is stoppage (*saṃvara*).
Furthermore, the intense engagement with this [state] in the form of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth,
as well as the practice of ascending heated stones and the like, constitutes that eightfold karma which is bondage.
The fourfold destructive karma consists of: first, knowledge-obscuring;
second, perception-obscuring; third, deluding; and likewise, obstructive.
Then there is the non-destructive karma, which is also fourfold.
(114) Furthermore,
that which is to be experienced, as well as the lineage and the lifespan—
these two constitute the cycle wherein right knowledge exists, yet there is no liberation.
That karma which obscures knowledge belongs to the Arhat upon his seeing [the truth];
through practice, there would be no liberation from the karma that obscures vision.

The third, however, is deluding (mohanīya), which is specifically said to be of nine kinds; it is described as occurring when one repeatedly fails to maintain resolve regarding the paths to liberation that have been prohibited.
They know that which is the fourth consciousness to be an obstacle for those engaged on the path to liberation; it is designated as "the internal obstacle."

These [four] are called destructive karmas (ghāti-karma) because they destroy spiritual excellence; likewise, the non-destructive karmas (aghāti-karma) are now described, beginning with the karma to be experienced (vedanīya).
Indeed, even the causal bond does not exist in the maturation of white (śukla) persons,
because it is contrary to their welfare and obstructs the knowledge of reality;
that [bond] which conforms to the experience-initiating karma of white persons [is absent].
He described the "nāmika" karma; he then undertakes that karma, which is the first stage of the white *pudgala*: the *kalala* and *budbuda*.
Beyond that is the primordial unmanifest (avyākṛta), which exists in the form of potentiality;
it is the lineage (gotra) and the lifespan (āyuṣka), for it indeed extends the life of human beings.
Because it leads virtuous beings in that manner through correct production,
and because it subsequently binds the person by depending upon white (pure) individuals,
it is called the eightfold karma of bondage.
The abiding of the self, whose entire mass of afflictions and habitual tendencies has been eliminated and which is solely intent upon perfect bliss, occurs through that which has been taught.
Others, however, maintain that liberation consists in ascending upwards; for when the soul is freed from its bonds, it moves upward, and thus it is called "mokṣa."
Because it is called "kāya" since the *jīva* itself exists as the body (*asti-kāyaka*), so too elsewhere; thus, the *asti-kāya* is traditionally held to be threefold.
The Buddha is liberated, the Arhat is eternally perfected, and the third is the Jain;
the other two are well-known as "the one who fills" and "the one who flows away."
That person which is accumulated by way of substantiality, as well as that which is diminished,
would be a person existing as a body, endowed with sixfold divisions.
The four elements beginning with earth constitute the stationary and the moving;
the category of merit (dharmāstikāya) is to be known as that which conforms to the nature [of motion]. The category of demerit (adharmāstikāya), however, is declared to be the cause of stability.
Space is of two kinds: the first is the space of the world (lokākāśa), and the other is the space beyond the world (alokākāśa), which exists above those situated one above the other.
That which exists within the worlds is called the world-space (lokākāśa);
above that, the place of liberation is termed the non-world-space (alokākāśa).

Introducing that logic of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) everywhere, [the word] *nipāta*— which appears as non-exclusive (*anekānta-bhāsin*) and is a substitute for a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*)— [is used]. If it were the case that "the thing exists indeed," then [it would follow] exclusively, in every way, and at all times.
If it is argued that [the self] exists everywhere with its entire essence, that is inconsistent;
for its activities and desires occur only in certain places and in certain respects.
"Since the acquisition of knowledge by discerning beings is thus postulated," he himself refutes this very method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī-naya*).

And by the sūtra, "Because it is impossible, not in one," the author of the sūtras [establishes] that for phenomena such as existence and non-existence, which consist of mutual non-existence, [simultaneous occurrence is impossible].
For there can be no coexistence within a single substratum [of contradictory qualities] like cold and heat;
and thus, since the self would not be omnipresent, it cannot have the same dimensions as the body.
Even if there is contradiction due to succession, it does not arise from transformation and the like;
for the final dimension of one established in liberation is eternal.
The permanence of both the initial and intermediate sizes must be asserted,
as well as the uniformity of the size of the body.
Otherwise, it would follow that there is no distinction; therefore, it cannot be so. Or rather, [this is said] while the final liberation and the ultimate dimension remain established.
In the two preceding states, however, the individual soul (jīva) would be of that same measure;
therefore, specifically, the soul exists as either minute or large according to its state.
Therefore, the view that [the soul] has the size of the body is untenable;
moreover, it is inconsistent to claim that the Lord is the presiding controller (adhiṣṭhātṛ).
That doctrine of mere signs (nimittamātravāda) is refuted because it contradicts reality; likewise, the doctrine of a non-scriptural Īśvara is refuted as it is imagined in various forms.
Yoga, Sāṅkhya, and other systems proclaim that the Lord is solely the presiding overseer of both the Puruṣa and the Pradhāna, and the instrumental cause [of creation].
The followers of Maheśvara, moreover, consider that there are five categories:
effect, cause, union, method, and the end of suffering.
"These [beings] have been commanded by the Lord for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the bound";
thus, Paśupati would be the Lord, the efficient cause, indeed the instrumental cause.
The Māheśvaras, however, are fourfold: the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, some who are Kāru-siddhāntins, and others who are Kāpālikas.
And because they follow the scriptures propounded by Maheśvara,
they are called Māheśvaras; in that system, Īśvara is the cause,
Pradhāna is the effect, and Yoga is proclaimed as the Great One (Mahat) and so forth.
The syllable Oṃ, knowledge, fortitude, and so forth; the ritual of the three ablutions; the culmination in secret conduct; and liberation as the end of suffering—thus [is the path].
"The soul is their substance; the bond is proclaimed to be their fetter.
Liberation from that is the end of suffering"—thus say the Vaiśeṣikas.
Furthermore, according to their own system, they hold that God is the instrumental cause.
Just as a potter and others who act as supervisors possess causality as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) with respect to jars and the like,
yet do not possess material causality (*upādānatva*), so too the Lord does not [possess both] with respect to the effect.

In this regard, the following occurs to me: Is the Veda merely the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) [of the world], or is it so through inference and other means? It cannot be the first, because both [instrumentality and material causality] are described [in scripture], as in the statements: "It is the instrumental cause and the material cause (*upādāna*)," and "It is also the material cause."
Since [the Lord] has been mentioned repeatedly in the Vedas, there is no need for inference here either.
If one were to postulate a Lord based on inference, he would be conceived merely in accordance with what is observed.
Therefore, in this case, just as in the case of a potter,
the Lord would also be subject to defects such as passion, as well as partiality, cruelty, and so forth.
Because [the world] possesses purpose, it would follow that Īśvara lacks sovereignty;
and because [he is claimed to be] a particular kind of puruṣa, he would share the nature of a puruṣa.

If it were argued that [the Lord acts] like an instrument due to the absence of a physical basis for control, then inconsistency would follow from His admission of indifference. Furthermore, if [He were to act as an instrument], the consequence of having an end would follow, because experiences such as enjoyment would necessarily ensue.
Whether there be a determination of omniscience or not,
the Pāñcarātra is considered inconsistent because its origin is impossible.
The Blessed One Vāsudeva is the embodiment of knowledge and is untainted;
he, who is the ultimate reality and the supreme essence, is divided into four forms.
Establishing himself as his own self through the form of the Vāsudeva array,
he [appears] in the form of the Saṅkarṣaṇa array and the form of the Pradyumna array.
Aniruddha is Vāsudeva, whose form is the manifestation; he possesses the supreme Self.
Saṅkarṣaṇa is named the individual soul (jīva), and Pradyumna is said to be the mind (manas).
Ahaṅkāra is Aniruddha; he is said to be their primordial nature (prakṛti).
Vāsudeva and the others are designated as the effects (kārya).
Having stated that Saṅkarṣaṇa is born from Vāsudeva as the mind (manas), and that Pradyumna is born from Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Aniruddha is born from Pradyumna; (p. 119)
Having worshipped the Blessed One here through self-surrender, through ritual sacrifice,
and through the yoga of Vedic study, the practitioner, with afflictions exhausted, becomes united with Him.
Regarding the statement "one should take refuge in the Blessed One" and so forth, it is said therein:
because [the self] is unproduced, defects such as impermanence and the like cannot possibly occur.
Furthermore, due to contradiction, in some places there is the state of being a collection of qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty; yet in other places, those very things are the Self itself.

Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are individual souls (jīvas), while Vāsudeva is likewise [a soul] in some instances; furthermore, because it contains censure of the Vedas, the Pāñcarātra is inconsistent [with the truth].

The systems beginning with Sāṅkhya and ending with Pāñcarātra have been refuted by many arguments; yet, according to the maxim that "a position remains established until it is refuted by one's own arguments," one's own doctrine [remains unrefuted].
Therefore, the linga should be worn upon the region of the heart by those seeking liberation;
this is established by authoritative means as well as by many logical arguments.
The independence from opposing positions has been stated by way of contradiction;
lest that [independence] be lost, this further elaboration unfolds.
Regarding the doubt as to whether there is an origination of space or not:
space does not originate because it is not heard [to do so] in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
however, let there be an origination of space in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
The scriptural statement regarding the origination of space is figurative, because origination is impossible [for it];
for that which has prior non-existence possesses origination, as in the case of a jar.
Nor is it the prior non-existence of space; therefore, the scriptural statement is indeed figurative.
Furthermore, because of the hearing of such passages as "and therefore it is immortal," it is indeed eternal.
Because [the attributes] such as "all-pervading like space" and "eternal" would be inconsistent [with a plurality],
there would be both primary and secondary application of the term "Brahman," just as in the case of the word "Brahman" [applied to different individuals].
In this case, there is no abandonment of the thesis, because there is likewise no exclusion;
for the existence of the clay is not excluded from the words [denoting] the jar.
Just as the cognition of a jar arises from the cognition of the clay, so too does that Brahman exist through non-distinction;
for the existence of space likewise arises from its non-distinction from the existence of Brahman.
From the knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of the ether arises with ease;
for as far as there is modification, there is division, just as in the world.
By this, Mātariśvan is also explained almost entirely;
for it is stated that "Vāyu and the intermediate space (antarikṣa) are immortality."
Since prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) does not exist in space, it is appropriately [said that space is eternal];
however, since prior non-existence of air does exist, how can its eternality be established?
In this regard, it is established that the scriptural statement regarding its origination is figurative,
because the scripture concerning immortality determines that air exists even prior [to creation].
Indeed, because it arises from that [preceding] scriptural statement, this scripture must be taken in a secondary sense;
for by the scriptural statement "From air, fire," fire would arise from the wind (mātariśvan).
From fire, water arises; from water, earth itself [arises].
Because of its function (*adhikāra*), it is dark in form; and because of another word [in the text], it is the Great Earth (*mahī*).
Since [the world] arises in this manner, He alone is the cause of the worlds by Himself;
it is not air or other elements, for He is the Lord because of His meditative contemplation of them.
From that characteristic mark, it is known that "He desired, 'May I be many,'" because of this desire;
and since water and fire are insentient, the act of seeing belongs to the Lord of the universe.
Furthermore, this sequence of origination is established by way of reversal;
thus it is described that "in this world, the universe arises from the Imperishable."
The Atharvaṇa Śruti says that they are born in that sequence:
"By austerity Brahman is built up; from that, food is born."
From food come life-breath, mind, truth, the worlds, action, and immortality;
he who is all-knowing, who consists of all, whose austerity consists of knowledge.
Therefore, from this Brahman are born name, form, and food; and from it arise, in sequence, the earth, water, fire, consciousness, and the mind.

If it is argued that "from food [come] breath and mind, [and from them] truth" is based on their characteristic marks, then the previously stated method applies here as well, since there is no distinction; and furthermore, the immediate sequence following food is established here too.
For it is established by scripture that food comes first, from which arises vital breath (*prāṇa*), and from that, the mind (*manas*);
and because the truthfulness of the mind is likewise heard [in the text],
there is no origination of either consciousness or mind in their own essential form.
Since beginninglessness is what must be expressed, and because that [Self] consists of the moving and the unmoving,
the body is not a transformation of food; therefore, there is no mention of the immediate succession of food.
Thus has been declared that which depends upon the origin of the moving and the unmoving.
The birth of consciousness and the mind is figurative, because they arise when that [body] exists;
for while the body is produced, there is the production of consciousness and the mind,
and thus their birth here is designated by way of their own nature.

Since there is no production of beings from a prior separation, and because the sequence of their arising would be broken, the doubt arises: does the individual soul (jīva) come into existence, or does it not?

Just as sparks fly forth from a fire, so too, according to the scriptural statement at the outset— "all these [souls] emerge having the nature of the Knower"— it might initially appear that the individual soul (jīva) is produced; however, there is no such origination of the soul.
Just as sparks issue forth from a fire, even so do the individual souls (jīvas) emerge from Him; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
There is a doubt as to whether the nature of the *jīva* is the Self (*ātman*) or the knower;
however, through such passages as "a mass of consciousness," its nature as knowledge is established.
For indeed, from the statement "He who is born knows through his higher intellect" and from such Vedic passages as "He is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, and the knower," [it is established].
The scripture cited with the intention of showing the difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality asks:
"Is the individual soul (jīva) minute in size, of intermediate size, or indeed great?"
But the intermediate size has been refuted in the sequence of the Arhat;
because of the scriptural mention of its departure, going, and returning, it is indeed atomic.
Departure from the body is not possible for that which is all-pervading;
likewise, going to other worlds and returning from them would be impossible.
The coming and going belong to the self alone; it is not enveloped by the elements or the instruments of action.

(123) If it is argued that the Self is indeed great because of the scriptural statement [of its magnitude] and not minute, listen: because the context concerns the Supreme Self, that [scriptural] hearing refers to Him; for the individual soul (jīva) is indeed minute.
This self is subtle; it is subtle by virtue of its verbal description and also by its measurement:
[it is subtler] than a hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold.
That portion is to be known as the individual soul (jīva), and it is capable of attaining infinity.
For it is described that even the smallest [self] is seen as being the size of the tip of an awl;
but if the soul were indeed atomic in size, how could it [pervade] all bodies?
If sensation were perceived [as distinct from consciousness], then this would indeed be a contradiction;
however, there is no contradiction, because of the connection with the quality of sentience, just as in the case of sandalwood.
If it is argued that [the objection does not apply] because of the distinction in the mode of abiding, it is not so;
for since [the soul] is admitted to abide in the heart, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Or rather, it is due to its quality, just as light [is attributed to a gem]; here, because of its connection with the quality of consciousness, just as the entire space is pervaded by the radiance of gems, lamps, and the like.

Because consciousness is all-pervasive, its pervasion of the entire body is logically consistent. But how can a quality exist apart from the possessor of that quality? Indeed, a quality such as whiteness cannot exist without the cloth.
This light is to be inferred from its quality; it is a distinct luminosity marked by rarefaction.
Its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is like that of fragrance, as it is not perceived when flowers and such are out of reach.
Even so, there is a separation of the quality of consciousness from the atom here;
but surely, if it is argued that this is merely a dissociation [of consciousness] from its substratum, like that of fragrance [from a flower].
In that case, however, a diminution would necessarily follow in flowers and the like;
yet it is not observed at all that they lose their weight and other such properties.
Nor is it the case that because the distinguished [substances] are few, their distinction is not perceived;
for if there were a perception of a distinct fragrance, it would be recognized in the world.

Just as there is the cognition "the fragrant substance has been smelled by me" and "the fragrance has been smelled by me," so too is the distinctness of the qualities [established] from their existence.
And thus the scripture shows: "even unto the hairs";
it [shows] that consciousness is an attribute, not the very nature of the Self.
If consciousness were all-pervasive here, then the individual soul (jīva) would also be all-pervasive;
however, this is not so, because of the teaching of their distinctness in such scriptural passages as "by means of intelligence" (prajñayā).
But surely, because of the statement "His [nature] is knowledge" (*vijñānam*),

it follows that He is denoted by the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*); thus, the designation "knowledge" would apply to Him on account of His having knowledge as His essential quality, just as the term "the Wise One" (*prājña*) applies to the Self, or as the term "salt-ocean" applies to the sea.
Furthermore, there is no fault in that [usage], because it is seen to be produced by the very nature of things;
for instance, from the word "cow" which denotes the universal *gotva*, the individual cow (*go-vyakti*) is likewise described.
Because of the absence of knowledge in states such as deep sleep, the nature of the Self is not [perceived] therein;
however, its manifestation is possible for that which exists, just like manhood and other qualities.
Just as masculinity, though existing in the state of a cause during childhood and so forth, becomes manifest in youth; and just as that same quality exists in the state of a cause during deep sleep,
yet becomes manifest upon waking and so on— therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
Thus, both its nature as a knower and its atomicity have been correctly established;
however, if it were of the nature of pure consciousness (jñapti), its omnipresence would be contradicted.
Otherwise, either constant perception or constant non-perception would result;
or else, a restriction regarding one or the other would necessarily follow.
When the doubt arises as to whether the individual soul (jīva) is the agent or not,
the Sāṅkhyas first describe that the soul is not the agent, because it is insentient.
Because that [Self] is devoid of any excellence to be acquired through action,
and because its state of non-attachment is described in such passages as "For this [Self] is indeed unattached."
It has been stated that because of the absence of conjunction with a cause in that [Self], agency belongs to the intellect alone; having reached this conclusion, it is now further explained.
Because it possesses scriptural meaning, that [Self] is the agent; [as stated in such texts as] "he should sacrifice" and "he should offer oblations.
Through the scriptures, the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is correctly understood.
Otherwise, if it were established in this way, the treatise would be entirely purposeless;
for an entity cannot be produced because it is incapable of having any excellence added to it.
It has been stated that because pleasure and so forth are perceived here by direct perception through their excellence,
the quality of being incapable of having an excellence added to it is unestablished.
The absence of the conjunction of signs is not thus; let it be recited by you:
"The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer."
It has been established by scripture that [the soul] is joined with the true causal signs;
this scripture concerning its lack of attachment refers to the waking state of this individual soul (jīva).
This was stated with the intention of showing the absence of a permanent conjunction, based on the observation that there is no connection with what is seen in a dream.
Furthermore, agency [is attributed] because of the instruction regarding its abiding, likewise because of the cessation of the instruments,
because of the appropriation [of materials], and because of the designation [of agency] in the action.
But surely, by such passages as "Consciousness is the sacrifice," it is the intellect (buddhi) that is intended by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna);
how then can the individual soul (jīva) be the agent?
And it has been stated that "it is not indicated"; this is the specification of that which has the form of the individual soul (jīva).
But surely, could this not be a specification of the intellect (buddhi) as the soul, rather than the reverse?
At that time, the Śruti declared "not in consciousness" for this very reason;
otherwise, a lack of restriction would follow for action as well, just as it does for perception.
For if the intellect were indeed the agent, then it would incur a reversal of its power;
it would possess the power of an agent and abandon its causal power.
When the state of being an agent belongs to the Self, there would be detachment from the objective world;
this occurs through the knowledge of the discrimination between Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
And thus it has been stated that, because the Buddha lacks the status of an agent, [he is not an agent];
yet, just as a carpenter acts in both ways, agency indeed derives from the Supreme One alone.
For his status as the impeller is heard in scriptural passages such as "He indeed...
[Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1]. Now, one might object: if the Lord were the impeller, the individual soul (jīva) would lack agency.
Agency belongs to one being carried away by a powerful current of water,
which depends upon the effort exerted for the performance of what is enjoined and the avoidance of what is prohibited.
Regarding the two [injunctions] thus acquired—"one should sacrifice" and "one must not kill"—the scripture would otherwise be purposeless;
therefore, on account of its non-frivolity and other such reasons, the scripture possesses meaning.
Just as sparks [emanate] from fire, the individual soul (jīva) is said to be a portion of the Lord;
this is established by such scriptural passages as "That is to be sought," and by the designation of manifoldness.
Moreover, in the Vedas, absolute non-difference is also stated:
"The slaves of Brahman, the servants of Brahman, those who gamble with Brahman."
Everything is proclaimed to be Brahman by way of the reasoning concerning low birth; for it is described as a portion of Brahman in the passage, "All beings are but one quarter of Him."
"An eternal portion of My very self, having become a living soul in the world of living beings"—
by such Smṛti passages, the individual soul is declared to be a portion of the Lord.
Now, if the non-difference of the Lord from the individual souls is accepted,
then the Lord would become miserable through the misery of the soul, because there is no difference between the two.
Furthermore, due to the particularity of its own nature, like light and so forth,
Vyāsa and other authorities maintain that the Lord does not experience the suffering of the individual soul.
In the Smṛtis that are difficult to traverse, the meaning has been made clear at will;
for the Supreme Self therein is indeed remembered as eternal and devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Nor is it stained by the fruits of action, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
however, that other one, whose nature is action, is joined with both liberation and bondage.
This is made clear by such passages as, "One of the two eats the sweet fruit," and so forth;
[it is further shown] by the two cases of permission and prohibition: "One should sacrifice" and "One should not eat."
[The fruit] is [determined] by connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth, due to the difference in location;
for otherwise, there would be a confusion of fruits arising after the death of the body.
Furthermore, there is no confusion between injunctions and prohibitions due to the lack of continuity;
moreover, their selves are many, distinct, and all-pervading.
Because they are connected with every body in its entirety,
there is a confusion of pleasure, pain, and so forth; therefore, those [bodies] alone are indeed the manifestations of the Self (ātmābhāsa).
Although there is no difference in all beings' connection to a body, nevertheless,
such specific distinctions are observed there only in the case of some particular individual.
The connection with pleasure and so forth belongs to others [the self] and not to other [elements], because of the absence of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa);
therefore, there is no confusion [of properties]. Thus he said: "Because of the restriction by the unseen."
And if the intention and so forth were to reside in the primary [cause], then, as before, there would be commonality; this would likewise hold true even if they resided in the self.
However, due to the non-distinction in the conjunction with the mind, there is only a commonality [of experience] for all selves,
even though they are omnipresent, within the specific locations delimited by their respective bodies.
Hence, pleasure and the rest arise without any confusion;
if it is argued that this is due to spatial location, we say no, because the individual souls are included within those very parts.
However, the difference between the individual soul and the Lord alone is universally accepted;
their natural distinction as individuals is desired by everyone.
There is a doubt as to whether the sense organs are produced or not; [for it is said:
"From this [Being] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs."
If you argue that this is because their origination is heard of in such Smṛtis, listen:
just as the Self is not born, so too are the vital breaths and the sense organs.
The scriptural statement regarding their origination is figurative, because the origination of the vital breaths is impossible,
in accordance with the meaning of such scriptural passages as "by this living self."
129) And because of the scriptural statement "The Ṛṣis were indeed the vital breaths," that [creation] is only figurative;
and since speech is preceded by that, there are therefore seven sense organs.
Furthermore, because their movement is specified, these [senses] such as the hands are distinct;
they remain so, and thus it should not be thought that there are only seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
These *prāṇas* are said to be subtle, whereas if they were gross, they would be composed of earth.
Emerging clearly from the body like a snake from its hole,
that supreme [breath] is designated as having five functions, just like the mind.
This chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is atomic, and it is neither air nor a mere function;
for, according to the scriptural statement, it is taught that the prāṇa itself is Brahman.
If the individual soul were the agent and the enjoyer, then the vital breath (prāṇa) would be merely an instrument like the eye and other senses;
as an instrument for all purposes, it is never independent.
The vital breath (prāṇa) remains together with those [organs] such as sight;
nor is there any fault in this, for the Śruti demonstrates it thus.
Just as light and other elements have a substratum, so indeed do they through the act of thinking;
if the deities are the presiding agents, then let them be the enjoyers here.

And since the status of being a presiding controller is established, the connection of the collection of organs with the master [the Self] alone— not with the individual soul (jīva)— is enjoined by scripture, just as it is with the vital breath (prāṇa).
Now, where this space and that memory correspond to one another,
because of the eternity of the individual soul (jīva), there is indeed no [separation] due to the injunction of the Śruti; thus,
the eternal connection of the vital breaths (prāṇas) with the soul itself has been proclaimed.

130) Because its persistence is observed at the time of departure [from the body] and dissolution, and because it is established by such scriptural passages as "When he has departed... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).
It has been described that the connection between the vital breath (prāṇa) and fire and the other elements is non-eternal;
for even in the absence of fire and the rest at the time of cosmic dissolution (pralaya), the vital breath continues to exist.

Therefore, the presiding agency over fire and the other elements is attributed to the preeminent vital breath (prāṇa), rather than to anything else, because of the designation of their distinctness from it.
The Śruti likewise [teaches] that speech and the other [organs] are indeed distinct principles from the vital breath (prāṇa):
"From this [Self], the vital breath, mind, and all the sense organs are born."
The vital breath (prāṇa) is designated as distinct [from speech and the other organs] in various scriptural passages;
thus, because the Śruti declares the prāṇa to be separate from speech and the rest, it is distinct.

Indeed, there must be a distinction on account of their specific characteristics; therefore, they are certainly distinct principles. When this doubt arises—whether the evolution of names and forms has the individual soul (*jīva*) alone as its agent, or whether it has the Lord (*īśvara*) as its agent—[the following is said].
The fashioning of name and form occurs here and there by the Lord who effects triplication;
for this is indeed taught in such statements as "This [is that]," and so forth.
Regarding that tripartition, how is it that the division into "this is earthy" and "this is watery" is made clear,
and how is there a further internal division following such a suspicion of differentiation?
From the earth, which takes the form of rice and other grains, the internal effects such as blood are obtained;
likewise from water, and likewise from fire, the bones and so forth are produced.

However, due to the predominance of this or that particular aspect, and by virtue of the distinction of those respective parts, there arises the designation of this or that [specific doctrine]; therefore, everything is consistent.

The entire grammatical derivation of those names and forms is established solely on the basis of inferential signs (*liṅga*), such as the "triple-making" (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and so forth. Thus it has been proven that [the creation] proceeds from inferential signs alone.
Therefore, the Liṅga, which is designated by the term Brahman, should be held within the lotus of the heart.

Thus ends the second instruction in the *Kriyāsāra*, within the *Nigamāgamasārasaṃgraha* composed by Nīlakaṇṭha, who is proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secret essence of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
Now follows the instruction on the three fires.
Salutations to the venerable gurus!
In the second [chapter], the contradiction with Smṛti and Nyāya has been refuted,
and the independence from the positions of opponents has been thoroughly demonstrated.
The contradiction with scripture has been properly resolved previously;
[so too have been explained] the non-produced nature of the individual soul (jīva) and its instruments.
Now, the manner of dissolution and its various intermediate states have been explained with respect to the individual soul (jīva) when it is enveloped by the instruments of perception.
Likewise, the state of being Brahman and knowledge; then again, difference and non-difference;
the combination of qualities and likewise their non-combination.
The accomplishment of the goals of human life proceeds from knowledge; thus, knowledge and the ritual procedure are established.
The various types of procedures, along with their auxiliary and cooperative factors, shall now be explained.
In this third discourse on instruction, the determination of the fruit, which is liberation itself, is also set forth through many logical arguments.
In this context, something else is first elaborated as a digression:
the path and the exhaustion [of merit] based on the knowledge of the five fires (pañcāgnividyā), and the dissolution [of the world].
The individual soul (jīva), together with the principal vital breaths, the senses themselves, as well as the mind,
knowledge, past actions, and prior cognition, having taken hold [of these], [departs].
Having abandoned his former body, this living being (jīva), indeed having entered another body and enveloped by subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), either departs or does not— so it is asked.
Since the elements would exist wherever the fruit is experienced, their [separate] appropriation would thus be purposeless. Therefore, this is indeed the case.
Upon entering another body, the individual soul (jīva) departs, enveloped by the subtle elements which serve as the seeds of the body.
From the statement in the form of a question, and from the description beginning with "heaven" and so forth,
[it is established that] in the fifth oblation, "the waters," meaning he is enveloped by water.
It is understood by all that it moves; how then is it said to be enveloped?
Because it consists of three elements and because of their predominance, there is much water in the semen and the blood, which are white.
Furthermore, there is the departure of the elements because the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is described;
for indeed, the vital breaths have no movement when they are without a support.
If it is argued that the movement of the vital breaths toward fire and the other elements does not occur together with the individual soul (*jīva*):
Nor is that journey to Agni and so forth figurative, because it is not metaphorical;
furthermore, in the first [section] concerning the world of heaven called Agni, water is not heard of.
Since it is heard that "they offer faith as an oblation," [the water] does not [consist of water] from this point onward;
or else, how could water be said to be present there in the fifth oblation?

If it is argued thus, [we reply]: the waters that are beneficial are described by the word "faith" (śraddhā). Otherwise, on account of the logical inconsistency, that scriptural statement would not be tenable; for it is observed in usage that "faith" refers to external water, as seen in that very context.
(133) "And those living beings are embraced [by the light], for there is no separation from them," according to scripture—
if this is argued, it is not so, because the destination of those who perform sacrifices, works of public utility (*pūrta*), and other such deeds is observed [to be different].
Furthermore, enjoyment is not possible for those who have been devoured by deities as if by tigers and other predators; therefore, the author of the Sūtras has spoken here [as follows].
Or [the term "enjoyment"] may be figurative, because he is not a knower of the Self; for scripture shows this as well.
Upon the exhaustion of his works, he departs with a remainder of karma, as seen from two scriptural statements.
Likewise, this very point—that it is not so—has been established by the Śruti itself.
If it is asked, "How then can there be a statement regarding descent from the *caraṇa* [world] here?", the answer is: "It is not so."
Now, as for the scriptural statement regarding conduct, it is for the purpose of indicating karma;
however, the teacher Kṛṣṇa himself indeed maintains that birth is the [primary] factor here.
Otherwise, conduct would be purposeless, for it is that very [knowledge] which is required;
"The Vedas do not purify one devoid of conduct," for indeed, the collections of good conduct are the causes.
Bādari declared that right conduct consists of the duties toward one's husband, characterized by the worship of Śiva and so forth, as well as good and evil deeds performed independently.
In the Śruti, the course of the moon is mentioned even for those men who have not performed sacrifices and other rites;
what then is the similarity between those who perform such rites and those who do not?
Even after experiencing suffering in the restraint of others,
the ascent and descent may also take place within the lunar orb.
The Śruti itself has declared that Vaiśvānara is the "confluence of all things";
likewise, the followers of Yama remember such torments in the Nāciketa fire.
Moreover, these seven hells, beginning with Raurava,
are further recorded by the authors of the Purāṇas as being lands for the experiencing of the fruits of evil deeds.
How is it that Citragupta and others are also remembered as presiding authorities?
It is because Yama’s status as a presiding authority derives from his specific functions.
There is no contradiction regarding [the practice] in Raurava and other such texts; in those cases, the Command (ājñā) is the regulating authority.
However, because it is the subject at hand, it has been stated in the Sūtra that this applies to the knowledge and action pertaining to that [state].
The word "tu" (but) functions by itself to set aside the prima facie position:
[the claim] that for those persons who do not perform sacrifices and so forth, there is an ascent to and descent from the moon.
"How do you know that world does not exist?"—
since both the question and the answer are heard in the Vedic text beginning with "nastaḥ."
Now, regarding the phrase "not by these two," it refers to those two paths;
and regarding the phrase "of those two," it refers to knowledge and action, because they are the subjects under discussion.
Knowledge and ritual action are the two primary means for the paths known as Devayāna and Pitṛyāna; thus it is said: "But those who know this thus... and so forth.
Regarding that, the description of the meaning is as follows: "The gift" refers to the ritual action consisting of sacrifices and works of public utility;
those who travel by the path of the gods through knowledge, and those by the path of the ancestors through ritual action.
Men are not at all authorized [for this]; it is declared to be for them alone. The third type is the nature of a lowly creature, who returns only once more.
Therefore, for those who have committed the most grievous acts, there is a path upon the lunar orb consisting of two [stages]:
ascent and descent; however, there is no third station.
Let a restriction of the number five be prescribed for the attainment of a body; however,
in the case of the third [birth], there is no restriction on the number of oblations.
And because of the attainment and perception of a body, as well as from such statements as "be born," the fourfold village is established by the Śruti.
Regarding those characterized as born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, and from sprouting—
among these, the latter two (those born from sweat and sprouting) possess the qualities of domestic life.
Furthermore, because their production is observed, there is no restriction on the number of oblations;
for this is described by the statement "Indeed, these [are the fires]" as being of three kinds.
How could its fourfold nature be established? Therefore, the author of the Sūtra stated here that the term "udbhijja" (born from a sprout) is intended to include those born from sweat as well.

Due to the similarity in their origin from earth and water, there is no difference between the two— namely the sweat-born and the soil-born— because one can be produced through the transformation of the other.

In this regard, concerning the practice of space and the subsequent elements prior to the practice of rice, there arises a doubt: does the similarity with each preceding element persist for a long duration?

Furthermore, regarding the question of whether it is for a short time, there is again no fixed rule; since there is an absence of any specific restrictive factor, this being the position reached, it is stated as follows.
There is descent in a short time, as well as the attainment [of the world] there;
this is because of the specific statement beginning with "vai khalu" and so forth.
By stating that "the emergence [of the soul] is difficult after its state as rice and so forth," he very clearly indicates that the duration prior to that was brief.

And since rice and other grains are presided over by another living soul, there is merely a clinging [of the deceased] to them; how then could those who explain the state of the *anuśāyin* (the lingering soul) describe it as being truly present there?
Just as action is proclaimed [to exist] in space and so forth, and likewise in the intermediate state,
so too is there verbal expression here, because verbal expression is observed [in this case as well].

If it is argued that [the body] is impure, we say no; for by the very injunction of the sacred word, there is merely a conjunction with rice-grains and the like, through the transformation into the state of rice and so forth.
And immediately thereafter, the state of being a "semen-discharger" (retassig) is recorded in the Śruti;
indeed, in this context, that state of being a semen-discharger occurs in its primary sense.

Since the meaning of the word *śiśna* is indeed established as "dust" (*rajas*) and refers specifically to the semen of youth, why then is that which was previously stated not considered a figurative usage? Indeed, it is so.
Let it be understood that one who possesses latent dispositions (anuśayin) attains those various states;
therefore, the very union with the progenitor is called the state of being a progenitor.
Even the existence of that rice and so forth consists merely of its connection with rice;
likewise, the body of a woman arises from the womb immediately following union with the seed-discharging male.
The body is shown to emerge from the womb by the words "that which is here";
even then, the statement regarding rice and so forth is appropriate as referring merely to the process of conjunction.
The second quarter of the third [chapter].
Now, however, the various states of the individual soul (jīva) are being elaborated upon, beginning with the passage where they declare: "He, having been approached, is made to lie down."
Does the living being (jīva) actually create chariots and other objects in a dream, or does it merely perceive them?
137) Dream is the third state, as it is seen in the Śrutis as being intermediate (sandhya).
When there is a junction between two worlds or two locations, it is called "sandhya" (the juncture).
Regarding that intermediate state, the Śruti declares: "He indeed creates a creation";
moreover, certain followers of specific Vedic branches maintain that he is the creator there.
"That which [exists] while [the senses] are asleep," and so forth; those desires, such as sons and the like, are mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), for their true nature is not manifested in its entirety.
Furthermore, due to the persistent clinging to a self, that sovereignty remains concealed for this individual soul;
for this very reason, bondage and its opposite [liberation] come to pass.
Or rather, the concealment of one's sovereignty arises from connection with a physical body;
for those who know it declare that this is indicated by what is stated in the Vedas.
When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for the sake of desired objects—
One should recognize prosperity in that dream-vision;
there is auspiciousness in mounting a noble elephant, whereas the opposite occurs when riding a donkey.
The fact that [the mind] is not able to create by itself is an auspicious sign for oneself.
Now, the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) is properly examined:
the absence of that dream is called deep sleep.

If it is argued that in this passage concerning sleep it was stated that [the soul] "slips into the channels," and that its return occurs "by means of them," then its entry into the pericardium must also be understood in that same way.
It has been declared that "being with the True" (*satā somya*) refers to attaining [Brahman], and "then" (*tadā*) refers to that time;
but are these [means], such as the channels (*nāḍī*), truly independent [of one another]?

138) Is it not clear that the states of deep sleep and the others are mutually dependent? Could "sleep" possibly exist when [the self] is combined with all [states], since there is a scriptural statement to that effect regarding the channels (nāḍīs)?
Furthermore, according to scripture, all things such as the channels (nāḍīs) are the locus of deep sleep;
yet, as in the expression "he lies on a couch," he lies enveloped [in the heart].
This very place is indeed accumulated for the sake of sleep; for it is certain that from this accumulated place, awakening occurs as if eternally.
Regarding the awakening just described: is it that very same person who was asleep who rises, or is it someone else within the body?

Due to the performance of the remainder of his karma and so forth, having reflected upon the action performed on the previous day, he proceeds once again toward that very same action on the following day.

Indeed, on account of the recollection [of the state], the word "previous," and the scriptural injunctions, this single state called "stupefaction" (mugdha) exists; it is described by all as being "fainted."
It is considered: in what state is he? There are four states:
first, waking; then dreaming; and after that, deep sleep.
And it is described that the fourth state of this living being is its attainment of perfection;
the dreaming state is not the same as the state of being stupefied, because [in the latter] there is no perception of objects.
Because he is devoid of perception, he does not see dreams;
for that reason as well, he is not considered to be in deep sleep, nor is he distinct from it.
With a serene countenance and eyes closed, he was like the very embodiment of innocence;
yet, while his karmic residue remained upon the earth, there was the attainment of all desired objects.
When speech and mind have returned to the non-existent sphere of the earth,
it is clear that from that point the vital breath and warmth depart.
For this very reason, the attainment of all objects is proclaimed as "mūrchā.
Now, the nature of Brahman is correctly described;
for there are scriptural passages [that speak of it] in two ways, [namely, as possessing] qualities such as the fulfillment of all desires.
Some [scriptural passages] are to be interpreted as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*) by virtue of their being endowed with attributes;
therefore, is that Brahman characterized by both marks (*ubhayaliṅga*), or is it characterized by one mark or the other?
Indeed, the Supreme Brahman cannot possess both characteristics by its own nature;
for there is no single entity in the world that is both with form and without form.
In that case, there can be no existence [of difference] either by way of location or through connection with limiting adjuncts such as earth and so forth;
for a thing cannot become something else merely through connection with a limiting adjunct.
A crystal gem would not possess a different nature and become non-transparent;
even through contact with lac-dye and the like, it does not itself become non-transparent.
Furthermore, because the impure superimposition is merely like a tree [in its diversity],
Brahman does not become diverse through such distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
If it is argued that it would possess both genders [of attributes], we say no;
for it cannot be so, since the non-difference [of the Self] is taught by the scripture despite the distinctions of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Moreover, because earlier distinctions were described by one who knows distinctions,
therefore Brahman cannot possess both characteristics; it is exclusively formless,
since such scriptural texts are primary, whereas others are intended for meditation.
The established position regarding that [scripture] is that it does not possess the intended meaning;
its futility is like that of a lamp, and scripture itself declares it to be "mere words."
Now, that statement which is remembered in the work of Yājñavalkya demonstrates this:
"Having made the mind, intellect, and consciousness free from other objects, [one perceives the Self] beyond the senses."

The Self is the object of meditation; it is that which is stable, the Lord residing in the heart like a lamp, solitary, devoid of minuteness and other qualities, and indeed luminous for that very reason.
Thus, the analogy "like the sun and so forth" is also appropriate;
for the single Self of all beings is established within every being.
It is seen as one and also as many, like the moon in water;
likewise, it is not equal to the sun and so forth, being [perceived] in an instant at the tip.
Even when there is the arising of a reflection, that which is distinct from and far removed from even embodied things such as the sun is seen there as an embodied form.
The Self is not material, nor are the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) distinct from it;
they do not exist at a remote distance, because [the Self] is all-pervading and non-different [from them].
"Therefore, the example is incorrect"—to this it is replied by me:
"The example is indeed correct, because it is an analogy based on a corresponding part of the subject under discussion."
For one should know that it partakes of increase and decrease, since it resides in the water;
indeed, the reflection of the sun expands when the water increases.
When there is diminution, it seems to diminish; when there is movement, it seems to move;
and when there is division, it seems to be divided—but in ultimate reality, it is not so at all.
(141) Maintain that the sun possesses suchness (*tathātva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for in that same way, Brahman itself is indeed one, yet [appears as many] through its own presence within bodies.
It likewise undergoes the properties of that [cause], such as increase and decrease;
this is consistent because there is no contradiction between the illustration and the thing illustrated.

For such is seen from the passage beginning with "Having created that," as well as from passages such as "Not this, not this" (neti neti); for "merely this much" (etāvatva) indeed constitutes materiality (mūrtatā).
Because it is the subject under discussion, the phenomenal world (prapañca) would be affirmed rather than negated;
therefore, Brahman alone remains as something vastly greater than its limited form.
For the Śruti declares that Brahman is indeed of the nature of the phenomenal world;
the Śruti speaks of this as unmanifest (avyakta), and they do not remember it as having a beginning in time.
"He is unmanifest, he is inconceivable," and so forth, has been heard many times in the Śruti;
moreover, yogis likewise [perceive] that Self at the time of meditation.
The Veda perceives Him here; therefore, the Veda praises Him.
The yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.
Just as there is non-difference between the quality of light and the like, and Brahman,
so too is there identity between Brahman and the phenomenal world through constant meditation on their being one with each other.
And here I shall establish grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*):
for this [coreferentiality] is primary when there is non-difference, whereas elsewhere it occurs through the connection of qualities;
such coreferentiality [is established] from the form [of the Vedic text], "May I become many."
And thus, from the perspective of non-difference, creation would not occur;
for light is certainly not a quality, but rather the very nature of Brahman itself.
Because it is established in that very way that "consciousness is bliss," the example is fully applicable; that example serves as a model for the practice of meditation.
"This quality of Brahman must indeed be explained as arising from practice alone—
He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge."

In the passage beginning with "tameva bhāntam," the status of being the agent of cognition is expressed; for by the use of the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) in the word "bhāti" (shines), it is precisely agency that is described.
For it is heard in such passages as "Then He thought," and likewise in the text, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. Therefore, it is indeed so.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two terms "infinite" (*ananta*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is indeed not contradictory; for that [coreferentiality] can only exist when there is non-difference (*abheda*).
For this reason, the Sage composed the aphorism "liṅgam" [Pāṇini 3.3.114];
it is derived from the root *jñā* with the suffix *lyuṭ*, signifying the act of making known (*jñapti*), and functioning as an abstract noun (*bhāva-sādhana*).
This word "jñāna" here [does not refer to cognition] because, if it were a derivative (pratyaya) ending in a suffix, it would be accented on the first syllable;
however, it is stated to be accented on the final syllable.

In the word "jñāna," the suffix *matup* (expressing possession) is understood as "that which has knowledge"; therefore, it is a term denoting one who possesses knowledge, and by virtue of the rule that such words are udātta on the final syllable,
it is known from this indicative mark of the final accent that Brahman possesses the quality of knowledge.
And likewise, because it possesses the characteristic of having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*), it is traditionally held to have the quality of knowledge of Brahman.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction in accepting both difference and non-difference, we say no; for...
Its lack of contradiction is stated on the basis of its being authoritative,
just as both "the serpent is the earring" and "the earring is the serpent" are remembered [as true] from two different perspectives.
The difference between the serpent and its coils is the same as the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world,
because both are designated as being "existent" and "non-existent" respectively.
Just as there is indeed no difference in the essential nature of light, of shade, and of the sun which is their support; so too [is it here].
Thus, through their nature as light, there is non-difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world,
just as there is none between a quality such as illumination and its possessor, Brahman.
The difference and non-difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world should be understood in this very same way;
how can a wise person accept these two, difference and non-difference, as being contradictory?
Indeed, non-difference alone is intended by the practice [of meditation], because [the object] possesses parts;
however, the designation of difference in that regard should be understood as figurative.
If this is argued, [we reply]: because of the repeated negations "not this, not this," its nature as a bridge is designated for the purpose of meditation, just like [the description of] the feet.
A quarter of a kārṣāpaṇa is likewise intended as the "quarter" (pāda);
the designation of weight and so forth depends on the specific context of its application.
Just as there is a distinction in manifestations due to the differences between palaces, gate-towers, and enclosures,
so too, for the one Brahman, there is a distinction based on its connection with primordial and other locations.
Due to the difference in its relations, even its own differentiation is designated.
Having thus refuted the arguments put forward by others with many logical reasonings,
Vyāsa indeed stated the reason that establishes the nature of being the Self of all.
Likewise, Brahman is held to be the self of all because other [entities] are negated;
by this [negation], its omnipresence is established through scriptural texts concerning ether and so forth.
The word *āyāma* signifies pervasion, according to the Vedic scripture "as far as this extends";
furthermore, the attainment of the fruit proceeds from the Lord by virtue of His being the sovereign supervisor of all.
Because He knows the specific distinctions of place and time, He bestows fruits upon those who perform actions in accordance with their karma; yet He does not perish along with the impermanent karma.
And because it is so heard, that fruit comes from the Lord alone;
for the teacher Jaimini says that He is the giver of the fruit, on account of logical consistency and scriptural authority, such as the observation of the injunction "one should sacrifice."
And that [unseen force], by means of an operation termed "unprecedented" (apūrva), bestows the fruit of action;
due to the diversity of actions, the diversity of fruits arises therein.
Since God is of a single uniform nature, there would be both partiality and cruelty;
therefore, it is not tenable that Brahman is the bestower of fruits.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that the fruit [of action arises] from the Lord,
because the scripture declares Him to be the impeller of action and the possessor of the fruit.
Whichever form a devotee desires to worship with faith, that very form I make steadfast for him.
Whatever be their wavering faith, I ordain that very same faith for them;
endowed with that faith, they strive for the propitiation of that [deity].
"And from that [the Lord], he obtains those very desires ordained by Me alone";
since this is stated in the Gītā, Maheśvara is the giver of the fruit.
The third quarter of the third chapter.
The reality of Brahman, as well as the means of valid cognition and other categories, have been explained;
now, however, let us see what remains to be said regarding each Vedānta text.
Whether there is a difference between the cognitions [of the various Upanishads] or not is correctly investigated here;
for all the Vedāntas are the means of knowledge (*pratyaya*), and that [knowledge] is, moreover, consciousness (*vijñāna*).
All that would indeed have a single uniform cognition based on the Vedānta,
because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth, and because they all take the form "one should meditate."
If it be argued that there is a multiplicity of knowledges due to the difference in their qualities, we say no;
for even within a single knowledge, the presence of different qualities is logically possible.
There is no distinction between the Atirātra sacrifice on account of the inclusion or non-inclusion of the sixteenth cup; therefore, the unity of the vidyā is indeed established.
Because of the scriptural statement regarding the practice of Vedic study in that manner,
and because of the qualification [of the person], there is a restrictive rule for that [study] there, as in the case of the *sava* sacrifices.
The Veda declares the oneness of knowledge because it teaches the oneness of the object to be known;
likewise, it speaks of the oneness of the days and similarly of the qualities elsewhere.
Since the cognition is indeed the same,
the sublation [of one by the other] must be understood by the wise as being due to the identity of purpose, just like the case of supplementary injunctions (vidhiśeṣa).
In that context, there is a plurality of knowledge (vidyā), as indicated by such scriptural passages as "But you are not [the breath]," and so forth;
for in one instance the vital breath (prāṇa) possesses the status of an agent, while in another it possesses the status of an object, and thus they are not identical.
There can be no distinction [between them] due to the fault of grammatical case endings, because there is no difference;
likewise, the designation "Udgītha" and "Vidyā" is specifically applied to that same thing.
If it is argued that there is unity of knowledge here because the remaining [text] is similar to the "parovarīyas" [passage], despite the difference in the introductory sections; |||

Thus it has been said: "In the case of [the word] *para* and so forth, which serves to distinguish the sequence of the *sāti* suffix, there is a unity of designation (*saṃjñā*) here because the force of the designation is weak."

For while there exist well-known distinctions among ritual acts such as the Agnihotra and others, there is indeed a unity of identity based on the single name "Kāṭhaka"; therefore, they are not different.
For the Udgītha of "Om" and so forth is indeed a qualification [of Brahman] due to its pervasiveness;
these qualities, such as bliss and the rest, belong to that [Brahman] because they exist everywhere and not elsewhere.
For increase and decrease are not beneficial in the case of "having the beloved as the head" and so forth;
these two are possible only if there is difference, yet that difference is not tenable.
Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind;
there is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.
The Supreme Puruṣa alone is to be meditated upon, and not others such as the senses;
for there is no purpose for the meditator in those, whereas there is a purpose in the Puruṣa.
For this reason as well, the Person is to be meditated upon, because of the hearing of the word "Self" (ātman);
for in that scriptural passage, "Or rather, the Self," the Supreme Self alone is understood.

(147) If it is argued that [the term "Brahman"] must refer to the Supreme Brahman because of its syntactical connection with the subsequent sentence, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*), then [we reply]: it is so because of the restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
The Śāṇḍilya-vidyā of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka belongs to the Vājasaneyins.
