In this way, because there is no difference, that which is considered to possess qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (manomaya) is the same;
likewise, through connection, it is so elsewhere, both in the internal self (adhyātma) and with respect to the deities (daivata).
The scripture itself shows that this very [Self] belongs to him;
and thus, the non-accumulation of vigor, as well as the abiding in heaven and other such prosperities, [are his].
In each respective instance, the manifestations pertaining to the deities are to be brought together;
and for the Tāṇḍins as well, there is the knowledge concerning Brahman designated as "Puruṣa."
Certain dharmas have also been stated by the followers of the Taittirīyaka branch.
Likewise, for one who knows thus, both the Puruṣa and the sacrifice are heard in the Śruti;
those duties which are prescribed elsewhere are to be combined here from the Taittirīya.
Or rather, when there is such a doubt as to whether [the rites] should not be combined at all,
there would be no combination for the others because they are not mentioned;
for the mantras are distinct in their purposes, such as piercing and so forth, in rites like malevolent magic (*ābhicāra*).
Therefore, those [details] employed in the Pravargya and other rites are not to be brought together [with the horse sacrifice].
Furthermore, there is the Tāṇḍin Śruti stating: "The horse has a black tail-hair; this is its form."
For the wise, the abandonment of mere evil deeds has been taught;
however, in the Kauṣītaki Śruti, both good and evil deeds [are mentioned].

It is described in that very same place: "When those who are dear kinsmen receive the merit of the two [who have died], and those who are not dear receive their evil, this is the loss for those who have passed away."
In some places, knowledge consists of the very distinction between those two [pleasure and pain] through likes and dislikes;
and since for someone there is the attainment [of results] through that very meditation, it is so stated in the Śruti.
In that case, there may or may not be a convergence of the "bringing forward" (upāyana);
for if it is argued that there is no convergence because of the absence of an explicit teaching (śrāvaṇā) regarding it there.
Likewise, if it is argued that there can be no synthesis because they are distinct sciences,
then this means of attainment would apply even to knowledge alone.
Because it is a supplement to that [preceding section], the statement regarding the "attaining" (upāyana) is a supplementary part of the injunction for its establishment;
furthermore, since there is no distinction regarding the kuśa grass, it is possible that it does not belong to that [specific context].
Just as in the supplementary statements "Audumbara stakes" and "Kuśa grasses," [the meaning is established],
so too are similarity and other factors demonstrated in cases such as the praise of a meter and the singing of the *upagāna*.
Thus has the method of ascent (*upāyana*) mentioned in other scriptural passages been explained.
For it is said: "Likewise for others, because there is no separation after death"; and "Because both are consistent according to the will of the wise, and likewise [in that manner]."
[Objection: There would indeed be the loss of good and evil deeds either in the next world or on the intermediate path.
[Response: But surely there would be the loss of good and evil deeds even in the next world.
In that case, that goal would be purposeless;
yet it is auspicious for its sake, because Brahman, being omnipresent, does not depend on a path for attainment.

Because the attainment of Brahman is impossible without an intermediate state of transition, and because the transition of the soul along with its subtle body occurs in both ways; otherwise, there would be contradiction.
Because the object characterized by that [light] is perceived, the meaning of "going" (gati) is consistent;
furthermore, all cognitions are considered to be constituent parts of the path of the gods.
There is indeed no fixed rule that one must hear [the teaching] only where it was heard; nor is there any contradiction with scripture in the statement, "Those who know thus... and so forth.
Both verbal testimony and inference are means for understanding the meaning already stated;
these two, the bright and the dark paths, are considered the eternal courses of the world.
By one [path] he goes to non-return; by the other, he exists again.
For those possessing an office, there is stability as long as the office lasts.
This is an exception to what was previously stated regarding merit and sin.
Having completed their office, these enter the supreme state;
all those [energies] whose intellects are subject to decay must be restrained everywhere.
It is considered [to be established] through generality and through its presence, like the attainment of that state;
the application of those [elements] established in the Udgātṛ-branch is stated by the Adhvaryu.
The offering of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) has been declared to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest;

here, while the subsidiaries (aṅgas) generally follow the lead of the primary rite (pradhāna), there is a deviation from that rule (atantratā). Even in those cases where specific details of the rite are joined with the syllable itself, this remains the case.
From this frequent mention [of the two birds] in the mantra beginning with "dvā suparṇā," and in the Atharva-śākhā mantra beginning with "ṛtaṃ pibantau," [it is established].
Indeed, it is said that the unity of knowledge becomes diversity when there is a distinction between the knowledges;
however, the unity of knowledge follows from the scriptural recitation (āmnāna) of that which is endowed with duality as being merely [one].
(150) There is identity of knowledge for one's own self as well, just as there is within the aggregate of beings.
If it is argued that, given this identity of knowledge, the mention of differences [in the Upaniṣads] would be inconsistent here, [we reply:]...
Furthermore, the unity of the knowledge [of Brahman] is not established merely by the lack of specific instruction, as in the case of "That thou art" (tat tvam asi);

for while there is a mutual exchange [of attributes], other qualities— such as "Being, Consciousness, and Infinite" (satya-jñānānantādi)— are indeed distinguished and then again combined within that same single [Brahman].
In that regard, through the equality of the sense-bases (āyatana),
the wise know that there is a single unification of desires both elsewhere than in desire and therein.
In the rite called Vaiśvānara, there should be no omission [of food] due to respect,
because of the scriptural statement "whatever cooked food is present" and the injunction regarding what has been set forth.
If there were an omission of food at the meal, there would likewise be an omission of the Prāṇāgnihotra.
In the case of a ritual, there would clearly be no restriction regarding the knowledge of its constituent parts;
for, as seen from Vedic statements, the fruit of the rite would exist independently [of such knowledge].
It is clear that there is no obstruction whatsoever to the accomplishment of the fruit of action;
this is stated [in the case of meditations on attributes] just as in the case of the primary [meditation], but in the meditation on the Saṃvarga, it is stated again [differently].
On account of the abundance of indicative marks, that [conclusion] is indeed stronger; this is also clear.
The previous alternative would follow from the context, as in the case of the mental [sacrifice], which is an action.
Moreover, because of the extended application (atideśa), it is declared that this is indeed knowledge and not a subsidiary to ritual action;
for it is further clearly determined by the statement, "He is built of that very knowledge" (tad-vidyā-cita eva).
Moreover, because direct perception is stronger than scripture and the like, there is no sublation;
for here, due to the [mention of] adjuncts and so forth, it is like the distinctness of other cognitions.
And [the status of being a subsidiary] is observed in the case of the Rājasūya and other rites; this has been stated in the Pūrvatantra:
"Because of its similarity to the mental cup-offering (mānasagraha), it is not accepted as a subsidiary of the sacrifice."
Because the purpose of the human agent is perceived, just as fire is said to be death;
for instance, by the mantra beginning with "asau vāva," the world is described as having the nature of fire.
Furthermore, by that subsequent [word], the nature of the word is indicated;
however, due to its abundance, it is a subordinate element and not a constituent part of the ritual action.
Therefore, the nature of the fire-altars built of mind and so forth is indeed established as being of the nature of nescience (avidyā);
for here, a self distinct from the body is clearly demonstrated.
In this regard, some say that consciousness and the like, which are indeed accepted [as real],
exist as attributes of the self internally within the body, and externally as well.
Therefore, those qualities such as consciousness and so forth must belong to the body;
thus, when it was concluded that "the body is the self," the author of the Sūtras stated:
But the negative concomitance [of the self] with the body is established because [the self] does not exist when that [body] is absent, just like perception;
therefore, it is clearly proven that the self is to be known as distinct from the body.
These [mantras], however, are not bound to the limbs [of the sacrifice] with respect to each Veda;
rather, they would apply across the various recensions (śākhās) because there is no distinction made in the scripture.
Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and the like;
for the meditation upon the entire plenitude, even when located in another recensional branch, is indeed authoritative.
It is declared that [the meditation] is endowed with all its constituent parts, like a ritual sacrifice;
for this very Śruti indeed demonstrates its superiority.
The meditations there are indeed distinct, due to the difference in words and other factors.
And because the fruit is not distinct, an option is appropriate here;
for indeed, those rites performed for specific desires may be combined according to one's wish, or perhaps they may not.
Or, due to the absence of the aforementioned reason, because it is connected with the performance of one's own will,
the meditation— whether bound to the limbs [of the sacrifice] or not— is to be combined.
When the categories (padārtha) based on those [six] substrates are thus combined, the suffixes (*pratyaya*) based upon them likewise follow; and it should be so according to the usage of the learned.
And because of the collective inclusion there, as well as the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities,
there is no "being according to the substrate," nor is there the absence of that nature, because of the lack of scriptural statement to that effect.
Furthermore, because conditions for coexistence are observed in both sight and hearing,
it has been explained at length that for this reason as well, [the order] may be according to one's desire.
The Fourth Quarter.
The fact that the statement arising from Vedānta is the sole cause for the human goal,
as well as its various auxiliary factors, are now being examined by me.
For the goal of human life is indeed accomplished through the higher knowledge produced by Vedānta;
this is what the teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains, based on the scriptural statement, "He crosses over."

Furthermore, because the self is subordinate to the ritual action by virtue of being its agent, knowledge is likewise a refinement of the agent, like the inspection of the clarified butter; such is the scriptural testimony.
Just as the statement "when he anoints [his eyes]" is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) concerning the eye itself, so too,
because we observe traditional practice (*ācāra*), knowledge is a subsidiary part of ritual action; this is also established by scripture (*śruti*).
It is certain that knowledge, because it is undertaken together [with ritual action], is an auxiliary part of ritual action.
For those possessing knowledge, according to the injunctions regarding ritual action, knowledge is declared to be an auxiliary to action;

because of the restriction of the lifespan and because of its application to action along with its constituent parts, knowledge is indeed an auxiliary to action. However, knowledge possesses independence as well.
Furthermore, because there is no [fixed] time for the attainment of the fruit,
and because it would follow that the practice of knowledge would be abandoned altogether,
it is stated here that knowledge is not the cause of the human goal.
Because of the teaching that the soul is the predominant factor, the self is the non-agent with respect to action;
yet it is not merely a refinement of knowledge, for its fruit is likewise heard [in scripture].
The Śruti demonstrates that it is appropriate for this to be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda):
"He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge."
That is the opinion of Bādarāyaṇa, for it is indeed more logical;
for the scriptural injunction regarding ritual action is equal [in its application] as a subsidiary element of knowledge.
Nor does the propriety of conduct alone establish that it is an auxiliary to ritual action;
for that [conduct] is not universal, as evidenced by such scriptural passages as "by knowledge" (vidyayā).

Wherever the objects of action require greater vigor, there the science of ritual auxiliaries (*karmāṅgavidyā*) applies; whereas that science which leads to a different result is [the science of] knowledge (*vidyā*).
And because liberation is the sole purpose [of the Vedas], it is clear that [the study of grammar] is not an auxiliary part thereof;
thus it has been described [in the Mīmāṃsāsūtra] as "the undertaking together [is established] from the words and so forth."
When it is said, "And a hundred is the sacrificial fee," it is distributed among the officiating priests;
in the same way, the distribution in this case is fully described.

In the passage beginning with "having studied [the Veda] from the teacher's family," the qualification for ritual action is stated to arise from mere study alone; it certainly does not pertain to one who possesses knowledge.
Since the injunction for study prescribes it as something to be seen, the understanding of the meaning is also a necessary cause;
therefore, eligibility belongs to a person possessing knowledge, and not otherwise.
It is true that the understanding of ritual action is not an auxiliary limb for the understanding of Brahman;
for the knowledge of one sacrifice does not depend upon another sacrifice.
Such [knowledge] is not a constituent part of action, but rather the means for understanding action;
this is established by such scriptural authorities as "Performing actions here indeed... and so forth.
Action common to those possessing knowledge is to be performed merely as such;
it is designated by the word "action" (karman) without distinction, and not specifically that which is performed for desire (kāmya).
Or, if there is the sacrifice of action (karmayajña) and so forth, it may be intended for the sake of praise or for approval.
The fact that knowledge is a cause for the goals of human life is not denied,
because in the subsequent statement, its status as a cause for the fruit is described.
Some [hold that knowledge arises] through the performance of one's own will, while others [say it arises] through the suppression [of the senses];
however, in the case of those in the higher stages of life (āśramas) who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), it is clearly heard in the scriptures that knowledge alone [is the cause].
But those great-souled ones have no desire-driven actions;
therefore, knowledge is not an auxiliary to action—so indeed the Śruti declares.
From that arise the aggregates of Dharma: sacrifice, study, and likewise giving.
The first is austerity itself; the second is the life of celibacy.
In the third [case], he excessively degrades both himself and his teacher.
For it is heard in the Śruti that "all these worlds belong to those who possess merit," and it is likewise shown that "one who is established in Brahman attains immortality."
The duties prescribed for one's own stage of life (āśrama) regarding the retention of vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), as well as those performed and proclaimed in the Vedas, have been fulfilled;
therefore, the doctrine of the Vīraśaivas is heard to be most worthy of honor.
Jaimini likewise [rejects] the grasping [of such views], stating "because there is no injunction";
for the Vedas themselves, beginning with the words "He is a slayer of heroes," indeed censure him.
Furthermore, the sage Bādarāyaṇa considers that the other stages of life must be practiced just like the householder's stage, because of the scriptural texts regarding their equality.
Or rather, this is an injunction, like the injunction regarding the holding [of the staff] in the case of the text "he should stand";
just as an injunction is resorted to there, so too an injunction is proclaimed here.
Gautama also declared that there is only one stage of life (aikāśramya) in his own dharma-code,
and likewise the sage Bodhāyana in the Prahlāda-hāda and other discourses.
Likewise, he also recites the invisibility of other stages of life [in the verse]:
"How [could one go] from the house or from the forest?"—which is established even by direct perception.
Āpastamba and others state: "One may go forth into homelessness while still remaining a student;
moreover, some even declare that there is an option regarding the stages of life (āśramas)."

For this very reason, the absence of the conduct of the [four] stages of life (āśrama) and many duties pertaining to the state beyond the stages (atyāśramīya) shine forth in the Vīraśaiva tradition within the Āgamas.
p.
156) Those very [practices] were perceived by the seers (*ṛṣi*) and fashioned into their respective duties;
for this reason also, O Hero, the conduct of the Śivas is superior to the Vedic.
Therefore, I have previously stated that the bondage of actions arises again,
and that liberation is attained through the knowledge of Brahman and not otherwise.
"Without knowledge, which is like fire for cooking, liberation is not accomplished"—
this has been stated by us alone, and likewise in the Agamas and Saṃhitās.
They say that knowledge possesses such power that it does not become subordinate to ritual actions;
for non-duality is not something to be produced, even in the performance of religious duties.
Therefore, they clearly say that the *liṅga* is the "immortal wood" (*kāṣṭha*) for those who possess knowledge of the eight enclosures and follow the five modes of conduct.
Indeed, by virtue of its equality with the Udgītha-vidyā, it attains power;
thus, the assembly of Vīraśaiva practitioners is said to be most powerful.
And having placed non-difference at the forefront, those dharmas are described within them;
for the Guru, the Linga, and the mobile [deity]—this triad is indeed one and the same.
Therefore, they perform the foot-washing consecration upon the Śiva-liṅga with the vision of non-duality;
for one who perceives duality incurs sin.
But he whose mind is firmly attached to Śiva, to his conduct, and to the Guru,
is a possessor of realized knowledge, a knower of Vedānta, and one who has mastered the divisions of sacred scripture.
Those who, through the vision of duality, conceive of the mortality of the Guru and the Linga in other ways,
are indeed turned away from the knowledge of reality.
He who knows the non-difference between the Guru and the *carya*, as well as the difference between them and the *liṅga*— he alone is that wise one who becomes Nīlakaṇṭha.
Therefore, let this web of proofs remain awake within the Āgama of the *Ukiraṇa*;
it exists in full detail within your own Smṛtis and Purāṇas.

If it be argued that this is merely a eulogy because it is based on [a prior injunction], we say no; for it is not so, because of its novelty (*apūrvatva*). Therefore, the meditation on the *udgītha* is indeed taught as having the highest purpose.
If it is argued that the scriptural accounts of narratives have as their purpose mere worldly diversion (*pāriplava*), [we reply:
because they are specified [as such], the scripture itself declares that the *pāriplava* consists precisely of these [narratives].
"This [scripture] does not have a wandering meaning; this is perfectly and well-determined.
Furthermore, because it is composed as a single connected discourse, there are likewise narrative accounts (ākhyāyikās).
For this very reason, it is said in the Āgamas: 'These are narrative accounts.'"
Consequently, there arose a clear conformity with the Nigamas and Āgamas;
now, however, the question is considered whether this new Vidyā is dependent upon ritual action (karman).
If it is argued that knowledge alone would be the cause of the human goal,
without requiring ritual action such as fire and fuel, listen to this.
And although it is stated in the Vedas that sacrifices and other rites require all [preparations] like a horse,
nevertheless, for one who is endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, such [rites] are likewise required.
Because of the scriptural statement, "Therefore, self-restraint and so forth [are required] as auxiliary parts of knowledge," and because they must necessarily be practiced accordingly,
it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that knowledge indeed depends upon ritual action.

It is heard in the *Chāndogya* [Upaniṣad], in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), in the passage beginning "One who knows thus" (*evaṃvid*) and so forth, that "food indeed does not perish" (*na ha vai... anaśanam*). Furthermore, [it is stated] that "nothing whatsoever remains un-eaten."
The meaning expressed is that everything becomes edible for him;
is this permission to eat all food stated because he is like a child?

Is it for the purpose of praising the ancillary part of knowledge, or is it mentioned again for some other reason? What, then, is the prima facie view? For now, it is established that this is an injunction.
Instruction is said to be that which brings about a distinction in right conduct;
for this very reason, it is likewise [effective] through the proximity of the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā).
If that were a constituent part [of the practice], no restriction would be prescribed in the form of abstention;
for if it were intended merely for the sake of distinguishing between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, it would result in a contradiction of the scriptures.
"Because sublation is established through the manifestation of the general and the particular.
This being the position reached, we say: "In accordance with the path of reality."
In this context, no such permission for all food whatsoever is prescribed;
nor is it appropriate to assume a distinction [between types of food] based on the Vedic scripture.
For here, because it prescribes an impossible object, the limit is set by "his own" and so forth;
having stated that food belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in that same way,
the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* scripture says, "He who knows thus does not eat non-food."
For it is possible to consume food with its limits, such as horses and so forth;
however, it is [only] possible to contemplate that "all this is the food of the vital breath."
Therefore, this [passage] here is indeed for the purpose of praising the knowledge of the fire of prāṇa.
159) The rule permitting the consumption of all food is a provisional injunction; the definitive conclusion is that this is not so.
However, in an extreme emergency, everything may indeed be eaten.
Therefore, the Vedic revelation stating that "when there is purity of food, there is purity of the being," and so forth, is not contradicted; moreover, it is likewise recorded in the Smṛti.
In many instances, there is no distinction whatsoever between the learned and the unlearned:
"When one's life is at stake, he may eat whatever food comes from wherever it may be."
He is not smeared by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
therefore, sound does not prohibit the exercise of one's own will.
Because it is prescribed, the action enjoined for the stages of life is the sole means to liberation;
furthermore, by acting as a cooperative factor, it serves as the sole cause for the human goal.
Because the statement "There is no other path" negates any alternative way,
the duties belonging to those beyond the [four] stages of life (atyāśramin) are proclaimed within Vīraśaiva.
It is certain that their status as auxiliary branches of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) has been declared and not otherwise;
it is certain that they alone, because they possess both characteristics, are so in every respect.
Because it is heard that one who is endowed with the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth cannot be overcome by the afflictions (*kleśa*);
furthermore, it is also recorded in tradition that [the Buddha] saw such a person even in the interval [between lives].
Furthermore, a special favor may arise from the ritual procedure;
however, one who possesses knowledge shall achieve perfection through recitation alone—of this there is no doubt.
One who acts otherwise or does not act at all is called a friend or a knower;
however, the worship of the Liṅga is superior to that, for it is the sole means to liberation.
Nor is even an authorized ritual act [a cause of downfall], because it can be inferred from the state of falling.
And because that [prohibition] is not applicable, everything stated therein is inconsistent;
for some maintain that the prefix *upa-* [in *upavāsa*] refers to the consumption of honey and meat, as in the case of the term *upabhukta*.
The violation of a vow is likewise said to be a lack of refinement;
it is excluded from both perspectives here, according to both the Smṛti and traditional practice.
Ātreya, moreover, maintains that the fruit belongs to the owner [of the sacrifice], because of the scriptural statement:
"Thus one meditates upon the fivefold Sāman with regard to rain."
Āuḍulomi maintains that it is the office of the officiating priest (ārṭvijya), because that is what is purchased;
and from the Śruti, "Whatever [desire] he may have," it follows that the fruit belongs to the sacrificer.
Furthermore, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, there is an injunction for additional auxiliary practices;
specifically, through their distinct classification, there is an injunction for scholarship (pāṇḍitya), childhood (bālya), and silence (mauna).
The third [meditation] belongs to one who possesses that [quality], as in the case of the injunctions and so forth;
however, because it exists in its entirety [only] in the householder, its application is stated to be restricted to him.
From instruction, silence is indeed spoken of, and it is clear that this applies to others as well;
for just as a child follows along clearly without manifesting [its understanding], so too is it here.
If there were no obstruction to what has been commenced, that [result] would be seen; however, since there is an obstruction, the result is experienced either in this life or in the next.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that the fruit may be obtained here or in the hereafter.
For it was previously established whether or not Brahman possesses liberation as its fruit;
first, the position that it does not was reached even by those who know the knowledge of Brahman.
And because [the states] of Vāmadeva and others were seen to persist even in another birth, such being the case, we reply: "Because that state is determined."
By the scriptural statement "for him, for so long," and also by "then he shall attain [union]," liberation is described as occurring once the *prārabdha* karma has been exhausted.
And for Vāmadeva and others, it was by means of their very *prārabdha* karma.
Furthermore, since liberation occurs upon the exhaustion of the *prārabdha* karma through the undertaking of another body, there is no contradiction; this has been correctly established.
The duties taught in Vīraśaivism are indeed for those engaged in the knowledge of Brahman;
they are certainly not the "paśu-dharmas" (animal-like duties) which, though heard in scripture, yield only the fruits of desire.
This applies equally to both the Sāmarasya-liṅga and the Aṅga-liṅga.
For in this matter, authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇas) indeed extend throughout the Śaiva scriptures;
however, in the section concerning the means and ends of spiritual practice, they appear in the form of questions posed by the sages.
O best among those who know all things, tell me the true nature of bondage and liberation;
I shall explain bondage, liberation, and likewise the means [to them], so listen with reverence.
The individual soul (jīva) bound by the eightfold bondage beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti) is called "bound";
one liberated from that eightfold bondage of primordial nature and the rest is called "liberated."
The wise declare that liberation is the mastery over primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest.
When the bound soul is released, it is called the liberated soul.
Beyond primordial nature is the intellect (buddhi), and then the ego (ahaṃkāra), which consists of the [three] qualities (guṇas).
The wise know these eight, beginning with *prakṛti*, as the group of eight starting from *prakṛti* and ending with the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The body is said to be born from the eightfold *prakṛti*, and action is said to be born from the body.
Furthermore, from karma arises the body, and from that body arises karma again and again;
the body is to be known as threefold: gross, subtle, and causal.
The gross [body] is said to provide activity; the subtle [body] provides the enjoyment of the senses;
and the causal [body] exists for the sake of the self's experience, in accordance with the karma of the living being.
Through merits and demerits, and through actions consisting of pleasure and pain, one experiences their fruit;
therefore, bound by the rope of karma, the individual soul (jīva) is fettered again and again.
The three bodies are constantly whirled about by karmas like a wheel;
for the sake of stopping the rotation of the wheel, one should praise the Maker of the Wheel.
The great wheel begins with primordial nature (prakṛti), and Śiva is beyond that primordial nature;
for Maheśa, the creator of the wheel, is indeed beyond primordial nature.
Just as a living being drinks and then vomits saliva,
so indeed does Śiva remain, having brought Prakṛti and the other principles under his control.
Because everything has been brought under his control, he is remembered as Śiva;
for Śiva alone is omniscient, eternally perfect, and constant.
Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternal undiminished power, and infinite power— these are the sixfold mental sovereignty of Maheśvara, which the Veda knows.
Therefore, by the grace of Śiva, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest shall come under one's control;
for the sake of obtaining Śiva’s grace, one should worship Śiva alone.
How can there be worship for him who is free from desire and full?
An action performed for the sake of Śiva becomes a source of grace.
One should worship Śiva, intent upon the devotee at the Liṅga-bera,
with body, mind, speech, and even with wealth.
Through worship, indeed, Maheśa— the supreme Śiva within primordial nature—
truly bestows his grace, especially upon the worshipper.
Through the grace of Śiva, karma and the rest shall come under control in due order;
when everything from the commencement of karma up to primordial nature (prakṛti) has reached its final state, [liberation is attained].
Then, declared "liberated," he shines, delighting in his own self by the grace of the Supreme Lord; when the body of action has become subject [to him],
that residence indeed in the world of Śiva is called *sālokya*.
When one approaches Sāmba and that [state] alone has come under control,
that is declared to be "proximity" (sāmīpya) to Śiva himself, by his very grace.
Furthermore, when one's own ego has been brought under control through the grace of Śiva,
then there is identity with Śiva by means of the weapons and so forth, as well as by actions and other attributes.
Through the attainment of great faith, the intellect also comes under control;
for the intellect is the agent, while its natural state is said to be its similarity [to the object].
Furthermore, through great devotion, one's own nature will come under control;
then, the sovereignty of Śiva’s mind will be attained by oneself.
Having attained the sovereignty of Śiva, beginning with omniscience, one shines within one's own self;
those devoted to the Vedas and Āgamas call this "union" (sāyujya).
In this way, liberation shall come gradually through the worship of the *liṅga* and other such objects;
therefore, for the sake of Śiva’s grace, one should worship Śiva with ritual actions and the like.
The performance of auspicious rites, the practice of auspicious austerities, and the constant recitation of auspicious mantras.
Practicing the knowledge of Śiva and the meditation on Śiva more and more,
one should indeed pass the time until death with constant contemplation of Śiva.
"By worshipping Śiva with flowers such as the *satya* and others, one shall attain him.
Having heard all this, the sages spoke again.
O you of noble vows, tell me the injunction for the worship of Śiva at the liṅga and other sites;
I shall describe the sequence of the liṅgas, so listen with respect as it truly is.
That very first *liṅga* is the *praṇava*, which leads everywhere;
for it is the subtle form of the *praṇava*, indeed the partless (*niṣkala*) subtle form.
The gross liṅga is indeed with parts (sakala) and is called the five-syllabled mantra;
the worship and recitation of these two are declared to be the direct bestowers of liberation.
The Puruṣa, Prakṛti, and the many elemental signs— Śiva alone is the agent capable of describing them in detail, and no one else.
I shall declare to you the known signs of the transformations of the earth:
the self-existent linga is the first, and the bindu-linga is the second.
The fivefold [manifestation] consisting of the established, the moving, and the guru-liṅga was indeed present there for the sake of proximity,
as the divine sage was pleased by his ascetic penance.
The seed of Śarva, existing within the earth in the form of sound,
becomes manifest upon the ground like the sprout of a stationary plant.
They know him as Svayambhū because he was born of himself;
through the worship of his *liṅga*, knowledge increases spontaneously.
165) A pure *liṅga* marked with the *praṇava* and the *yantra*, drawn with one's own hand upon gold, a wooden board, the earth, or even on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Beginning with the mechanical linga (yantralinga), one should perform the rites of installation and invocation;
for the linga consists of the Bindu and Nāda, whether it be stationary or mobile.
For this indeed consists of cultivation; Śiva is the witness, there is no doubt.
As long as Śambhu is trusted therein, He bestows the fruit upon him.
In a yantra drawn with one's own hand, the deities are both stationary and artificial.
Having invoked Śambhu, one should worship him with the sixteen types of service;
one attains sovereignty for oneself, and through practice, wisdom shall arise.
Indeed, by the gods and the sages as well, for the sake of their own spiritual perfection,
that which was performed with mantras by their own hands upon the pure earth—

The supreme *liṅga* established through pure contemplation alone is called the *pauruṣa-liṅga*, and it is said to be "installed" (*pratiṣṭhita*). By constantly worshipping that *liṅga*, one shall attain human sovereignty.
That linga which has been fashioned by skill by great kings who are knowers of the Śaiva scriptures and possessors of great wealth, and which has been consecrated with mantras;
For that which is established as ordinary bestows ordinary sovereignty and enjoyment;
indeed, that which is powerful and eternal is called "Prākṛta" (the Ordinary).
The linga is the navel, as well as the tongue, the tip of the nose, and the crest-lock in sequence;
among the triangular regions beginning with the hips, the linga is the final one pertaining to the inner self.
p.
166) A mountain is declared to be *pauruṣa* (supernatural), while the surface of the earth is known as *prākṛta* (natural).
Trees and the like are to be understood as *pauruṣa*, whereas shrubs and the like are known as *prākṛta*.
The common sixty-day rice is to be known as natural, while the Śāli and wheat varieties are produced by human effort.

Theists declare that sovereignty consisting of the eightfold perfections such as *aṇimā* is the result of human effort (*pauruṣa*), whereas objects such as beautiful women and wealth are called "natural" (*prākṛta*).
First, among the mobile liṅgas, the rasa-liṅga is proclaimed;
the rasa-liṅga bestows the fruit of all desires upon Brāhmaṇas.
An auspicious liṅga made of jewels bestows great sovereignty upon Kṣatriyas;
a liṅga made of gold, however, bestows the status of a great lord of wealth upon Vaiśyas.
They know that a stone liṅga bestows great sovereignty upon Śūdras;
a crystal Bāṇaliṅga, however, grants all desires to everyone.
In the absence of one's own [liṅga], the use of another's for worship is not forbidden;
however, for women, an earthen liṅga is prescribed, especially for those whose husbands are living,
and for widows who have renounced worldly desires, it is the sequence of the mercury-liṅga (rasaliṅga) and so forth.
Whether in childhood, youth, or even old age, O observers of noble vows,
a pure crystal liṅga bestows all enjoyments upon women.
For those engaged in practice, the worship of the *pīṭha* bestows all desired objects on earth;
one who has entered the path should perform the entire worship using only the vessel.
At the conclusion of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should offer the food offering (*naivedya*) consisting of *śāli* rice.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should place the *liṅga* in a pure casket in a separate room. For those who have completed the ritual worship with their hands, one should offer one's own food.
For those who have withdrawn from external activity, the supreme, subtle *liṅga* alone is distinguished as superior.
One should perform worship with sacred ash and offer sacred ash as the oblation;
having performed the worship, one should then always carry that *liṅga* upon one's head.
The threefold manifestation (vibhūti) is declared by the worlds, the Vedas, and Śiva-Agni;
one should employ the ash of the world-fire for the purpose of purifying substances.
Of objects made of clay, wood, or metal; likewise of grains and other [items];
of sesame seeds and the like, as well as liquids, and similarly of garments and so forth.
Likewise, purification by means of ashes is prescribed for things that have been kept overnight;
purification by means of ashes is also prescribed for things defiled by dogs and the like.
He should apply water, dry ash, or ashes produced from the Vedic fire as appropriate;
likewise, he should wear that ash at the conclusion of those rites.
The action produced by mantra and ritual assumes the form of ashes in the fire;
by wearing those ashes, the twice-born man should internalize that karma within his own self.
One should cause wood from the *bilva* tree to burn with one's own *aghora* mantra;
this is renowned as the "Śiva-fire," and what is burnt by it is born of the Śiva-fire.
First, one should take the dung of a tawny cow, or exclusively that of a cow,
or else [the leaves] of the *śamī*, *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, *vaṭa*, *āragvadha*, and *bilvaka* trees.
One should burn purified [wood] with the Śiva-fire; that indeed is the ash born from the Śiva-fire.
Or, reciting the Śiva-mantra, one may burn pieces of wood in a fire of darbha grass.
Having thoroughly cleansed it with a cloth, one should place it in a new vessel;
for it is considered that [the substance] should be collected for the sake of its brilliance, and it is also worshipped.
The meaning of the word *bhasman* (ashes) is indeed Śiva; for in this way, he previously acted so that a king takes only the essence from a subject, which is the tax (*kara*).
Just as humans, having burned down crops and the like, resort indeed to their essence;
and just as the digestive fire [consumes] various and abundant kinds of food.
Just as one's own body withers after consuming the very essence of its essences,
so too does that Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who is the creator of the phenomenal world.
Having burned away the essence of the phenomenal world that was to be presided over by him, Śiva took hold of it; having burned the phenomenal world, he cast its ashes upon his own self.
Under the pretext of smearing himself with ashes, he seized the essence of the world;
indeed, he placed his own jewels within his hair and upon his body.
The hair [is formed] by the essence of space, the face by the essence of air,
the heart by the essence of fire, the waist by the essence of water,
and the knee by the essence of earth; in that same way, every limb is likewise [constituted].
The Tripuṇḍra is the very essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Rudras;
likewise, Maheśvara [is present] at the edge of the forehead in the form of a Tilaka.
Through its increase, he indeed considers all this as "I" myself;
by this very [power], the *Prapañcasāra*, the essence of all things, has been brought under control.
Therefore, because there is no one who can bring him under control, he is remembered as Śiva.
Just as one who harms all wild animals is called a "wild-animal-harmer," yet for him there is no animal to harm, he is therefore called a "lion."
Beyond peace, the syllable *i* is remembered as the blissful Puruṣa;
the syllable *va* is Śakti, the nectar, and their union is called Śiva. (p. 169)
Therefore, having made one's own self Śiva, one should worship Śiva;
for that reason, one should first apply the holy ash (uddhūlana) and thereafter wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
For at the time of worship, that which is with water is for purification, while that which is without water is for the purpose [of the rite];
whether by day or by night, and whether it be a woman or even a man.

For the purpose of worship, one should apply wet ashes as the *tripuṇḍra* mark itself. He who performs worship after applying the *tripuṇḍra* with wet ashes certainly attains the full fruit of the worship of Śiva, including all its constituent parts.
Indeed, by wearing the sacred ash with the Śiva-mantra, one becomes a true transcendent ascetic (atyāśramī);
he is proclaimed a "Śiva-ascetic" (śivāśramī) because Śiva alone is his supreme goal.
For one who is solely devoted to the vow of Śiva, there is neither impurity nor birth-impurity;
he should always wear a white ash mark upon the forehead.

The etymological analysis of the word *guru* is declared to be: "one who obstructs the qualities" (*guṇān rundhe*), characterized solely by devotion to Śiva, whether [bestowed] from one's own hand or from the hand of a teacher.
He obstructs and casts aside the qualities such as rajas along with their modifications;
having taken refuge in the form of the Guru, he is the Supreme Śiva who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta).
Because he first dispels the three qualities (guṇas) and awakens one to Śiva,
he is called the Guru of those disciples who place their trust in him.
Therefore, O wise ones, the body of the Guru is indeed the Linga of the Guru;
the worship of the Guru-Linga consists in service to the Guru.
One makes it heard through service performed with body, mind, and speech;
that which was previously spoken by the guru, whether it be possible or indeed impossible [to carry out].
For one whose soul is purified indeed acts [righteously] even at the cost of his life-breaths and even his wealth.
Therefore, one who is fit for the Vaiśasana [initiation] is called a disciple;
having given everything, including his body and possessions, to the Guru, he becomes a true disciple.
Having first offered the finest portion of the cooked food, the disciple should eat with the permission of the Guru;
for it is said that a disciple is called "son" (putra) by virtue of his connection to discipleship (śiṣyatva).
Having indeed emitted the white mantra-semen from the tongue-linga into the ear-womb,
the son thus born is a "mantra-son" (mantrotpanna) who should honor his father as his guru.
The biological father, the progenitor, indeed causes his son to sink into the cycle of existence;
but the teacher who provides awakening is the true father who delivers one from saṃsāra.
Having understood the difference between the two,
one should honor the father with service to his limbs as well as with wealth and other things acquired by oneself.
From the feet up to the hair, one should indeed honor the other signs of the Guru by means of wealth such as sandals and so forth,
and by acts such as clasping his feet.
One should worship with ritual bathing, consecration, food offerings, and meals;
indeed, the worship of the Guru is itself the worship of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
All that remains from the Guru becomes a means for purifying the self;
the remnant of the Guru is the leavings of Śiva—whether it be water, food, or even waterless [substances].
O twice-born ones, for disciples who are devotees of Śiva,
that which is to be accepted or consumed becomes like that of a thief if it is devoid of the permission of the guru and other such requirements.
A wise person should indeed accept as a teacher even one who is superior to their current teacher, provided that teacher is a knower of distinctions;
for liberation from ignorance is the goal to be accomplished, and only a knower of distinctions is a liberator.
Therefore, having specifically learned the knowledge of ritual action from the mouth of the Guru,
one should perform everything for the sake of the perfection of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
For knowledge of ritual action obtained through service to the guru leads indeed to happiness;
however, that which is obtained by other means is said to be futile, and it may result in inauspiciousness.
Furthermore, I shall speak again of the beneficial action that must be performed by one who desires auspiciousness:
a wise person should pray for nothing other than auspiciousness through the meditation on Śiva.
The gods, who fully uphold the command of Śiva, bestow everything;
one should worship with ritual action those gods who uphold Śiva’s command for the sake of enjoyment.
And at the outset, the pacification of obstacles must be performed for the completion of the ritual action;
indeed, an action performed without obstacles and with all its parts complete shall become fruitful.
Therefore, at the beginning of every rite, one should worship Gaṇanātha;
however, at the conclusion of the rite for Śiva, one should perform the great consecration and the offering of food.
One should liberate the devotees of Śiva by means of a grand feast;
thereafter, one should offer salutations to Śiva one hundred and eight times with the mantra.
One may have a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even ten million [recitations] performed by the wise;
through this sacrifice consisting of prostrations, the Supreme Lord shall be pleased.
"Projected by the intellect as my own nature, it does not exist in the void of the Supreme Consciousness;
yet, thinking 'it burns me,' that [delusion] ceases when You are seen."
Salutations indeed to my own body; salutations, O Lord, you are the Great One.
My own nature is certainly not empty; I am now your servant.
One should perform the self-sacrifice and prostration as is appropriate;
thereafter, one should perform one thousand and eight circumambulations.
One should cause ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million circumambulations to be performed by devotees of Śiva.
By circumambulating Śiva, every sin is destroyed in an instant.
For disease is indeed the root of suffering, and sin is the root of disease.
For it is Dharma alone that is declared to be the remover of evils.
Dharma performed for the sake of Śiva is capable of removing sins;
it is declared that circumambulation is the foremost among the religious duties dedicated to Śiva.
Indeed, by means of ritual action, the *praṇava* in the form of recitation is circumambulated;
birth and death, this pair, is declared to be the wheel of *māyā*.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is indeed the wheel of Śiva’s Māyā;
through its emergence, birth is attained, and through its entry, there is the offering of one's own self.
Birth and death are a pair bestowed by the Māyā of Śiva;
this pair, bestowed by the Māyā of Śiva, shall never again partake of its own true nature.
As long as the soul is dependent upon the three bodies, it is called "bound";
the mastery over the three bodies is called "liberation" by the wise.
For Śiva, the supreme cause, is indeed the director of the wheel of Māyā;
the pair [of Śakti and Puruṣa] is offered to Śiva’s Māyā, and Śiva alone wipes it away.
One should offer the pair fashioned by Śiva back into that very [Śiva];
the wise should know that circumambulation and prostration are extremely dear to Śiva.
Circumambulation and prostration to Śiva, the Supreme Self,
as well as worship performed with the sixteen types of offerings, bestow their fruit.
Indeed, there is no sin on this earth that cannot be destroyed by circumambulation;
therefore, one should destroy all evil through circumambulation alone.
By circumambulating Śiva alone, one shall accomplish all desired goals.

Devoted to the worship of Śiva, observing supreme silence, and endowed with virtues such as truthfulness, one should practice each of the following: ritual action, austerity, recitation, knowledge, and meditation.
Sovereignty, a divine body, knowledge that brings about the destruction of ignorance,
and proximity to Śiva— such indeed shall be the fruit of the ritual actions and other practices.
The instrument does not proceed toward the fruit because of the abandonment of that darkness;
by the complete wiping away of birth, and through the non-conceit of the intellect,
and likewise through meditative reflection— not "that"— such shall be the meaning of these [terms] in sequence.

A devotee of Śiva should perform his rites and other duties according to his physical capacity, according to the time, according to his body, according to his wealth, and according to what is appropriate.
A wise person should dwell in a sacred place (śivasthala) by means of acquiring wealth earned through righteous means—
a place free from injury to living beings and devoid of excessive hardship.
They know that food consecrated by the five-syllable mantra is easily digested;
or else, for one who is poor, even alms-food shall become a giver of knowledge.
The food obtained as alms by a devotee of Śiva increases devotion to Śiva;
they say that the alms-food of a Śiva-yogin is the very essence of Śambhu.
By whatever means possible and wherever on earth he may be,
one who has attained perfection should always eat his food in silence and must not disclose the secret.
Indeed, Śiva alone reveals the greatness of Śiva to his devotees;
for Śiva alone knows the secret of the Śiva-tattva, and no one else.
A devotee of Śiva should dwell eternally taking refuge in the Śivaliṅga;
by relying upon the Sthāṇuliṅga, one becomes a radiant Sthāṇu. Perform the worship of the Liṅga, and you will certainly become perfect in due course.
Everything that was previously proclaimed by Vyāsa in detail, and all that was heard by me in the past— the supreme means and the goal— has now been told in brief.
Through these and many other proofs, this Vīraśaiva practice alone is the primary means of realization; all others are secondary means.
Therefore, O Vyāsa, a wise person should extend their intellect toward the Vīraśaiva doctrine;
the practice of Vīraśaivism is clearly elucidated here according to its essential purport.

Thus ends the third instruction in the *Kriyāsāra*, within the *Nigamāgamasārasaṃgraha* composed by Nīlakaṇṭha, who is proficient in the one hundred and one stages of the secret doctrine of the glorious Viśiṣṭādvaita Siddhānta.
May there be prosperity.
The investigation of the means of knowledge was established in the third chapter;
now, in this fourth chapter on instruction, I shall conduct an investigation into the results.
175) And by how many topics does the author of the Sūtras follow there that which remains as a supplement to the means [of knowledge], wherein the Śruti of the knower of Brahman is present?
Regarding the passage beginning with "he crosses" and so forth, which teaches [the means] as a means to liberation:
does the cognition produce its effect once, or repeatedly? And what is the case here?
It is established that the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by performing [the rite] once;
likewise, this remains true even when the repetition is not explicitly heard in the text.
If [the practice] were performed only that many times, it would not constitute the meaning of the scripture;
for the repetition of the mental realization must be performed repeatedly, as indicated by the instruction.
"It is to be heard from the words of the Vedas, reflected upon through reasoning,
and meditated upon as such"— through such repeated instruction,
this repetition is indicated again by many scriptural passages.

"One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self' (ātmeti), and one should also contemplate the Lord (dhyāyīteśānam). Regarding these two injunctions—meditation (*upāsti*) and contemplation (*dhyāna*)—there must be repetition again and again, because it is precisely a qualified cognition that is the subject under discussion. Thus it is indeed.
The etymological derivation of the words *vid* and *upāsya* has been explained by those learned in the scriptures who perceive the ultimate truth,
through their application in the Vedānta treatises.

The practical application is seen somewhere; the commencement is recorded as being according to the prescribed rule, and the conclusion is by means of worship, as stated in the Śruti: "He who knows that."
In passages such as "The deity whom you worship," the sequence begins with the term *upāsana* (meditation),
while the conclusion is made with the term *vid* (to know), as in the Śruti statement, "The mind is Brahman."
In such passages as "He who knows thus," the word "veda" (knows) signifies meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
Therefore, this is also the case in the Śruti passage beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."
The accomplishment of the repetition of the cognitive state has indeed been correctly undertaken;
now hear that sign which indicates the repetition of the cognitive state.

Furthermore, you should turn back the knowledge of the *udgītha* currently under discussion and the statement "you are the rays," by indicating the repetition of the cognitive realization (*pratyaya*).
In this regard, this very conclusion brings forth Vīraśaivism:
from the statement of the Immortal One, that [the soul] is held within the region of the heart by means of the *liṅga*.
By the statement "You are the rays," and by the *Jyotiścaraṇa* Sūtra,
the sign of light (*jyotiliṅga*) was bestowed by the Guru, whose self is of the nature of equanimity.
Having seen it again and again every day, and having meditated upon it repeatedly,
[one realizes] the state of essential identity (sāmarasya) between the Liṅga and the Gaṇi, which is the nature of the fruit.
Likewise, in the Śruti it is said that "the knower of Brahman attains [it]," where the term "knower" (vid) is used as an indicative mark;
for it is established that "knowing" (vedana) means the wearing of the name-mark (nāma-liṅga).
And in the sūtra "āvṛttiḥ," this meaning shall become clear:
that in the phrase "namo 'tmane," there is also the sense of "to the one who possesses the marks of the Self."
"Salutation to Jvala," and so forth,
as well as "to the blazing Liṅga," in accordance with the intended meaning declared in the *Jyotiścaraṇa* Sūtra.
For since the term "liṅga" has been repeatedly taught in reference to the lotus of the heart,
it should be worn, meditated upon, and worshipped day and night by those seeking liberation.
177) However, the activity of vision is said to belong to the very *liṅga* that has been sustained;
and this vision occurs through the mind and with the stainless eye.
Because of the Vedic declaration that "it pervades all this,

both within and without," there is indeed a fruit through a person who is equal in both the external and internal; otherwise, a discrepancy between the external and the internal leads to the destruction of the fruit.
Therefore, the wise man should pray for inner and outer equality;
in Vīraśaiva, everything proclaimed by the Vedas is fully realized.
But for those other than Vīraśaivas, there is indeed no conformity with the Vedas;
[for they hold that] the Puruṣa is only the size of a thumb, adorned within the space of the heart.
The form of the *liṅga* is indeed light, Śiva himself, characterized by truth and other such qualities;
even the *liṅga* worn externally—herein lies the equality between these two.
The wearing of an external or internal liṅga is not at all possible for men without the internal wearing of the liṅga; therefore, one should wear the liṅga within the lotus of the heart.
An external mark (liṅga) is declared to be that which is suitable for the external senses, while an internal mark is said to be that which is suitable for the internal senses;
this is in accordance with the general reading in the Śruti and the Vedāntasāra.
That sign does not otherwise apply to those who do not manifest it externally;
likewise, the introduction and conclusion, as well as the revealed scripture (*śruti*) and the secret doctrine (*rahasyaka*),
[are established] out of fear that many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) might fall into confusion.
The repetition of the *liṅga* in accordance with such scriptural injunctions is what is meant by that term;
and this repetition consists in the uniformity of form toward the one who dwells within the lotus of the heart.
Clearly manifest externally within the *sajjikā*, shining forth in the form of a *liṅga*; and internally within the *daharākāśa*, shining forth in the form of a *liṅga*.
"Vision is said to be knowledge through the external [senses] and the internal eye;
thus it has been accepted by those desiring liberation that such a state of being must be cultivated."
In this sūtra, "He is known from the word alone," this very intended meaning is indeed to be understood according to the natural sense of the sūtra itself.
In this regard, the essential conclusion is as follows: those Vīraśaivas who seek liberation should rotate the Liṅga held within and without by means of the pair of eyes.
Because of the repeated utterance of the formula beginning with "Salutation to the Self" (ātmāya namaḥ),
and because of the indicative mark of her being established within the space of the heart in the form of a needle (sajjikā).
This repetition of conviction is established through the description of the two modes of perception by means of the external and internal eye,
according to the path taught in the Śaiva scriptures.
The Vedic scholars, however, accept [the existence of] the self and cause others to grasp it;
they speak of the meditation on Brahman as being both different from and non-different from the individual soul.
Does the part not eat there? What else is Brahman other than me?
Or rather, what is to be worshipped? "I am Brahman"—such is the meditation.

What, then, is the prima facie position? That "Now, what is that other than this [world]? and "Brahman" refer to different things, because they are described as distinct in the passage beginning with "The other within."
This being the case, we say: in the analysis of the meanings of words, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are described as being mutually distinct.
Moreover, even at the time of meditation, one should indeed meditate thus: "I am Brahman," because those ancient knowers of Brahman declared the Self to be Brahman.
One should know that "He is the Self," or likewise, "I am Brahman";
and the teacher [should instruct] in this way: "That thou art" (tat tvam asi).
"The Self is within all; the Self itself is indeed that"—thus they cause one to grasp [the object] through non-difference, and because of that non-difference, there is meditation upon it.
Also because of the censure of the view of difference in the Śruti, "Then [he is born] again in another womb," and because of the Śruti, "He thinks, 'That one is one and I am another; he knows.'"
One desiring the realization of the Self should not fix the notion of the Self upon symbols such as the sun;
for the auspicious Self, characterized by truth and other attributes, is not identical with those symbols.
And because one should contemplate [the world] as being of the nature of the womb (yoni) through its transformation from Brahman,
there is likewise non-difference of Brahman with respect to the symbols (pratīka), as well as the non-difference of those symbols from Brahman.

For this so-called "difference of self" is imagined through ignorance; even though there is no mutual difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the reflection (pratīka) of Brahman, it is still perceived as such.
Just as foam, waves, and so forth lack non-difference from one another,
even though they exist within the ocean which possesses non-difference [from them], there is nevertheless no mutual non-difference among them.
Therefore, the understanding that "Brahman is the creation because of its excellence," and so forth,
should likewise be applied to the Udgītha and other such elements within the sacrifices, as this is logically consistent.
But in the case of meditations connected with ritual acts, because of their arising from sitting,
this meditation— being bound to its auxiliary parts— is to be performed while seated.
Having likewise observed immobility from the Śruti, "He meditates,
as it were," the sages remember that meditation is indeed an ancillary limb [of knowledge].
Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place—
at whatever time and in whatever place one may indeed attain one-pointedness of mind— there [one should sit].
Because there is no mention of any distinction [in the scriptures], those seeking liberation must perform the repetition of meditative realization until death;
for the scripture does not permit one to stop in the interim.
Since it is seen that "he departs from this world according to his resolve" (yāvat-kratu),
that which remains as the third stage having been traversed is now being examined.
When that Brahman is attained, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is the non-clinging of future sin and the destruction of past evil.
As seen in such passages as "like a tuft of grass-stalk thrown into a fire," there is indeed the non-clinging and the destruction of other merit as well.
Because it is known that [the body] at the fall of the physical frame is the means for its bondage,
and because of the scriptural statement of non-separation, "his actions are exhausted," [it follows that there is no further rebirth].
Regarding the destruction of non-attachment [to karma] as previously explained in the prior section:
this applies only to those karmas whose effects have not yet begun, until the fall of the body;
for it is seen both in the scriptural text, "For him, [it lasts] only so long," and elsewhere.
The Agnihotra and other rites are for the sake of liberation alone, as is seen in the Śruti;
for it is heard in such Śruti passages as "He who knows this," which speaks of those who possess knowledge.
Indeed, there is no rite whatsoever, even among the obligatory ones like the Agnihotra, that is distinct from this.
181) For some, as well as for Bādarāyaṇa and Jaimini, it is thus:
"Whatever [is done] by knowledge," regarding the previously mentioned optional rites.
For merit and demerit that have not yet begun to bear fruit are destroyed through the power of knowledge;
however, merit and evil deeds whose effects have already begun are exhausted only after they have been experienced.
Having exhausted [the fruits of karma] through experience, the wise one attains the state of Brahmā.

First, he states the sequence of departure according to the scripture;
for from the Veda, which begins with the topic of departure, there arises the scriptural teaching concerning the process of dying.
By the statement beginning with "O Somya," the merging of speech alone into the mind is declared; and by the word "speech-and-mind" (*vāṅmanasī*), [the merging of both is indicated].
And for this reason, even when the activity of speech and mind has ceased upon seeing [an object],
one observes the continued operation of the collection of the other sense organs.
Speech first merges into the other sense organs;
there, the mind, together with the merged sense organs, merges into the vital breath (prāṇa).

For it is established in that very manner by the scripture stating "mind [merges] into breath," and by the statement "breath [merges] into heat," breath is declared to be merged into the presiding deity (adhyakṣa).
And that [self], conjoined with the vital breath (prāṇa), abides among the elements;
it should be understood as the "living one" (jīva). According to the scriptural statement, the vital breath [abides] in heat (tejas); this living self does not abide in the heat alone.
However, this matter has indeed been observed in many instances in the Śruti; moreover,
following the commencement with "non-remembrance" (asmṛti), it is identical for both cases.
Between the wise man and the ignorant man, the wise man is indeed superior;
for even without having practiced the austerity of immortality, the result for both is exactly the same.
The light that has arisen within exists as far as the attainment of Brahman,
because of the designation of *saṃsāra* and the Vedic scripture stating, "going from here.
That light which has arisen within is subtle in its dimension.
Likewise, as it emerges from perception, it is not perceived by those standing nearby;
this is because its gross body has been destroyed through the very process of subtle speech.
And by such signs as burning and so forth, it is not at all destroyed;
for precisely because of this logical possibility, there would indeed be warmth in the body. For one who is to live will be warm, while one who is to die will become cold.
Therefore, when one is about to depart from life, the vital breaths do not indeed depart;
rather, it is stated that they remain together with him—this is the meaning expressed.
And thus, the departure from the body of one who still possesses vital breath is indeed recorded; moreover, the destiny of the wise man is described by the illustrious ones in the Mahābhārata:
"But Śuka, having attained a speed swifter than the wind, traveled through the atmosphere."
Having displayed his own power, he became one with all beings;
for him who had become the self of all beings, all beings were seen correctly as he beheld them.

"He is produced by that very [Self]," because of that scriptural statement in the Chāndogya; and "Now, the liberated one," because of the passage beginning with "the Self which... and so forth.

for, though seen as non-differentiated, its establishment occurs precisely through differentiation.

He is liberated and has no other lord, because of the scriptural statement that he possesses true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatā*). Furthermore, he [creates] merely by his will (*saṃkalpāt eva*), because of the scriptural mention of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛ-loka*) and so forth.
Thus the teacher Bādarāyaṇa declares the absence of a body,
also because of the meditation on the alternatives such as "he becomes singlefold" and so forth.
The wise Jaimini maintains that the body exists [after death] just like the mind,
because both types of characteristics are observed in the case of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, which is both an *ahīna* and a *sattra*.
Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there are two kinds [of liberation] because of the twofold nature of the Vedic statements;
for even in the absence of a body, experience is possible for the liberated one.
Just as in the twilight state of dream there is indeed the activity of the body and certain experiences, so too,
when the body exists, the occurrence of experience arises just as in the waking state.
Just as a single lamp can produce many lamps through its capacity for transformation, so too does the Knower, though one, [manifest in many ways].
Having attained mastery over manifold states through the application of his power,
the wise one indeed enters all bodies by means of his capacity.
How can it be so? For the scripture speaks of [the path] as being single, twofold, fivefold, and so forth; how could there be many paths for one who is liberated?
That dissolution is deep sleep, for scripture says, "He has gone to his own self";
furthermore, there is merging [of speech] into mind and so forth, as well as departure, according to scripture.
With reference to the state of either one of those two, this qualification—
the statement regarding the absence of consciousness— was further revealed.
And because of that [Lord] being absent, just as from the context [of the individual soul],
his sovereignty— consisting of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth— would be devoid of the activity of governing the world.

If it is argued that in the Śruti, "He attains self-sovereignty" (svārājya) is used in the sense of "thus indeed," just as "instruction and so forth" is used in the sense of "perceptible," [then the same applies here]. If it were so, [the term] would likewise reside within a modification (vikāra).
190) That which belongs to the sun presiding over the maṇḍala exists there;
that very thing is what is expressed here by the word "Brahman," but not that [other] one again.
For that Śruti indeed declares that Brahman— characterized by truth and so forth— is both unchanging and attainable by the liberated, and likewise exists within the realm of modification.
Thus, the Śruti and Smṛti, demonstrating that the supreme light is likewise free from modification,
declare: "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines it."
In the same way, the wise man, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equanimity— that which has been described as equanimity.
But that [enjoyment] is not for the sake of activity in the world, but solely for the purpose of experience;
for it is heard in scripture that "he enjoys all desires" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21),
and through knowledge, by the path of the gods, he attains the supreme Brahman, which is unchanging.
Furthermore, the return of those who have attained [the goal] is nowhere seen;

There is no returning for them, according to the Vedic revelation that they go "by the word itself.
Such is the state of equilibrium between the two: the primary sign (liṅga) and its subordinate member (aṅga).
Through discernment, even a hundred [verses] of the *Sthala* will certainly be mastered;

Because the categories taught in the scriptures are seen to be non-different from one another,

Having protected all beings, she who is the essence of knowledge clearly manifested this very meaning, which is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Now, therefore, O twice-born one, I shall fully declare to you the sequence of creation;

At the time of dissolution, this entire world remains within the Supreme Lord,
who is distinct from Māyā, in a form non-different from His own causal nature known as Svasā.
By way of the non-existence of latent impressions, through the nature of the non-existence of latent impressions,
by the ripening of time and karma, and also by the power of latent impressions.
By means of Māyā, the Great Self produces within this [being] the two ears;
the knowledge of the objects to be created, born of sattva, is the means to liberation.
He who is seen by the wise as the Great Self is that supreme Śiva;
as the creator, Śiva himself entered into the Great Self.
Furthermore, that Supreme Lord, Maheśvara, is recited by the learned as "the Omniscient One" (Sarvajña) because his essential nature is primarily characterized by that [omniscience].
The Supreme Lord, whose primary nature is Pradhāna, observes through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Tamas;
yet He observes the quality of Sattva by means of His own self-nature alone.
He conceives himself as the destroyer of all through darkness (tamas),
and likewise, he constantly identifies with the quality of darkness (tamoguṇa) as his very self.
And Śiva shall always be the protector through the quality of goodness (sattva) alone;
through goodness and passion (rajas) together, he becomes the creator of all.
Brahmā is proclaimed as the creator; Viṣṇu is called the protector;
and Maheśāna Śiva is the destroyer, yet he is the supreme common [principle] of all.
Rajas is the cause everywhere in origination, sattva everywhere in preservation, and tamas everywhere in dissolution; of this there is no doubt.
For whatever cause has been proclaimed for anything, Maheśvara indeed remains as its direct presiding presence and thus renders assistance.
Merit and demerit, time, latent impressions, and Maheśvara always assist in the activities of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
But following the creation of the three forms,
the creation of the elements proceeds as before, preceded by sound, from Māyā.
The five objects, beginning with sound, arise from the five elements through the quality of sattva;
and just as they were produced before, so too are the powers of knowledge.
O best of the wise, in that same way as previously described, the powers of action arise from the five elements— sound and the rest— through the influence of passion (rajas), time, and karma.
The powers of cognition that perceive sound and the other [objects] within the five elements are unified with their own cause, which is called Māyā, and rendered manifold by means of Vidyā.
Having attained a state of oneness through the ripening of time and karma, it becomes the aggregate (samaṣṭi) of the individual internal organs (vyaṣṭi-antaḥkaraṇa); of this there is no doubt.
The creative powers (kṛti-śakti) born from the five elements, beginning with sound,
having attained a state of uniformity through time and action as before, [proceed].
The collective (samaṣṭi) of all individual vital breaths (vyaṣṭi-prāṇa) is undoubtedly the same;
the powers of knowledge born of sattva reside within the five elements, beginning with sound.
There are also collective unities (samashṭis) for all the organs of knowledge;
from these, the internal organ (antahkarana) arises in fourfold form in succession.
The mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (citta)— likewise,
these become fivefold in succession through the divisions of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth.
And those who are excessively conceited regarding these very [beings] have the designations of the universal aggregate (samaṣṭi) and the vital breath (prāṇa);
they are known as Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sūtrātman, the quarters, the wind, and the sun.
Varuṇa, as well as Bhūmi, and the god Trivikrama;

The Lord Kālāgnirudra, who bestows the enjoyment of Śivā,

The Blessed Lord Sāmba, whose characteristics are truth and the rest, is the one who identifies with all;

Having known that golden-hued one, who is accessible only to subtle intellect, a person is liberated;

And by Rudra, as well as by all others, that [recollection] is performed incessantly;

The divisions of the cosmic eggs arise, and likewise the divisions of the worlds;
