The distinctions of caste and stage of life, as well as the divisions between dharma and adharma;
the distinctions between pleasure and pain, and even the divisions between heaven and hell.
The Lord Śambhu is the cause of all, characterized by truth and other such qualities;
he is neither Viṣṇu, nor Viriñca, nor Rudra, nor any other person.
That very [Self] is respectfully propounded by all the Vedāntas,
as well as by the Smṛtis following the Veda and by the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata, and so forth.
That very [Brahman] is worshipped by the twice-born through the practices prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti;
and all other [deities] are also to be worshipped as being subordinate to Him.
In certain places and at certain times within the Vedas, all other deities besides Him are likewise mentioned as objects of knowledge and as objects of meditation.
Their reality and form are never described as belonging to them [the individual souls],
but rather through the lineage of Śiva himself, Rudra, who is accompanied by Ambā.
O best of beings, the Śrutis and the Purāṇas, such as the Mahābhārata and others,
indeed always proclaim Śiva alone, together with Ambā, keeping him in their hearts under names such as Śiva,
Śaṅkara, Rudreśa, Brahmeśāna, and so forth.
The supreme state is described by the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other scriptures,
using all the names such as Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and so forth.
The supreme state is not described by the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth;
however, words such as "Rudra" and others are applied to the Supreme Lord through conventional usage.
By means of figurative usage alone, words such as Viṣṇu and others are declared to be true;
yet this Sāmba, whose characteristics are truth and so forth, is the witness within all forms.
He stands manifest as the objective ground; this entire world is dependent upon Him.
Abandoning Him through great delusion, people worship deities such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
And they declare that the Vedas speak because they have another as their source.
Likewise, the Smṛtis, Purāṇas,
and the Mahābhārata and other texts declare that mortals are like illusions; indeed, that illusion is truly difficult to cross.
For men burdened by great sins, Śiva— characterized by truth and other virtues—
does not appear as the supreme reality along with Ambā, O Self-Master.
To those who have attained perfection over many lifetimes and who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti,
the eternal Śiva, together with Ambā, appears as the Supreme Reality.
The vision of Śiva should be maintained toward everyone by all living beings,
just as the vision of a king is maintained toward a minister by all people;
for Tryambaka, the destroyer of Tripura, is the King of Kings for all.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, are his very attendants;
the thorough knowledge of the cause of manifestation arises solely through his grace,
and not through the grace of Viṣṇu and the other gods— of this there is no doubt.
Those who strive for liberation while abandoning the Lord Sāmba-Īśāna are overcome by great darkness; for them, there is no supreme goal.
Having abandoned Īśāna, the Lord of Jambūdvīpa, those who worship other deities fall,
utterly deluded, into this most terrible cycle of existence.
All deities should be meditated upon by the wise as being nothing other than the state of being the remains (śeṣa) of Mahādeva accompanied by Ambā; this is well to be understood.
"Having abandoned everything else, Śiva alone is the bringer of auspiciousness;
he is to be meditated upon—so indeed says the supreme Atharvaṇa Śruti."
Now, what is the use of saying more? Śiva Jāmba is eternal; he is indeed the direct final goal of all scriptures, and there is nothing higher than him—this is the truth that has been declared.
Everything else besides that is the entire universe; for he is Śiva, who transcends the universe. He alone is the Lord of the worlds, for he is the liberator from saṃsāra.
Now, moreover, I shall respectfully proclaim another superiority of the deities,
by the mere knowledge of which Maheśvara becomes pleased.
The conscious are held to be superior to all that is unconscious;
among the conscious, humans are superior, and among humans, the twice-born are superior.
Among the twice-born, those who are brahmins are considered superior; among them, those of noble lineage are remembered as superior; and superior to them are proclaimed to be the human gandharvas.
Higher than them are the gods and the Gandharvas, and beyond those, the Pitṛs;
then the Karmadevas are enumerated, and after them, the Devas.
Indra is superior to them, and Bṛhaspati is superior to him;
the wise Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) is remembered as being even superior to Bṛhaspati.
Brahmā is even greater than Prajāpati, and Viṣṇu is greater than Brahmā;
and Hara is even greater than Viṣṇu—therefore, Maheśvara is the manifest wielder of Māyā.
The Smṛtis and Purāṇas, as well as the Mahābhārata and others, indeed surpass the entire universe, yet they do not transcend the Supreme.
Other treatises and systems of logic that support the Vedas—
even all such means of valid knowledge— are [insufficient] without Śiva, together with Ambā, being directly present.
O great sage, all the Purāṇas never declare anyone else to be superior to Maheśvara.
With an uncommon form and a common name,
they speak of the supreme reality: Śiva, accompanied by Ambā, the three-eyed one.
He saw Candraśekhara dancing with the joy of supreme bliss for himself and others,
the destroyer of the three forms (Trimūrti), who is both their portion and their presiding deity.
Furthermore, they always declare that even a portion of those [Purāṇas] is auspicious,
as are all the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas.

By the name of Hari among the three forms, they proclaim his supreme state; and by this same method, two Purāṇas—the Brāhma and the Vaiṣṇava—do so as well. Maheśvara is the ultimate foundation and the final limit of the eighteen Purāṇas.
Indeed, the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas describe the majesty of the three forms, as well as that of Hari himself,
and of each of his respective portions.
O best of men, although a diminution of Hari is observed even in all the Śambhava Purāṇas,
that which is seen as a diminution in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas pertains to Hari himself, who is the primordial source.
This excellence of Rudra, even of Hara,
which is seen in the Purāṇas and the Śaiva scriptures, belongs solely to his manifestation (vibhūti).
O Sage, that excellence of Rudra which is seen in the Purāṇas and in the Vaiṣṇava texts, exists both in his own essential form and through his nature as the ultimate reality (tattva).
O best of men, that [manifestation] belongs to Viṣṇu by way of his essential nature (tattva), not by way of his own specific form;
thus has the direction regarding Brahman been directly shown in the two Purāṇas.
O best of beings, in the Purāṇa of Pāvaka as well as in that of Saura,
the preeminence of Śiva, the God of gods and the Supreme Self, is established.
In ancient times, men, failing to understand Rudra’s superiority and failing to recognize Viṣṇu as the most excellent, mistakenly considered Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa [to be superior] due to delusion.

Thinking "I am Brahman" and "I am Viṣṇu," he engaged in battle out of delusion. Overcome by great anger and utterly bewildered, Brahmā, the Lord of the entire universe, cursed Viṣṇu, saying, "May you be born from a womb."
Your devotees, the Brahmins, would constantly turn their faces away from the ash-marked Tripuṇḍra,
even though it is established by the Vedas and bestows liberation.
Whether the mark is triangular, quadrangular, or like a bamboo leaf,
those twice-born who always delight in the intervals between the *puṇḍra*s shall become [liberated] at the end.
Due to great delusion, people might mark both shoulders with your weapons, such as the conch and the discus, heated by fire.
Through the path of Vedic study, O twice-born ones,
those devoted to you shall become eternally averse to the worship of you, utterly deluded.

O Hari, those twice-born who are initiated in your Pāñcarātra Tantra and also in the Bhāgavata [Tantra] shall always be fearless regarding the auspicious conduct prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti, which grants immediate liberation.
"May those devoted to you be eternally turned away and utterly deluded. Thus was Viṣṇu cursed by Viriñca;
overcome by delusion and filled with great wrath, he in turn cursed the four-faced one.
Your fifth head will be severed by Śaṅkara,
and for a specific reason, it shall be done by the Lotus-born One as well, before long.
O Four-faced One, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of mixed castes in this world shall always be your devotees.

nor, O Padmasambhava, would your independent establishment endure.
Thus, O twice-born one, both of them stumbled due to delusion,
failing to recognize the superiority of Śiva because of the power of great ignorance.
He who considers Śaṅkara to be superior to all the gods crosses over the ocean of saṃsāra and goes to the further shore of liberation.
He who always perceives Rudra as superior to all, as the manifest witness of all,
and indeed as greater than everything— that person is Śaṅkara himself. Those who do not declare the Pināka-wielder to be superior to all [shall suffer].
Those joined with great sins speak of him as equal to others; yet, O sinless one,
just as there exists a superiority of the Veda over all forms of knowledge,
so too does there exist a superiority of Rudra among the gods.
Thus, the essence of all the Vedas has been declared to you with devotion and solely out of compassion;
if this shines forth within the heart of Śuka, then people shall cross the ocean of their own sorrow.
Henceforth, I shall respectfully declare the *liṅga* of the deity,
by the mere knowledge of which Maheśvara becomes propitious.
Deities are said to be of two kinds, according to the division of Śrauta and Aśrauta;
for those who are solely devoted to Śrauta dharma, the deities are indeed established by the Śruti.
For those devoted to non-Vedic systems (*tantra*), there are no deities established by the Vedas;
for those devoted to non-Vedic dharma, the deities are indeed non-Vedic.
However, for those solely devoted to Vedic dharma, the *liṅga* is indeed Vedic alone.
For those who are devoted to non-Vedic dharma, a non-Vedic emblem is prescribed;
however, for those deities established in the Veda, their emblem must be Vedic.
For those who are devoted to non-Vedic systems, their practice is indeed non-Vedic;

however, the Vedic mark (liṅga) should be understood as consisting of the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) and smearing with ashes (uddhūlana). Non-Vedic marks such as the vertical line (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and so forth are not the horizontal triple-tilaka.
Mahādeva is established by the Vedas; he is the direct liberator from saṃsāra, his body half-formed with Umā, pure, and adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
For the benefit of the worlds, he bears the Vedic mark;
and for Viṣṇu, who is established by the Vedas, there is only the Vedic mark and nothing else.
Indeed, even regarding his specific manifestations,
that alone— namely the Veda— is the authoritative mark of Brahman as established by scripture, and nothing else;
for even regarding his specific manifestations, that alone is indeed [the proof].

The deity of the Siddhāyā is divine, and her *liṅga* is Vedic; for even regarding their specific manifestations, it is indeed that same [Vedic form]. Mahādeva is established by the Tantra, according to the path established by the Tantra.
Mahāviṣṇu, who is established in the Tantras and is affectionate toward his devotees, applies the horizontal *tripuṇḍra* with ashes and the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* as a trident.
Viriñca, accomplished in the Tantras, applies a square mark on the forehead for the sake of protecting his devotees, while [another] applies a circular mark according to the Tantric method.
The treasury of compassion places it upon his forehead for the sake of protecting his devotees.
(201) Furthermore, for deities such as Indra, the vajra, noose, kusha grass, and so forth,
are not indicated as their emblems at all according to the path taught in the tantras.
One who is devoted to Śiva and established in the Tantras should always wear the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead with sacred ash alone, following the very path prescribed therein.
One who is established in the Tantra and is a devotee of Viṣṇu by way of the Tantric path should wear the trident-shaped or quadrangular vertical *puṇḍraka*.
Likewise, one who is constantly devoted to the Tantras and directly to the Four-faced Lord (Brahmā) should devoutly wear a circular mark on the forehead according to the Tantric path.
A person who is devoted to deities such as Indra, or likewise one who is established in the Tantras,
should always wear the thunderbolt, noose, goad, and other symbols upon his forehead.
For all practitioners of Tantra, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with sacred ash alone is superior to all other marks; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
O Mahādeva, one who is devoted to the Tantras but,
out of delusion, wears another sectarian mark (puṇḍra) instead of the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead with ashes, shall become a denizen of hell;
for that triple mark made with ashes upon the forehead is identical with Me.
The Liṅga is declared to be of Maheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, and Brāhma;
it is proclaimed as Śaiva, Bhāgavata, and Brāhma.
A follower of the Vedic path should wear it upon his forehead according to the Vedic method.
In men who possess great sins, hatred arises toward the Great Lord established in the Vedas, as well as toward the application of the Tripuṇḍra and the smearing of ashes.
O Father, if anyone harbors hatred toward Śiva, the teacher of the worlds,
his own birth must be inferred by the wise to be purposeless.
But if one considers any other path to be equal to, or even superior to, the path of the Veda,
his confusion of traditions (sāṃkarya) should be inferred by the wise.
He who considers the names Śiva, Rudra, Maheśāna, Brahmēśāna,
and so forth to be identical with the words Viṣṇu and others— he indeed is Śaṅkara.
If one feels aversion toward this sacred ash, as well as toward the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and its smearing,
a wise person may infer that there is a mixture of castes (*sāṃkarya*) in his birth.
That man who considers Viṣṇu to be superior to Mahādeva—
by a wise person, the impurity of that man’s lineage should be inferred.
Indeed, due to the abundance of sins and because of the curse of the sage Gautama,
the Vedic linga did not please Dadhīca.
And in response to this, regarding the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* which is not based on the Śruti,
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas shall place their faith in it hereafter.
For those who have attained perfection through many births and follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti,
devotion to the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) arises solely by way of what is declared in the Vedas—
the application of the triple mark and the smearing [of the body] with ashes accompanied by Vedic mantras.
For one who achieves the state of Śambhu through diligent effort,
the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with sacred ash is more abundant than the mastery of the Vedas and Vedāntas.
The wearing of the Tripuṇḍra with ashes while reciting the Vedic mantra bestows right knowledge quickly; this has been truly stated, there is no doubt.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes while reciting Vedic mantras is a fierce sun to the mass of darkness consisting of the great sins (mahāpātaka).
It is declared that the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra with ashes while reciting Vedic mantras removes all sins; this has been spoken as the truth, there is no doubt.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash and Vedic mantras is a cause of satisfaction for Śiva, Viṣṇu, the gods,
and Brahmā; it is also a cause of satisfaction for Bhāratī, Mahālakṣmī, and Pārvatī.
(203) Without the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes and Vedic mantras,
liberation is not accomplished for humans or even for the gods.
Without the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra with sacred ash and Vedic mantras,
liberation is not attained for either human beings or gods.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes accompanied by Vedic mantras never arises for anyone without the realization of Vedānta.

The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes accompanied by Vedic mantras, as well as conduct prescribed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis, [is essential]; otherwise, such conduct becomes a cause of misfortune.
O wise sages, you should endure this: the learned proclaim that the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes and Vedic mantras constitutes the path of the virtuous.
The wise and learned proclaim that the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes and Vedic mantras constitutes the duty of the social classes (varṇadharma).
The application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes while reciting Vedic mantras is said by the believers to be the duty for all stages of life (āśramas).
The great sages declare that the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes according to the Vedic path is for the sake of protection and for the sake of auspiciousness.

What is the use of saying more here? Apart from the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), which is supreme and brings about all perfections, that man who desires liberation makes his own self eternal through the objects of the senses.

Therefore, a man desiring liberation should always joyfully fashion the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with white ash— well-known in the Vedas— following the path of the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and Śaiva traditions.
By such words as these, the well-spoken sayings of Parāśara,
one should worship the Śiva-liṅga in the Kali age for the destruction of impurity.
One who knows the eight syllables and is devoted to the fivefold conduct.
A Vīraśaiva should perform Vedic rites as a means for attaining the singular fruit of knowledge;
he should never perform animalistic (pāśava) rites.
Just as those who know the Vedas do not perform the practices of ascetics,
so too one devoted to the scriptures should perform only those actions that are accomplished through knowledge alone.
The Vedic rites established by the meaning of the scriptures and those proclaimed in the Āgamas—
being skilled in the knowledge of both, the wise man should practice their dharmas.
Averse solely to the path of liberation, their minds defiled by the impurities of the Kali age, they revile one another rather than acting for their own spiritual welfare.
O Parāśara, those dharmas declared in Vīraśaivism are augmented by the Purāṇas;
they are established in the Vedas and indeed exist within the Smṛtis as well.
Therefore, I shall describe individually those auspicious dharmas that are desired, as they are declared in the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Smṛtis, and enjoined by the Āgamas.
The connection of these [mantras] is indeed as a limb of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), according to the description of the mantras;
furthermore, their status as limbs of the knowledge of Brahman is established again within their respective contexts.
The truth will become clear through lofty arguments according to the path of reality;
its conformity with the Vyāsa-sūtras has been described in each individual aphorism.
Their status as Vedic is already established by their uniformity;
because they are Vedic, their practice is beyond reproach.
Tantric [practice] is of two kinds: that which is enjoined by the Vedas and that which is contrary to them;
both are authoritative because they originate from the instruction of the Supreme Authority.
The Vīraśaiva system is proclaimed as both Tantric and ordained by the Vedas;
it excels even the purely non-Vedic dharma.

Just as the Agnihotra is the formal worship for men who possess wealth according to their means, so too is it for one who has established all the sacred fires; for him, however, there is only the Śrauta rite, which is worthy of both.
Just as one does not incur any distinction [of fault] from the omission of domestic (gṛhya) rites,

so too the Vīraśaiva, who is worthy of both [Vedic and Tantric paths], is the best among the Vaidikas. One who is merely Vaidika and has not been initiated is not at all entitled to the Tantric duties.
Furthermore, whatever is prohibited in the Veda, such as the Kāpālika and other doctrines,
which pertain to those not authorized by the Vedas— that has been correctly stated.
In this regard, the following is considered:

by some it is held that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) has already been set forth in the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), even though it was not explicitly stated there.

This is because the first aphorism indicates both the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), and since the subject matter consists in the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpaikya*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.
It must be said that since both the definition [of Brahman] and the knowledge thereof depend upon superimposition (*adhyāsa*), that [superimposition] is indeed implied by the Sūtra itself.

However, because there is no identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, it cannot be accepted as the subject matter (*viṣaya*) [of the inquiry]. Indeed, the identity of essential nature between the individual soul and Brahman is nowhere stated in the Sūtras; on the contrary, [the Sūtra states], "The part [is] manifold... (*aṃśo nānā*).

Regarding the statement "on account of designation," it was said that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman and both different and non-different from it, like sparks from a fire. For there is no identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) between fire and its sparks, such as would exist between the individual soul and Brahman;

nor is it impossible for difference and non-difference to coexist in one place due to their mutual contradiction, because [this distinction] is produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*).

It should not be said that only a false distinction is stated there; for [the Lord] is designated as both [the cause and the effect], like a snake and its coils, or like light and its substratum. Furthermore, because He possesses the nature of light (*tejastva*), the permissions and prohibitions [of actions] apply as before, due to His connection with bodies, as in the case of light and so forth. His assumption of those states is possible because it is logical, as in the case of a lamp. And so too is His location.

For it demonstrates that there is no contradiction, since difference and non-difference are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and are observed in illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). And so it will be stated in that very same [section]:
"If non-distinction were to result from the identity of the enjoyer, it would be as in the world," where the lack of contradiction is likewise supported. Likewise...

For this very Sūtra has been explained by them in this manner: otherwise, the doctrine of Brahman as the cause is refuted solely on the strength of reasoning (*tarka*). Even though scripture (*śruti*) is authoritative with respect to its own subject matter, it must nevertheless yield to another means of knowledge when its subject matter is sublated by that other means. As, for example:

[The Veda consists of] mantra and arthavāda. Reasoning (*tarka*) as well would be unstable regarding anything other than its own proper domain, just as it is with respect to *dharma* and *adharma*. If this is so, what follows? Therefore, this [position] is untenable. Furthermore, regarding the Veda's communication of an object already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): what, then, is an object established by another means of valid cognition that is [further] communicated by the Veda?
It is said that [the self] is oppressed. For this distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is well-established in the world:
the enjoyer is the conscious embodied being, and the objects of enjoyment are sound and so forth; just as Devadatta is the enjoyer.

And [the objection that] the boiled rice would become the object of enjoyment: it would follow that this distinction between the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment would cease to exist, if the enjoyer were to undergo the state of being the object of enjoyment, or if the object of enjoyment were to undergo the state of being the enjoyer. This mutual transformation of the two would follow because they are not different from Brahman, the supreme cause.

If someone should say, "And it is not proper to subvert this well-known distinction; therefore, it is not logical to maintain that Brahman is the cause," one should reply to him: "It may be so, as in the world.
This distinction is indeed possible even in our view, because it is observed thus in the world. For example:
Although foam, waves, and the like are non-different from the ocean, which consists of water, a mutual distinction between them is nevertheless observed.
Furthermore, although they are non-different from the ocean, which consists of water, it does not follow that foam, waves, and the like attain a state of mutual identity with one another.
Nor does their failure to attain such mutual identity imply that they are not non-different from the ocean, which consists of water.
In the same way, here too, there will be neither the mutual transformation of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, nor the absence of non-difference from Brahman,
which is of the nature of Being.

[Objection: Is this not merely an argument based on a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), incapable of resolving the contradiction? For, by the sūtra "The non-difference from that [Brahman] is established on account of such scriptural passages as 'originating with speech' (*vācārambhaṇa*)," it is demonstrated that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated by scripture. [Reply: No; for by this sūtra, the entire phenomenal world is not...
The fact of its being sublated is now established:
for the manifold of difference, established by means of valid cognition such as perception and the rest, cannot be sublated by the Śruti.
Because it is observed that when there is a contradiction with perception, the scriptures themselves have another meaning;

for example, in the injunction "one should cook the *kṛṣṇala*," since the act of splitting the gold bean (*svarṇamāṣa*) is contradicted by perception, the injunction has the purpose of merely heating it. Or, as in the case of "one should sacrifice with *soma*," [the word *soma*] refers to the sacrifice.

Because of the partial acceptance [of the injunction] "one should meditate," when there is a grammatical coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two—namely, "with Soma" and "by means of sacrifice"—the identity between the *Soma* creeper and the sacrifice is contradicted by direct perception. Therefore, in the expression "with the *Soma* sacrifice," the word "Soma" is understood through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to that which is related to it. This is likewise accepted by others in the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

Because the identity between the expressed meanings [of the two words] is sublated by perception, it is accepted that [the sentence] has as its purport the identity with the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*).
Furthermore, if the sublation of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were admitted, then the very nature of the Vedic revelation,
the recollection of word-meanings produced thereby, and the knowledge of the sentence-meaning would also fall within the phenomenal world.

If even those [sublated objects] were sublated, how could the sublation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) be established? Or how is it not a contradiction to say, "My mother is barren" or "I have no tongue"? Nor can it be argued that even when the phenomenal world is sublated, its essential nature remains, and therefore its effects also remain possible; for negation (*abhāva*) does not exist without the negandum (*pratiyogin*).

Because designation is merely a conventional term (*paribhāṣā*), the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not sublated by scripture (*śruti*), which would otherwise result in contradiction. Rather, it must be said that [the world] is real;
for even in the absence of sublation of its nature, the quality of reality—defined as being unsublated—is admitted in the case of the phenomenal world.

Because the sublation of reality is utterly untenable, it follows that this [scripture] does not establish the sublation of the phenomenal world (prapañca), but rather establishes non-difference alone; thus it is established that there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference.

Likewise, in another place, there is the objection that because of the designation of identity, the fault of not performing what is beneficial and so forth would follow. Since the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is designated in the text "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the creation performed by Brahman would be as if performed by the individual soul; thus, one might suspect that the creator would create only what is beneficial for the soul and not what is harmful, such as hell. Anticipating this, [the Sūtra] states, "But there is more, on account of the declaration of difference," whereby the individual soul...

It is not the individual soul (*jīva*) that is the agent; rather, Brahman alone is the agent, and it is that which creates even what is disadvantageous for the *jīva*. Having stated this, [the opponent asks]: "How can there be a relationship of inferiority and superiority if there is non-difference? Or how could the Lord, perceiving all *jīvas* as his own self through his omniscience, create sorrow, delusion, and so forth in them? [The answer follows: Regarding sorrow and the like...

Anticipating the objection that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the self] being experienced as its own mode of existence, [the author] states: "And like stones and so forth, that is untenable.

By this, it is shown that although there is no difference among stones such as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*) in their common nature as stone, their essential forms (*svarūpa*) exist in middle or superior natures depending on the distinction between individual instances (*vyaktibheda*).

And there is diversity. Thus, it has been stated that even for the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), the state of being distinct and the diversity of their effects are established based on the difference between their manifestations (*vyakti*).

Nor is it the case that while the generality of "stoneness" (*pāṣāṇatva-sāmānya*) is non-different, the individuals (*vyakti*) are indeed different, such that [the properties] do not reside in one and the same [individual].

It must be stated that there is both difference and non-difference; for it is universally accepted that among individual instances, there exists a non-difference consisting in the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the generality of "stoneness," as well as a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by "lapis lazuli-ness."

And thus, there is no undesirable consequence of applying the grammatical relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even to "vajra" and "vaiḍūrya," because such a relation must necessarily be admitted for that [term] which expresses a particular within a universal, whereas there is no cognition of a particular [in this case]. Therefore...

Even with respect to the Lord (Īśvara), the Sūtra has taught the vision of non-difference from the individual soul (jīva) precisely as being the Self, in the words: "But they recognize [Him] as the Self, and they cause others to grasp Him as such.

For this very reason, even by our opponents, having set aside the aspect of egoity (ahaṃkāra) which stands in the place of the individual, the non-difference of consciousness alone—which stands in the place of the universal—is admitted.

And thus, although the object of the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is either a qualified nature characterized by the absence of difference or the [individual] nature itself, nevertheless, where there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apprehending difference in every respect, identity of nature is the object— as in cases such as "This is that Devadatta. However, where there is a means of cognizing difference...

There is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding cause and effect and so forth; in that case, the object is either two natures characterized by the absence of difference in the delimiters of their respective existences, or two natures characterized by the absence of difference from the universal (*sāmānya*). And in the present context, by the single cognition [arising from] "Have you asked for that instruction?"...

Having asserted the identity of all things through the statement "All is consciousness," even though the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "All this has that as its self" is repeated nine times in the explanatory text,
such a designation does not take as its object the absolute oneness of the essential nature of Brahman and the phenomenal world. The same applies to the statement "That thou art."

Designation as well is identical in both cases, because the designation of both difference and non-difference is equal in both instances. This is because [the scriptural statements] such as "There is no other seer than this," "Where one sees nothing else," and "There is nothing whatsoever higher than this" indicate difference; and because the possession of contradictory attributes—such as sentience and insentience, or being a transmigrating soul and not being so—is likewise equal in both cases.

Consequently, because difference is negated and difference is also established, both difference and non-difference are proven. Therefore, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference.
As for the claim that the false distinction is produced by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) characterized as ignorance (avidyā):
this is not tenable, because nowhere has it been stated in the Sūtras that ignorance is such an adjunct, nor that its status as an adjunct is itself false.

Nor should it be argued that ignorance is indeed mentioned in the Sūtra at the passage, "And for some, [the self is known] through inference" (BS 1.1.24), where it says, "But that [self] is subtle, because it is worthy of that" (BS 1.4.3); for that refers to something else.

In this regard, concerning the doubt that in the passage "beyond the Great is the Unmanifest" (*mahataḥ parataḥ paramavyaktam*), the word "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers to the *pradhāna* consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), [the author] states: "because of the apprehension of what was set forth as the metaphor of the body. By this, it is shown that it is indeed the body—which was described as a chariot in the mantra, "Know the Self as the rider, and the body as the chariot"—that is intended.

It is grasped [as such], but not as the *pradhāna*. Having stated this, when the inquiry arises—"Since the body is manifest (*vyakta*), how can it be unmanifest (*avyakta*)?"—it is said by the sūtra "But that [body] is subtle, because it is capable of that" (*sūkṣmaṃ tu tadarhatvāt*) that it is precisely the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) that is denoted by the word "unmanifest," and not the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*). Not... [the gross body].

Since the three qualities (*triguṇā*) are understood by the term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and because it is impossible to include "knowledge" (*vidyā*)— which is not established as being present in the formation of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*)— in that sense, and since ignorance (*avidyā*) is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*), and because the all-pervasiveness of Brahman is admitted through the universal perception "I am ignorant," [the unmanifest] is subtle (*sūkṣmatva*) and unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Furthermore, because [the terms] "sound" (śabda) and "worthiness" (arhatva) would be inapplicable; otherwise, there would be a contradiction if, having stated in the preceding sūtra that the body is grasped by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta), one were to state in the subsequent [sūtra] that ignorance (avidyā) is grasped.
Moreover, it would result in the acceptance of the doctrine of Pradhāna.

Nor should it be argued that by the statement "it is not like the [Sāṅkhya] principle because it is dependent on that," a distinction is being made such that the *pradhāna* is independent while ignorance is dependent on the Lord; for even in the systems of the Sāṅkhyas with God (Seśvara-sāṅkhya) and the Yogins, the dependence of the *pradhāna* upon the Lord is accepted, and thus no distinction can be established merely on that basis.
Because of its establishment:
just as objects are superior to the sense organs because the activity of the sense organs is dependent upon objects, so too is the Self [superior].
Because the Sūtra has the meaning that the body is superior to the self since activity is dependent upon the body; furthermore,
if ignorance were indicated here, the subsequent section would not need to be commenced.
Since it is possible that the same [Māyā] is being referred to even in the *ajā* mantra, there is no specific reason for taking it as the *pradhāna*,
and thus the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) does not arise. On the contrary, because of the mention of "the power of the divine Self,
established by its own qualities" in the preceding passage, and "know Māyā to be Prakṛti, and the world to be what is begotten of Māyā" in the subsequent one...

Since the dependence of *prakṛti* on Īśvara is established by the passage beginning with "Maheśvaram" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10), it is logical that even in the *ajā* mantra (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5), the reference must likewise be to Him. Consequently, [the claim] that "because it begins with light, as some read, and because of the teaching of a conceptual construction, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth" would be entirely untenable. [The principle of] being without beginning (*anādi*)...

Furthermore, since it is possible to understand the word "unborn" (*ajā*) as referring primarily to primordial ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the subject under discussion, it would be improper to abandon that meaning; rather, following the usage in other Vedic branches, one might take the word "unborn" to refer to the primary cause characterized by fire, water, and earth. However, because that [triple-element cause] possesses birth, it lacks the quality of being unborn, and thus [the term *ajā* cannot apply to it].

Regarding the doubt that the word [“goat”] is inappropriate, it is because the conceptualization of the sun as honey— as in “this sun is indeed honey”— is a mere metaphorical construction, and likewise, the conceptualization of the mind and so forth, which have light, water, and food as their material cause, as being of the nature of a goat (*ajā*) is an impossibility.
Therefore, primordial ignorance (*avidyā*), which is beginningless and distinct from the material nature (*prakṛti*) characterized by fire, water, and food, is not intended by the Sūtra;
nor does it exist, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that without ignorance (*avidyā*), the transformation of the partless Brahman into the world is impossible; for this very objection has been raised and refuted by the Sūtra itself in such passages as "There would be the consequence of [Brahman] being entirely transformed, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness. Nevertheless, what is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is the abandonment of the previous form of things...

It is the attainment of another form. In that regard, does Brahman transform in its entirety, or does it transform by way of its parts? It must be stated that it remains with some other part remaining. Regarding the first case, Brahman would not exist at the time of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because the whole would have abandoned its own nature and assumed the form of the effect.

Having raised the objection that [if Brahman were] partless, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts, this is resolved by the sūtra: "But because the scripture is the root of the word" (ŚBh 2.1.27).
Thus, while such reasoning may apply to matters accessible through inference, in a matter that can be understood solely through scripture, the meaning is determined by scripture alone.

The reality must be established; there is no need for reasoning (tarka). As it has been said: "Those entities which are indeed inconceivable, one should not attempt to apply reasoning to them. Furthermore, the Śruti declares that Brahman, which is partless, undergoes transformation and abandons its dense form. For instance, after describing the creation of fire, water, and food, [the text] immediately thereafter—

This is recorded in the tradition: "That Deity thought: 'Well, let me enter these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms. For it is stated that the Supreme Lord, the thinker, exists as distinct from the transformation characterized by fire, water, and food; even in the world, [transformation does not occur] by the abandonment of the prior form.

Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the attainment of another state. This is because transformation is impossible for that which lacks a substratum once its material cause (*upādāna*) has perished. Rather, transformation is simply the production of an effect capable of being designated as non-different from that [cause], while the material cause itself remains. As it was said regarding the motion of an arrow and so forth: "And likewise in the Self, there are various [powers]," just as follows:

In the living self (*jīvātman*), without the destruction of the very nature of the living soul, there arises the production of various other effects; namely, specific transformations such as cognition, desire, and so forth, come into being.

And so it is with clay, threads, and the like, in relation to jars, cloth, and so forth. Where, in the production [of one thing], another effect that is opposed to what is being produced exists, there the production of the other effect occurs only through the destruction [of the former]. For example, the production of a jar occurs through the destruction of the lump [of clay]. But where no opposed other effect exists, there—

The arising of another entity occurs precisely through the destruction of the previous entity. For example, the production of a cloth from threads occurs only through the destruction of the non-existence of the cloth within those threads.

Even in the case of a sprout and so forth, the seed and such are not the material cause (*upādāna*), because they persist in the effect and because only that which persists in the effect is the material cause. Rather, it is the parts themselves that are interwoven in both [the cause and the effect]. And thus says the Śruti: "Of this indeed..."

In the *Tarkapāda* of the Sūtras, it is stated by the author that "the non-existent [cannot produce] because it is not observed," explaining that even from a single seed, such as a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*), a great tree arises, and yet its capacity to produce sprouts and so forth occurs without the destruction of its own essential nature. And their vow is likewise the same. Thus it is also for Brahman, which is partless.
The transformation of the world is possible precisely without the destruction of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Furthermore, the refutation of the opposing view has already been stated, as has the defect in our own position: if the *pradhāna* and its constituents (*sattva*, etc.
were to transform in their entirety, it would entail the destruction of their essential nature; however, if one admits transformation only in part, [the aforementioned fault does not arise].

This would contradict the accepted doctrine of its being partless. This same defect applies equally to *avidyā* (ignorance), since *avidyā* is also equivalent to *pradhāna* (primordial matter). Nor can it be argued that transformation is possible for *avidyā* because it possesses diverse powers, but not for Brahman; for it is heard in scripture: "His power is indeed declared to be manifold."

Because such scriptural passages as these, along with the sūtra "And [Brahman] is endowed with all [powers], for that is seen," establish that Brahman alone possesses diverse powers; and because there is no evidence for such power residing in ignorance (avidyā). Thus, since the meaning of the sūtra is established as Brahman being the subject of transformation (pariṇāma), it is [incorrect to say] that "ignorance transforms" or "Brahman undergoes illusory manifestation (vivarta)."
Thus, this designation is improper; furthermore, it contradicts the Sūtra: "Because of the transformation [of the Self] by its own action" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.26).
If it were the case that avidyā alone undergoes transformation and not Brahman, then, because of the difference in nature between them, Brahman could not possess such a character.
The section concerning "Sound" (Śabdādhikaraṇa) would be untenable, because there would be no distinction between ignorance (*avidyā*) and the world (*jagat*),

and because the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman is not admitted. Furthermore, if some beginningless entity called ignorance were accepted, it could not be distinct from Brahman, as it would lack the status of being a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman.

Even if Brahman were known, that [ignorance] would not be known; thus, the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" would be undermined. Therefore, ignorance does not exist at all, nor has the view that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) is merely adventitious (aupādhika) been stated anywhere in the Sūtras.

Nor should it be argued that for this very reason the analogy "like the sun and so forth" implies that the state of being conditioned (*aupādhikatva*) was not indicated anywhere in the Sūtras; for in that context, the conditioned nature of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is not what is being pointed out. Rather, since there is the perception of both minuteness and magnitude through such statements as "Brahman is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great," both of these [attributes] exist.

Regarding the doubt that the Supreme [Self] cannot possess both characteristics even on the basis of location, it is stated that because Brahman is one, two contradictory forms cannot exist within it; then, as an illustration for the appearance of the fields (*kṣetra*) having distinct transformations, the example "like the sun and so forth" is adduced here. Thus...

Because water and the sun are material substances and possess form, a reflection is possible therein; however, since Brahman is not a material substance and lacks form, a reflection is impossible. Anticipating this objection with the words, "But because it is not apprehended like water, it is not so," [the Sūtra] states: "For here... [and so forth].

The distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is intended here as that of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*); however, it has been made clear by means of this illustrative example that the intended meaning is precisely this: that the various transformations of the field (*kṣetra*), such as the manifestation of forms, are merely the appearance of transformations belonging to Brahman alone.
p.

216) [The opponent argues: "That [distinction] is figurative (bhākta), because it is included within [the primary sense] and because both [explanations] are consistent. Therefore, there is no real difference;

its nature as being based on limiting adjuncts (upādhika) is precisely what is established. For this very reason, the distinction between the two who have entered into the one and the same [Self] is taught.

In passages such as "The two entered the cave," it is because of the perception of that [distinction] that [the difference is established]; therefore, since the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is inherent, there is no identity of essence (*svarūpa-ekya*) between the individual soul and the Supreme. If that were the subject matter of the scripture, then that alone would be propounded in every section (*adhikaraṇa*). Yet it is not so propounded; rather, in each section, by means of this or that...

When a doubt arises as to whether the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord (īśvara) is being propounded by the subject passage, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is the individual soul; however, having established that because the attributes propounded by those various passages are impossible in the individual soul, the Lord— who is distinct from that— is what is being propounded.

It is not the other [the individual soul], because that is untenable; and it is different because of the designation of difference. If it be argued that it is not so because of the marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath, [we reply] no, because of the distinction between deep sleep and departure. But it is not the embodied soul, because of the impossibility [of its being the cause]; and because of the designation of action and agent; and because of Smṛti and the specific word. If it be argued that it is not so because of its small abode and because of the designation of that, [we reply] no, because it is to be meditated upon in this way.

"And like the ether. If it be argued that [the Self within the sun is] not [the Supreme Self] because of the marks of attaining the state of enjoyment, we say no, because of the difference in nature. And because of the impossibility of its being stable, it is not the other. For both [scriptural traditions] teach this [Self] as distinct from the embodied soul. And because of the designation of distinctive attributes and difference, it is neither of the two others. And because of the designation of difference from the individual living being.
"And because of the context, and because of abiding and eating; he [is the Self], because of the designation of Him as the object of seeing.

"If it be argued that He is not [the Self] because of the reference to the other, we say no, because of impossibility; if it be argued that it is so because of what follows, [we say] rather that His nature has become manifest;

and the reference is for another purpose. "If it be argued that the soul is not atomic because of scriptural statements to that effect, we say no, because of the context of the other; moreover, there is a distinction."
Because of the detailed exposition; and because of the superior teaching of Bādarāyaṇa himself, as stated in such passages as "for it is seen thus" (Brahmasūtra 3.4.8).

It cannot be argued that because the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*), its status as an object of instruction is denied only in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and not in its conditioned form;
for if this were so, since God (*Īśvara*) also possesses adventitious adjuncts, He too would not be an object of instruction even in His conditioned form.

Since the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone is innate, it would be what is to be established; however, it is not established in that way, because there is no possible means for establishing it as such. Rather, it is established precisely in the form of Lordship (*īśvaratva*), which distinguishes it from the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because of the teaching of its attributes within [the passages concerning] the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), such as those regarding the divine realm (*adhidaiva*), and so forth. "Because of the teaching of its attributes within... [refers to] its attributes in the sections on the Inner Controller, the divine, and so on.

By the passage beginning with "because of designation" (vyapadeśāt) and so forth, it follows that the identity of nature between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is not the subject matter of the scripture, nor is this [identity] its purpose. This is because, according to the context and due to their lack of proximity, there is a distinction between the Lord and those who are not yet liberated, as indicated by such signs as the equality regarding mere enjoyment (bhoga). Thus, it is precisely their difference that is established.

Because it has been established [as such]. Therefore, since superimposition (adhyāsa) is not useful for either the subject matter or the purpose [of the treatise], its lack of being enshrined in a sūtra is proven.
Likewise, by the sūtra "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Janmādy asya yataḥ), the definition of Brahman as the cause of the world was stated. What [is that]?

Upon investigating what that cause is, it was stated in the passage beginning with "prakṛtiśca pratijñādṛṣṭāntānuparodhāt" (And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction between the initial proposition and the illustrative examples) that Brahman is both the efficient and the material cause. Thus, when it has been established by the Sūtras that Brahman alone possesses this twofold causality, some have asserted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the material cause, while others have asserted [the subtle body].

That the phenomenal world of consciousness and unconsciousness (*cidacid-prapañca*) is the material cause (*upādāna*), or that *prakṛti* is the material cause, as asserted by others—this mention of alternative material causes is disconnected from the Sūtra.
Likewise, regarding the Sūtra "Because it has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*), some have asserted that Brahman’s being the source of the scripture implies its unknowability—

a claim that is directly contrary to the meaning of the Sūtra itself. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because "being known through scripture" means being the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by scripture,
whereas "unknowability" means not being an object of pure consciousness (*caitanya*), since these two are different types of knowledge.

Because the differentiation of knowledge is not mentioned anywhere in the Sūtras, it belongs to the Tantric tradition. Nor should it be argued that "that which is other than the known" refers to the state of being unknowable; for that passage aims to establish the [Brahman's] nature as the Self of all by negating its being merely the known or the unknown. As it is said: "If you think 'I know well,' then surely even what is slight you do not truly know."

Because of the designation "the form of Brahman," so too, that which has been asserted by some—that the Vedāntas possess an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) after first refuting injunctions for knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*) on the grounds of "But that [is established] because of the harmony" (*tattu samanvayāt*)—is also contrary to the Sūtra.

For it is stated: "There is a single cognition from all Vedāntas because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth"; thus, the mere scripture (*śruti-mātra*) is what is accepted as the basis.

Because it is something not previously known (*apūrva*) and because the injunction to know is indicated by the word "being" (*bhāva*), as stated in the Sūtra. Nor should it be argued that knowledge cannot be enjoined because it is dependent on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for if knowledge were to be accomplished through an injunction, liberation would necessarily be non-eternal.
This objection will be refuted in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*. Furthermore, the claim that [the passages] have a merely miscellaneous (*pāriplava*) meaning is not tenable.

This is because they possess a specific character and are connected within a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyopabandha*). For instance, the narratives found in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), such as "Prajāpati cut out his own omentum," are connected in a single syntactical unit with injunctions such as "one should sacrifice a hornless animal," through the means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.
Thus, [the purpose] of Vedic narratives such as "Now Yājñavalkya had two wives" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.1) and so forth,
is knowledge [of Brahman], beginning with the statement "The Self is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).

Because it has been stated that [the Upanishadic texts] form a single syntactical unit with the injunctions, and because they have likewise been explained in that very manner by those [commentators]. Likewise, through such [Sūtras] as: "On account of seeing, [Brahman is] not that which is non-scriptural"; "If it be argued that [the term 'Self'] is figurative, no, because of the word 'Self'"; "[Brahman is] the possessor of qualities such as invisibility, because of the mention of its attributes"; "[Brahman is] the abode of heaven, earth, and so on, because of its own word"; and "It is known from the word itself."

Even when the determination of Brahman is being made through unique scriptural aphorisms (*sūtra*) concerning the attributes of Brahman and through words denoting Brahman, the assertion that Brahman— which is devoid of attributes— is not the denotable object of any word whatsoever is contrary to the *sūtras*. Nor is it the case that, although Brahman lacks real attributes, [it cannot be designated].

It cannot be argued that there is no contradiction because the attributes [of being the cause of the world] are superimposed, for since the superimposition of attributes such as being the cause of the world is possible everywhere, it cannot serve as a means of definitive determination. Furthermore, because attributes such as being the cause of the world are not established elsewhere, their superimposition is impossible. Thus, the Vedāntas [refer to] the superimposed...
Because if it were to have dharma as its object, it would result in the loss of its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*).

Nor should it be argued that its validity is established just like the notion of the body being the self (*dehātma-pratyaya*), which persists until the realization of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva-jñāna*);
for indeed, apart from the Lokāyata materialist, no one accepts the validity of the notion of the body being the self.

Validity is accepted by someone [as inherent]. For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) never becomes an invalid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*). Indeed, that whose object is uncontradicted is a valid cognition, while that whose object is contradicted is an invalid cognition. For contradiction and non-contradiction cannot coexist in one and the same place. Contradiction, indeed, is a negation throughout the three periods of time. For that which [is negated] in relation to something...

The negation of its existence across the three periods of time is possible only where its existence might otherwise be presumed. Therefore, that which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is always a means of valid cognition; that which is not a means of valid cognition is always not a means of valid cognition. Consequently, the notion of the body as the self is always invalid. If, therefore, the Vedāntas are also invalid, then for the sake of determining their meaning—
There would be the futility of the science of inquiry (*vicāra-śāstra*) and the consequence of falling into nihilism (*nāstikatva*).
Likewise, in the sūtra *ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt*, if the state of being Brahman for the *ānandamaya* were not [explicitly] stated in the sūtra... its... (p. 220)

The designation of Brahmanhood [for the ānandamaya] is contradicted by the Sūtra. Nor should it be argued that because the statement "from whence words turn back" establishes the featureless nature of Brahman as being beyond speech and mind, the ānandamaya—which is characterized by having joy as its head and so forth—cannot be Brahman; for the statement "from whence words turn back" does not [mean that Brahman is entirely unnameable].

By means of the sentence, Brahman’s transcendence of speech and mind is established; otherwise, the statement "the knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing whatsoever" would become incoherent. For it is not possible for Brahman to be inaccessible to any means of knowledge other than speech and mind, since there are other means of knowledge regarding Brahman.

Because [the world] proceeds from it; and because of the contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "One who does not know the Veda does not conceive that Great One," and "It is to be seen by the mind alone," and so forth. Rather, what is meant by its immeasurability is that the extent or limitation of the bliss of Brahman is beyond the reach of speech and mind; therefore, it is of such a nature.

"He who knows the bliss of Brahman with the mind (*manas*) has no fear from anything whatsoever"—thus the knowability of [Brahman] by the mind is stated. Nor is there a lack of evidence for supplying the word "with the mind" (*manasā*); for the introductory statement, "On this point also there is this verse," serves as such evidence. Having said, "On that point also there is this verse," it continues: "Bliss... [and so on].

In the phrase "knowing Brahman," it is understood that he is "knowing" by means of the mind; otherwise, no praise would be conveyed. On the contrary, there would arise the implication of censure, as in the passage "together with the mind which is to be attained," where the mind is understood as something to be reached [rather than a means of knowing]. Furthermore, in the seventh section of the *Āraṇyaka* of the Taittirīyas, the mantras for the *pravargya* rite are recorded.

At the beginning and at the end of those [mantras], peace (śānti) is recited by means of the two sections beginning with "namo vāce" and "śaṃ no vātaḥ pavatām. In the eighth praśna, the application (viniyoga) of those very mantras for specific ritual acts is recited.

Peace (śānti) is not recited there again. Just so, in the fifth book (pañcama-praśna), the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) along with its accessories is handed down in ten sections (anuvāka); [the peace] is [recited] both before and after it.

The two pacifications (*śānti*) are recited by means of the two sections beginning with *śaṃ no mitraḥ śaṃ varuṇaḥ*. The passage beginning with *sahanāva vatu* is a supplement to that very [section] and is not a separate pacification. Words ending in the dual number, such as *nau* and so forth, refer back to what was previously recited in the mantra: *tan māṃ tadvaktāram*.

Because it must be stated that these constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) due to their mutual expectancy as speaker and listener, and because all the world practices [them] in that very manner; furthermore, the two sections beginning with "Bhṛgu, the knower of Brahman" (*brahmavid bhṛguḥ*) are supplementary to that very [text] by providing the required meaning. For this very reason, the *śānti* is recited again there.

"He who knows those [Vidyās] as the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), he knows Brahman; all the gods bring him tribute"—thus it is recited. And it is universally accepted that this [knowledge] takes the form of meditation (*upāsanā*), as seen in the passage: "Therefore, O Yājñavalkya, meditate upon the ancient one. If meditation were not to have liberation as its fruit, but rather only the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahmavidyā*) had liberation as its fruit, then...

In that very context, two preceding and subsequent *śāntis* (propitiatory verses) would have been recited; yet they are not recited. Therefore, meditation (*upāsanā*) alone has liberation as its fruit. In that regard, the phrase "he knows Brahman" (*sa veda brahma*) declares the knowledge of Brahman. Then, in response to the inquiry—how one should know it, where one should know it, or what kind of fruit results—the section beginning with "the knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*) follows. And therein:

"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite; he who knows It as hidden in the secret cave of the heart within the supreme ether, he enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman"—this is the concise presentation of the desired meaning. "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" indicates the nature [of Brahman], while the rest is the manifestation. In that context, "Truth" means:

That entity which, having been determined in a certain form, does not abandon that form even at another time is called "true. However, that which abandons that form at another time is called "unreal. For instance, one...

For an object consisting of cause and effect—such as clay and a jar—is determined both in its causal form and its effected form. At another time, following the blow of a hammer, the effect in the form of the jar abandons that state; therefore, the effect is said to be unreal (*anṛta*). The cause, however, does not abandon its own nature. Therefore, the cause...

Truth is indeed spoken of; and that truth is of two kinds: relative and absolute. The nature of clay and so forth is relative truth, because even that ceases to exist at the time of dissolution. The nature of Brahman is absolute, because it is eternal. And therefore, by the word "truth," [it refers to the latter].

Its causality and eternity are stated; the meaning is that it is to be known in that form. And the causality of Brahman has been established by such passages as, "From this very Self, space was produced," and "It created all this. Its eternity is also [established] by such passages as, "He becomes non-existent indeed if he knows Brahman as non-existent; [Brahman] exists..."

"If one knows it as Brahman, then they know him as existing. He who knows Brahman as non-existent becomes a partaker of non-existence regarding the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). The word "iti" in the phrase "Brahman exists" has the sense of "in this manner. He who knows that "it truly exists, it is indeed Being"—he becomes a partaker of the goals of human life. And so says another Śruti:

Regarding the statement "it should be perceived as 'it exists'": here, by the word *jñāna*, the knower—the Self—is meant. For this word *jñāna* is not derived from the verbal root *jñā* with the suffix *lyuṭ* (ana) in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva-sādhana*), signifying "the act of knowing. If that were the case, it would be udātta-accented on the first syllable; however, it is recited as having the udātta accent on the final syllable. Therefore...

The word *cit* ends in an acute accent because it is formed with the suffix *yac* (the *arśādya* group), which expresses the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), as in "one who possesses knowledge" (*jñānam asyāsti*). Consequently, the self (*ātman*) is the knower (*jñātṛ*).
That [Selfhood] has been established. Therefore, from this very Self, space was produced;

it desired, "May I be many, may I procreate"; it performed austerity; having performed austerity, it emitted all this—by virtue of possessing knowledge, desire, and volition. And likewise, another Śruti says:

"One should worship [the Self] as 'I am the Self'. Regarding the term "immediate" (*anantaram*): that from which the cognition of something ceases is its "end," just as the cognition of a cow ceases upon reaching a horse; thus, it is said to be a limited entity, like any other distinct object.
That from which the cognition does not turn away from anything is "infinite" (*ananta*), being the self of all; and this has been established.

"May I be many, may I procreate"—thus, by such passages as "He made Himself by Himself; He became the existent and the non-existent," one knows Brahman as truth, as the Self, and as the Self of all. And so says another Śruti:
"All this has that as its essence; That is Truth; That is the Self. And thus, for this restating [text]:

The status of being a supplement to what precedes [is established] by the cessation of the expectation regarding [the nature of] the "kind" (*prakāra*) and so forth. Since the subsequent section (*anuvāka*) ceases the expectation of "What is that Brahman?", its status as a supplement to what precedes is indeed clear.
Thus, since both sections are supplements to what precedes and lack the capacity to establish a Brahman devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), [the term] "bliss" (*ānanda*)...
To establish [the effect] as being without distinction from its substrate is contrary to the Sūtras and contrary to the Śruti.
Thus, in the Sūtra "The non-difference of that [effect] from that [cause], on account of words such as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa)," the non-difference of the effect from the cause is aphorized.
However, some say that the non-existence of the effect apart from the cause is its falsity (mithyātva). That too—

This contradicts the Sūtra; for the term "non-difference" (ananyatva) does not denote existence, but rather denotes non-distinction. Furthermore, if the effect were not distinct from the cause, how could the proposition that "by knowing one, all is known" be sustained?
For if there were non-difference between cause and effect, it could be said that when the cause is known, the effect is also known,
because the effect is non-different from the known cause. But if the effect is non-existent, how [could there be] a cause?

All effects are known through consciousness, because everything indeed has consciousness as its essence. Furthermore, by the definitive statement that "only the clay is real," which establishes the reality of the cause alone, and by the declaration of the unreality of the effect through such expressions as "a mere modification of words" (*vācārambhaṇam*), it is shown that the effect does not exist apart from the cause.

It must be said that this is not what is being propounded by the scripture. For this scripture does not first establish the reality of clay and the unreality of its modification; rather, it restates as an example precisely what is already observed in the world, such as a clod of earth, because only what is well-known can serve as an illustration for both common people and investigators.
As the learned have stated: "That in which there is a consensus of understanding regarding a certain meaning is an illustration (dṛṣṭānta).

Therefore, it must be said that [the scripture] merely restates exactly what kind of reality is well-known in the world for clay, and what kind of unreality belongs to its modification; it does not [assert] an unreality consisting of sublated nature for the modification.

This is established by worldly consensus (*lokasiddha*). For at the time of the jar, no sublation (*bādha*) is perceived such that "the clay is not the jar. Furthermore, the correspondence with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is observed [in both]. Nor is the truth (*satyatva*) of the clay said to consist in its being unsublated (*abādhitatva*), because they do not admit that even that [clay] possesses truth. This applies to both the clay and the jar.

Furthermore, because they accept conventional reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*), they do not admit any specific kind of ultimate reality (*satyatva-viśeṣa*). However, since a jar and the like do not exist independently apart from clay, their lack of such existence constitutes their unreality (*anṛtatva*);
whereas the reality of the clay consists precisely in its independent existence prior to and subsequent to the jar.
And thus, apart from clay—that is, in the absence of the nature of clay—the characteristic of unreality is the non-existence [of those things] elsewhere.

With the intention that, by virtue of having that [clay] as its self, existence (*sattva*) therein conveys non-difference, it was stated: "The non-difference from that [cause] follows from such words as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*)," and so forth. Nor should it be argued: "It is not the case that there is an absence of existence elsewhere apart from the nature of clay; since even absolute non-existence (*atyantāsattva*) would not be tenable, how could this establish non-difference?"

Because absolute non-existence is untenable as an effect, and because the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in expressions such as "the clay jar" results in the determination of non-difference; thus it has been stated by those very [authorities] in the *Vākyānvaya* section:
having proposed that "by the knowledge of the Self, all is known," the subsequent text establishes that very point.

The scripture beginning with "Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as other than the Self" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10] refers to one who perceives the world— consisting of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth— as having its existence established independently, apart from the Self. Indeed, for such a person of false vision, that very Brahminhood, Kṣatriyahood, and the rest, which were falsely perceived, [desert him].

It effects the transcendence of the world by removing the perception of duality, leading one to realize that "all this is indeed the Self," thereby establishing that the entire range of existing things is non-different from the Self.
Furthermore, by the very statement that "the beginning is merely a modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), it demonstrates the unreality of the transformation and the reality of the material cause.
It is said: because it is not applicable to the subject at hand. Rather, non-difference alone is being stated. For this is the meaning of that sentence:

"ārambhaṇam" means that which is begun (ārabhyate). And this is a qualification of the name (nāmadheya), due to its neuter gender. Thus, a name such as "pot" and so forth is merely begun by speech; it is not [produced].

And it is not distinct from the clay; for an object such as a jar is derived from clay, and that modification, the jar and so forth, is truly only "clay. Thus, the internal non-difference of the modification from its material cause is established.

Non-difference alone is being established here. It is not the reality of the clay that is being asserted; for the scripture states, "Clay is real. Nor does the determination of the reality of non-difference entail the unreality of difference. Rather, in the passage "by which the unheard becomes heard," the term "unheard" denotes that which is different from what is heard; thus, by stating it as something entirely distinct, non-difference [is affirmed].
By the exclusion of the apprehension of difference, non-difference is indeed real;

or rather, the particle *eva* (only) is connected with the word "real" (*satyam*). Thus, only the exclusion of unreality (*asattva*) is perceived, and not the unreality of difference. Furthermore, if the jar were unreal apart from the clay, then it would simply be "not-jar."

Regarding what is perceived, it must be stated what its objective support (*ālambana*) is. It cannot be the clay alone; for since that [clay] exists even prior to the activity of the potter, it would follow that there is the perception "this is a jar" even at that time. Now, if it is something distinct from that [clay], does it exist within that clay or not? If it does not exist, how can there be the perceptual cognition "this is a jar"? For in the case of perception, the object must be present.

Because it is a cause. If it exists, how can it have existence (*satva*)? For the meaning of the word "existence" applies only to that which is already present, since terms such as *asti*, *bhavati*, and *vidyate* are synonyms. If you argue that this is something else entirely—a technical definition—namely, "the state of being unsublatable" (*abādhyatva*), then that too certainly exists in a jar; for it has already been stated that no sublation is observed in the case of a jar.

Now, [the opponent claims that] existence (*sattva*) consists in being uncontradicted at all times and in all places. But that does not belong to a jar. If you argue that its contradiction occurs only in another location, then, given its permanence, it would follow that it possesses omnipresence (*vibhutva*), and its contradiction would likewise imply non-existence (*asattva*).
And such non-existence is indeed accepted in the case of jars and the like; for who could ever maintain that an effect is both permanent and omnipresent?

This is indeed accepted. Now, if it is argued that "unreality" (asattva) is simply the non-existence of the jar's independent existence elsewhere apart from the clay, and that this very state constitutes its falsity (mithyātva), then this too is not undesirable.

For no one accepts the existence of the derived elsewhere as something independent, apart from its material cause. If it is on this ground that you call it "false," then let it be so called; however, even this has not been stated in the Sūtra, because the word "false" (mithyātva) does not appear in the Sūtra.

[Objection: Even if falsity is established through the statement regarding "the beginning of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), it is nonetheless established by other statements as well—such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'Not this, not this'"; for from these passages, the absence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in Brahman is perceived. [Reply: No.

Therefore, [the text] "one only, without a second" establishes falsity (*mithyātva*). Although this [text] conveys the non-existence of that [world] prior to the origination of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it does not convey its non-existence at the time of the phenomenal world; rather, it conveys the falsity of the very absence of that [world] existing at that time. This is because [that absence] is the determinant (*prayojaka*) [of falsity], being co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with itself.

For it is defined that falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) co-temporal with itself. Nor is its establishment [attained] from the statement "There is no diversity here whatsoever" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*), because that [text] conveys the absence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in Brahman; it conveys precisely the absence of difference from Brahman. For it is said: "Not even in respect of place... (*na sthānato 'pi*).

Regarding the statement, "The other [scriptures] show both characteristics everywhere," it means that in Brahman there is no inherent or positional contradiction of two opposing forms; rather, it is that same single Brahman everywhere. For it has been stated that two contradictory forms cannot possibly exist within this [Brahman]. [Objection: Well then, let Brahman be different with respect to each limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); it is not one and the same. Therefore—
