(228) Having raised the objection that two forms might exist, it was stated that there is no duality in Brahman because scripture teaches precisely the non-difference [of Brahman] with respect to each limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This is further clarified in that very same passage: "If it be argued that [the difference of the world] is due to difference [of adjuncts], we say no, because [scripture] declares the opposite for each."

Another scriptural passage has been cited as corroboration. Furthermore, the meaning of the phrase "And some indeed [say] thus" has been stated by those very same [authorities]. Moreover, certain followers of particular recensions (śākhins), after first censuring the perception of difference, declare the non-duality of Brahman:
"What is here, that is there; what is there, that is here. He goes from death to death who perceives any diversity here."
Thus, since this [text] does not negate the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) with respect to Brahman,

the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the world is not established by it. Nor is the falsity established by the sentence "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), because that too establishes that Brahman is distinct from the formed and the formless (*mūrtāmūrta*), rather than establishing its absolute non-existence.

For it is thus: "It denies the limitedness of that which is under discussion, and then it speaks further. Since the word "only" (*eva*) has the sense of restriction, the Śruti—"Not so, not so"—denies that the Brahman under discussion consists merely of these two forms, namely the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), or merely that much. Thus, it negates that Brahman is limited to just the formed and the formless.

It does not mean that [it] does not exist; rather, the sentence "He speaks of what is even more abundant, more numerous, and greater than even that which is both formed and formless" (na hy etasmāt) has this meaning: there is nothing else superior to this Brahman designated by "No" and so forth; this alone is supreme to everything. Thus, by this sentence, [the text establishes] the [supremacy of Brahman over] the manifested world of the formed and the formless.
It is understood that by refuting the absolute non-difference of Brahman, difference alone is established; and this will be demonstrated in that very place. (p.

Therefore, when there is the suspicion that "absolute difference" follows from the negation of absolute non-difference, [the Sūtra] states "And non-distinctness, like light and so forth" (*prakāśādivaccāvaiśeṣyam*). Having stated non-difference as well by means of the Sūtra "And light [is non-distinct] in the act [of seeing], because of repetition" (*prakāśaśca karmaṇyabhyāsāt*), then, when there is the suspicion that there is a contradiction between difference and non-difference, [it is answered] by "But because of the designation of both, it is like a coil, etc. (*ubhayavyapadeśāttvahi kuṇḍalavat* etc.).
The lack of contradiction with the Sūtra has been established.

Thus, it has been stated in the sūtra *anyabhāvavyāvṛtteśca* that even by sentences such as "not gross" (*asthūla*), only the exclusion of grossness and so forth is perceived. Consequently, the falsity [of the world] is not established even by this sentence.
Therefore, it is established that falsity lacks any basis in valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*) because it is not supported by the sūtras. Furthermore, if—

The meaning of the word "otherness" (*anyatva*) is not the non-existence of the effect apart from the cause. If it were intended that the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) does not exist apart from Brahman, then a contradiction with what precedes and follows would arise; for later on, in the section beginning with "There is no non-existence, because [the world] is perceived," the actual existence of the world-phenomenon apart from Brahman is established. Likewise...

For in that regard, according to the Vijñānavādin, there is no external object distinct from consciousness; even if an external object exists, since the practical application of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is impossible without its ascent into the intellect (*buddhi*), the entire practical application of means of knowledge and the rest is established as being internal, by way of a form mounted upon the intellect. Indeed, there is no external object [independent of it].

It is possible [that it exists]. For that external object must be either atoms (*paramāṇu*) or their collection, such as pillars and the like. First of all, they cannot be atoms, because the appearance of something gross and so forth would be untenable in them, and because it would follow that cognition would have the appearance of atoms. Nor can it be their collection, because of the dilemma of whether those [collections] are different from or non-different from the atoms.
Because it is difficult to define.

In this way, there is likewise the non-existence of birth and so forth. Furthermore, since cognition arises as something common in its essential nature through mere experience, this partiality toward each respective object—such as "cognition of a pillar" or "cognition of a wall"—is not possible without a specific distinction inherent in every cognition; therefore, [this distinction must necessarily exist].

One must admit that cognition possesses a similarity of form (*sārūpya*) with its object. And once that is accepted, since the form of the object is already encompassed by the cognition itself, the postulation of an external object is purposeless;
this should be understood as being like dreams and so forth. For just as in dreams, illusions, and the water of a mirage...

Just as the cognitions of a city of Gandharvas and the like occur without any external object corresponding to the forms of the grasped and the grasper, it is understood that even the cognitions pertaining to the waking state— such as those of pillars, walls, and so forth— must likewise exist [without external objects], because there is no difference in their being cognitions. Such being the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) reached:

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "There is no non-existence, because [things] are perceived. Its meaning has been stated by those very same [masters]: "Indeed, it is not proper to accept the non-existence of external objects. Why? Because they are perceived. For in every cognition, an external object—such as a pillar, a wall, and so forth—is indeed perceived. And for that which is being perceived, non-existence is not possible."
This must be understood as follows: just as someone who is eating,

while personally experiencing the satisfaction that is the result of eating, might say, "I am not eating, nor am I satisfied," so too, even while personally perceiving an external object through the contact of the sense organs, one might say, "I do not perceive it, nor does it exist."

How could one who speaks thus be considered a person whose words are to be accepted? I do not say this: "I do not perceive an external object. Rather, I say: "I do not perceive anything distinct from the perception itself.
"Indeed, you speak thus; however, it is due to the unrestrained nature of your tongue, for you do not speak in accordance with reason. Since—"
The existence of an object distinct from its apprehension must also be accepted by necessity, precisely because of that apprehension itself.
231) For no one perceives the apprehension itself as a pillar or a wall; rather, [they perceive them] as the objects of apprehension.

All worldly people perceive pillars, walls, and so forth; however, it has not been stated that external objects are impossible. For possibility and impossibility are preceded by the operation of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but the operation or non-operation of valid means of knowledge is not preceded by possibility and impossibility. If...

That which is apprehended by even one of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as direct perception, is possible; however, that which is not apprehended by any [means of valid cognition] whatsoever is impossible. But here, since the external object is apprehended by all the means of valid cognition according to their respective natures, how could it be [denied] through conceptual constructions such as "distinct" or "non-distinct"?

It is said that [the object] exists because of its perception. Furthermore, the existence of an object does not depend on the cognition’s similarity to that object, for such a similarity to the object is untenable; moreover, the object is perceived as being external.
As for what was stated—that waking cognitions might occur even without an external object, like cognitions in dreams and the like—[that is refuted].

"Because there is no difference in their being conditions. To this he replies: "And because of dissimilarity, it is not like dreams and so forth. Cognitions of external objects cannot be like dreams. Why? Because of dissimilarity. What, then, is the dissimilarity? It is sublation and non-sublation. For an object perceived in a dream is sublated by one who has awakened.

"The gathering of the great multitude was perceived through delusion; for there is no such thing as a gathering of a great multitude. My mind, however, became weary with sleep, and by that this error arose. In the same way, sublation occurs accordingly even in the case of illusions and the like. But it is not so in the case of what is perceived while awake.
The pillar and so forth are sublated at some stage [of waking].
Furthermore, that which is the seeing of a dream is memory (*smṛti*), whereas the seeing of the waking state is perception (*upalabdhi*).
And the difference between memory and perception is experienced by oneself directly.
(232) I remember my beloved son, whose nature consists of both separation from and union with his objects; I do not perceive him,
yet I desire to perceive him.

This being the case, it cannot be argued that "the perception of the waking state is false because it is a type of perception, like the perception of a dream," for one who personally experiences the difference between the two. Furthermore, it is not proper for those who consider themselves wise to deny their own experience; moreover, if the perception of the waking state were an illusion, it would simply not exist.

The perception in a dream would be a sublater [of the probandum]. For an error does not become a sublater, according to the definition that "sublation by a valid cognition consists in the absence of the probandum. Consequently, the example of seeing things in a dream and so forth would be devoid of the probandum.

Thus, by the author of the Sūtra establishing an external object as distinct from consciousness, an external object that is distinct from [the internal] has indeed been established as being unrefuted. Nor should it be said that its "unrefuted" status therein refers merely to conventional truth (*vyāvahārika-satya*); for even by the proponents of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavādin*), the external object is admitted as conventional.

Because they accept its truth; for they employ the term "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) precisely to denote "transactional truth" (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*). Consequently, by first refuting their position and then establishing an uncontradicted object, it is ultimately the absolute truth (*pāramārthika-satyatva*) itself that has been established.

Furthermore, what else? Because it is impossible to define it as being "other" and so forth. Or is it unreal because it is sublated? For the determination of the true nature of things does not depend on verbal definition, but rather on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Even if a thing is inexpressible—either due to the limited intellect of persons or because of the extraordinary nature of the object itself—[it remains real].

This is because it would be established as ultimately real, like a specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇya*) or a universal (*sāmānya*), existing as something present before one's face in contradiction to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is the latter [option] tenable, because such a thing is not perceived.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that the scriptural passage, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone," serves as a sublation [of this view].

For this [text] does not teach the absence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) during the state of knowledge (*vidyā*); for if that were so, it would follow that others would likewise not perceive it. Nor does the phrase "of this" refer to a specific person or a particular individual.

It makes the existence [of the self] known. For it is said: "Having arisen from these very elements as a mass of consciousness alone, one vanishes again into them; after death, there is no consciousness. Upon hearing this, Maitreyī said, "In this very matter, sir, you have bewildered me; that there is no consciousness after death implies the destruction of the self, which partakes in liberation, and that is not tenable."
Thus questioned, Yājñavalkya said: "Indeed, I do not speak of liberation here;
rather, O venerable one, this Self is indestructible, for its nature is non-perishing. Non-perishing means it is not subject to destruction.
What, then, does it mean to "perish along with"? It means that it does not cease to exist after death.
It has been stated that "perception exists. Therefore, he says: "But there occurs for him a union with the mother. The meaning of this is as follows:

there is a union of this Self, residing in the heart, with the "mothers"—namely, the elemental matrices (*bhūtamātrā*) and the cognitive matrices (*prajñāmātrā*), which are the sense organs together with their objects—once they have departed from their respective locations.
There is a merging into oneness like that of water and milk. For thus it is heard in scripture: "Speech merges into the mind;

the mind into breath; breath into heat; heat into the deity that is the Sun. In this very way, at the time of death, all the vital breaths gather together into this Self. He, taking up these particles of light...

It descends into the heart itself. When this person consisting of sight turns away, then one becomes unaware of forms; "he becomes one," they say, "he does not see. And the author of the Sūtras will state this, beginning with "Speech [merges] into the mind, because it is seen [from scripture] and because of the word," and ending with "non-distinction, because of the statement."
By the perfection of the sense-organs as perceivers, the perfection of the objects to be perceived should also be understood.
234) Thus, for all tactile sensations, the skin is the single point of convergence; these are indeed the ten elemental constituents (*bhūtamātrā*).

With respect to higher wisdom, they are merely the ten forms of wisdom. With respect to the elements, if they were merely the elements and not merely wisdom, [they would not be established]; and if they were merely wisdom and not the elements, [they would not be established]. For form cannot be established from either one alone. It is not that these are different; it is just as, for example, the spokes of a chariot wheel are fixed upon the hub, and the rim is fixed upon the spokes.

In this very way, these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are deposited in the cognitions (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the cognitions are deposited in the vital breath (prāṇa). Regarding the mutual dependence of the objects denoted by the term "elements" and the sense organs denoted by the term "cognitions," [this dependence exists] in their relationship as the grasped and the grasper.

Furthermore, by demonstrating the non-presentation of objects, it is established that even with the perfection of the perceiving sense-faculties, the non-perfection of the perceived object is necessary;
for this very reason, even in deep sleep— as when one who is asleep sees no dream whatsoever— in this [state]...

"Prāṇa alone becomes one; then speech, together with all names, passes away into it," and so forth. By this, through the dissolution of the perceiving organs, the dissolution of the objects of perception is also expressed. At that time, the dissolution of the object consists precisely in its lack of being perceived; it is not that the other things are destroyed or dissolved into the Brahman within the heart in their own essential form.

Because it would follow that there is no perception of objects; for those two [dream and waking] came to a sleeping man. Furthermore, because the existence of the body and so forth is established by the scripture and the sūtra stating, "The absence of that [dreaming] occurs in the channels, and in the Self, according to scriptural testimony," and as it has been stated in the *Kalpataru* under the section on the Deities (*Devatādhikaraṇa*) regarding the origination of waking and deep sleep through the presence and absence of cognition.
Regarding the expression "layābhidhāna" (designation as dissolution):
this very contact with the *mātrās* is metaphorically designated as "destruction" because it is the cause of perception. And of this...

He demonstrates through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the cause is the absence of knowledge: "For where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see?
Here, in the waking state and so forth, there is "as it were" duality, but not oneness. Or, the word "as it were" has a comparative sense: just as duality [is perceived].

A jar, a cloth, and so forth become distinct; likewise, the sense organs as well. Having emerged from the heart and gone to their respective locations, they perform their own functions because the instruments are differentiated; thus, one perceives the other. In that state of death, everything becomes the Self alone, by virtue of being the material cause of all, according to the path previously described.
Or, because the individual soul (*jīva*), whose organs have been withdrawn by means of the non-different Brahman, attains oneness with it;

then, due to the absence of division, who could see whom? For this very reason, it is heard in scripture that even during deep sleep and similar states, there is an absence of knowledge due to the absence of division such as agency, for "there is not a second thing there, other than that which is divided."
"Whatever one might see," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: how can there be an absence of knowledge in deep sleep? For it has been stated that "there is no loss of vision because of its imperishability," and so on, thereby declaring that vision and the other faculties are indestructible. To this, we say: no.

Because the non-destruction of vision (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth is not established therein; for vision and the rest are not merely cognition (*jñāna*). If that were the case, then from a statement such as "the cloth is white," there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the blind and others, upon cognizing whiteness, would employ the linguistic convention "I see white. Rather [vision and so forth] are produced by specific instruments (*karaṇa*) such as the eye.
It is knowledge alone;
and its impermanence is not possible. Therefore, it possesses the nature of being the seer and so forth.

This is intended to mean the absence of the loss of capacity; otherwise, since one hears such statements as "there is no destruction of the speaker's speech," it would follow that even actions such as speaking are eternal. Indeed, no one accepts that an action, like knowledge, is eternal. Therefore, the absence of knowledge during deep sleep is indeed established.
The author of the Sūtras will state this: "Because it is declared [in scripture] that [the soul's state] depends on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or union with the Supreme (*sampatti*).

Therefore, since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). Furthermore, falsity (*mithyātva*) contradicts the Sūtra: "Because [contradictory attributes] cannot coexist in one [entity]" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.11), which refers to a single reality.

Because [the scripture] states that "neither existence nor non-existence, etc., can be predicated of the Supreme even in terms of location," and because it explicitly rejects the doctrine of falsity by declaring that neither form and so forth nor their absence are possible in Brahman— since He is devoid of both characteristics in every respect.

Some, however, assert an absolute non-difference between cause and effect. For instance, no distinct substance called a "pot" arises within the clay; rather, a single substance, having abandoned its state as a lump, attains the state of a pot, and then, having abandoned the state of a pot, attains the state of shards, and so forth.

Thus, the production of a substance is nothing other than the attainment of a different state, and destruction is nothing other than the relinquishing of that state. In this regard, are these states absolutely distinct from the substance, or are they absolutely non-distinct?
In the first case, how could the states be adventitious, given their absolute non-difference from the substance which exists [permanently]? In the second case...

How is it that through the knowledge of one [substance], there is the knowledge of all? Because even when a substance is known, its various states are also known. Yet, it should not be said that through the knowledge of one there is literally the knowledge of all; rather, "the knowledge of all" refers to the knowledge of [all] states as well.

237) Because there is no reason for such contraction, and because it is impossible for a single substance to possess the property of being "all" [simultaneously]. As for the third [alternative], what offense has been committed by substances such as jars, which are established by worldly experience? Furthermore, [it is untenable].

If origination were merely the attainment of another state, then there would be no origination of states, because [the substance] lacks other states. If one accepts that states possess other states, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Alternatively, if origination is the substance itself attaining a state, then as for the states, they do not exist previously...

If it is argued that "becoming" (*bhavana*) means "origination" (*utpatti*), we say no. Let origination be simply the coming into being of a substance after not having existed; enough with the conceptualization of a distinct origination. Furthermore, by such passages as "It created fire," the origination of substances alone is taught in the scripture (*āmnāya*).
This is because words such as "fire" denote substances possessing form (*rūpa*), and do not denote states, since those [states] lack form.

If one accepts that [Brahman] possesses form (*rūpavat*), it would result in merely giving a different name to the state of the substance itself. Nor can it be argued that it is the substance—which possesses those states—that has form, and not the states themselves; for Brahman is devoid of form, and since it lacks parts (*niravayava*), the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of its states would be impossible.

Therefore, it is established that only substances are produced, and that they are distinct from one another. Thus, beginning with the sūtra "And because the arrangement is impossible, there is no inference" and ending with "and because of contradiction," [the author] demonstrates that [the Sāṅkhya system is untenable] due to the mutual contradictions among the tantras, the internal inconsistencies between earlier and later parts, and the contradictions with the Śruti.

Even though their authority has been established, those commentaries by Tantric authors which— by assigning different names to the very subjects of the Tantra and through the application of definitions, ellipses, and so forth to the Sūtras— aim at the meaning of the Tantra, are indeed in contradiction with the Sūtras.

(238) Likewise, although the Sūtra has already indicated that the individual soul (jīva) is a knower by stating "for this very reason [the soul] is ignorant," the subsequent description of it as being of the nature of knowledge is also contrary to the Sūtra. Furthermore, although the Sūtra has indicated that the soul is atomic by stating "[it possesses] departure, movement, and return,"...
The assertion of [the soul's] greatness contradicts the Sūtra.

Nor should it be said that, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) on the basis of its atomicity (*aṇutva*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached through its "having the quality of goodness as its essence" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*) because of its greatness; for that [Sūtra] does not establish greatness. To explain how this Sūtra [functions]:

It must be considered what is intended by "the engagement" (*pravṛtti*). Is this begun because of the inquiry: "If the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of knowledge, what is the status of the designation of its non-difference from knowledge? Or is it more appropriate to say that this is begun because of the inquiry: "Once the greatness of the individual soul is established, what is the status of the designations such as 'atomicity' (*aṇutva*)?"

For instance, having established the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*) through the passages concerning its departure, its movement, and its going, as well as through the subsequent two [sūtras] regarding its own nature, a doubt arises: "Is it not the case that because of the scriptural statement of its greatness—'This very Self is great and unborn' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22)—it cannot be atomic? To this, [the sūtra] states:

"It is not atomic, on account of the scriptural statement to that effect" (BrSū 2.3.21), meaning that since the scriptural statement regarding greatness refers to Brahman, there is no contradiction with its atomicity.

Having stated "because of the context of what is other than that," and having further reinforced the very atom-like nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) through both its own scriptural designation and inference, [the Sūtra] addresses the doubt as to how an action pervading the entire body can occur if the soul is atomic,
by stating "there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood. This refers to a drop of sandalwood paste situated in only one part of the body.

Having stated that just as [the fragrance of sandalwood] produces delight by pervading the entire body, so too can this be established for the individual soul (jīva), [the opponent replies]: "Let it be so in that case, since the fact that a drop of sandalwood occupies only one location is established by direct perception; however, in this case, since there is no evidence for the soul's occupation of only one location, its all-pervasiveness must be accepted in accordance with the effects observed throughout the entire body."

(239) Anticipating the objection, "Why should this not be so?", [the Sūtra] states: "If it be argued that it is because of the difference in state, we say no, because it is accepted [by scripture], as in 'He is in the heart'.

For even with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*), its abiding in a specific part of the body—the heart—is established by such scriptural passages as, "That very Self is in the heart," and so forth.
Because [the Lord] is already established, He does not perform any further action, according to the maxim of the drop of sandalwood paste; thus, another supporting argument has been stated:

"Or [He acts] through His quality, like light. Even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic, its capacity for pervasive action is achieved through the pervasion of its quality of consciousness (*caitanya*).
Now, to address the doubt as to how a quality can exist apart from the substance possessing that quality, it is said: "The separation [of the quality from the substance] is like that of fragrance."

This would be so if consciousness were a quality distinct from fragrance; however, consciousness is not a quality, but rather the very nature [of the self]. Thus, in response to the doubt that if it were all-pervasive, the self itself would necessarily be all-pervasive, [the sūtra states] "because of the separate instruction," namely: "having withdrawn the body by means of intelligence."

It has been stated that because of the teaching of the difference between knowledge and the Self, [knowledge] is not the essential nature [of the Self], but rather a mere attribute (guṇa). If, then, knowledge is an attribute, how can there be the designation of non-difference from knowledge in the Self in the passage, "Knowledge performs the sacrifice"? In response to this inquiry, the following is set forth: "But that designation [of the Self as knowledge] is due to its having that [knowledge] as its essence."

In the phrase "like one who is wise" (*prājñavat*), the word "that" (*tat*) in both instances refers to the knowledge mentioned previously, because pronouns denote what is proximate. The compound *tadguṇa* is a *karmadhāraya*, meaning "that which has those qualities.
One whose essence (*sāra*) consists of those qualities is *tadguṇasāra*. The state of being that is its "nature" (*tattva*); from that [nature] comes the designation (*vyapadeśa*).

The designation "knowledge" [is applied] because of its essential nature as the quality of knowledge. Just as a lump of rock salt (*saindhava-khilya*) is designated as "salt" because its essential quality is salinity, so too the omniscient Lord is designated as "knowledge" because His essence consists of the quality of knowledge. In passages such as "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*), this very position is the appropriate one.
(240) When the intention is to address the question of what the status of the designation "atomic" (*aṇutva*) is, it is appropriate that this [section] has commenced;
for previously, the greatness of the individual soul (*jīva*) was asserted and proofs were presented, [only] if the Self were great.

One might ask: what is the status of that designation of the self as "atomic" (*aṇu*)? It cannot be said that the greatness of the self was previously asserted, nor has any proof been adduced [for it]. How, then, could such an expectation arise all of a sudden? Nor can it be argued that because Brahman is great, the greatness of the individual soul (*jīva*) has already been stated due to its non-difference from Him.

For in this way, the sūtra "If it be said that [the soul is] not atomic because of scriptural statement, we say no, on account of the reference to the other" would indeed be untenable. For that sūtra was intended to establish that the soul does not possess magnitude— responding to the objection that its atomicity is contradicted by the perception of magnitude in the scriptural text, "Now, this great unborn Self"— by showing that the scriptural mention of magnitude refers to Brahman and not to the individual soul.

[The discussion] has proceeded. For if the greatness of the individual soul (*jīva*) were not indeed [identical to] the greatness of Brahman, how could the doubt regarding the greatness of the soul have been resolved by the statement, "Because of the reference to the other"?
Therefore, since the greatness of the soul was previously asserted without the presentation of any supporting authority, [the opponent suggests] that it must then be atomic (*aṇu*).
It has already been stated that this sūtra was composed because of the inquiry as to what the status of the designation (*vyapadeśa*) is.

Furthermore, the meaning of the sūtra is also inconsistent with that [opponent’s] view. For, according to that view, the meaning of the sūtra is as follows: by the first word *tat*, the suffix *-ant* is understood; and *tad-guṇāḥ* (its qualities) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

By the second word "that" (tat), qualities such as atomicity (*aṇutva*) and so forth are referred to. Thus, because the individual soul (*jīva*) has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its substrate, it is designated as atomic and so on, just like the Supreme Lord (*prājña*). Furthermore, it is not appropriate for the first word "that" to refer to the internal organ, because that has not been previously introduced in the context.

Furthermore, because the word *tat* (that) refers to the subject at hand, if it were a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the fault would be that one must resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the prior member for the meaning of the elided genitive case.

In the second [interpretation], there is the fault that the word "that" (tat) refers back to "atomicity" (aṇutva), which is separated [in the text]. Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "because its essence consists of the qualities of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa-guṇa-sāratvāt*)—is unestablished (*asiddha*). For it is not established in the world that the individual soul (*jīva*) has the internal organ as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), nor is it accepted by anyone. Nor is it so in the case of the "wise one" (*prājña*) in the illustrative example.

There exists the state of having the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Nor is it possible for those who assert that the greatness of the individual soul (*jīva*) is due to the greatness of the Supreme Lord (*prājña*) to maintain either a relationship of illustration and illustrated (*dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika-bhāva*) between the Supreme Lord and the individual soul. Furthermore, the subsequent sūtra is indeed consistent with our own position: "And because it persists as long as the self exists, there is no fault, since that is seen" (*yāvad-ātmabhāvitvācca na doṣastaddarśanāt*), regarding knowledge.

Even if [the opponent] were to concede [that knowledge exists], the quality of existing as long as the self (*yāvad-ātma-bhāvitva*) is possible there; nor should it be argued that because knowledge is absent during deep sleep and so forth, how can it exist as long as the self?
For, like the power of burning and so forth, that which already exists becomes manifest; thus, while it is non-existent in its causal form, it exists in its complete, manifest form.

This has already been refuted by the statement that manifestation occurs at the time of awakening. Furthermore, on that view, since the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) undergoes absolute destruction upon liberation, it is impossible for it to persist as long as the self exists; for it has been shown by you yourself that its limitation consists in its persisting only as long as the transmigrating self exists.

Likewise, the aphorism stating that "otherwise there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or non-perception, or the restriction to one or the other" is indeed favorable to our own position. For it has been established that the self is atomic and possesses cognition as its quality. If that were not accepted—namely, if the self were omnipresent and of the nature of cognition—then by an omnipresent self...

Because the object would be in constant contact with consciousness, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perpetual perception. On that [opponent's] view, however, if the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) were not admitted, there would be perpetual perception whenever the self, the senses, and the objects are in proximity; therefore, [the size of the self] must be restricted. Consequently, the meaning of the Sūtra is precisely its atomicity (aṇutva), and thus the demonstration of the individual soul's (jīva) greatness [is refuted].
This is indeed contrary to the Sūtras;
for instance, by the Sūtra "The Self is an agent because the scriptures have purpose," etc., the agency of the Self has been established.

The designation "non-doer" (akartṛ) is indeed made out of adherence to the Sāṅkhya doctrine. Nor should it be argued that, as in the case of the carpenter, agency in the Self is merely adventitious (aupādhika), for adventitiousness is not perceived in the Sūtra. And as for the example of the carpenter, [agency exists] only when there is a desire [to act].

Just as one performs work with the perfection of instruments such as an axe only when there is consciousness [of purpose] and not otherwise, so too the living self (jīva) performs actions only when desire exists and it is endowed with instruments such as the mind, and not otherwise;
for this much alone is understood from the Sūtra, and because the term "conditioned" (aupādhika) is absent [therein]. This is because the carpenter lacks conditioned agency [in the absence of tools].

Furthermore, by the force of that very example, agency is also established as being adventitious (*aupādhika*). Moreover, if the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) is adventitious, then whose is it natural? If you say it belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*), that is not so; for in both common worldly usage and the Veda, that [intellect] is well-known as the instrument (*karaṇa*), being designated as the "internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Because agency is impossible. And it has been stated by the author of the Sūtras: "Because of the reversal of capacity" (*sūtrakṛtāśaktiviparyayāt*). Its meaning was explained by those very [commentators] as follows: "For, by virtue of the intellect's capacity as an instrument (*karaṇa-śakti*), this [intellect] would incur the capacity for agency (*kartṛ-śakti*). And if the capacity for agency were present in it, then it alone would become the object of the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*). [This is] egoism (*ahaṃkāra*).
Because we observe that activity proceeds everywhere from that very same [consciousness] alone, as in "I go" and "I come.

Furthermore, for that [consciousness], which is endowed with the power of agency, some other instrument must be postulated to accomplish all objects, for even a capable agent in the world proceeds by employing an instrument. Consequently, the dispute is merely over a name.
"There might be no difference in meaning, because agency is admitted for that which is distinct from the instruments. [To this it is replied:
"But surely, by the scriptural text 'This person is indeed unattached,' there is an absence of all connection in the Self."

If it is argued that since [the scripture] teaches [the absence of desire], how can there be agency in the Self in the absence of the conjunction with causal signs (*nimitta*), we say no; for this scriptural passage establishes the absence of desire in dreamless sleep, not the absence of connection [to causal signs]. To explain: when Janaka asked, "Now, speak further for the sake of liberation," he was inquiring about the means to liberation.
Yājñavalkya, intending to show that action alone performed with attachment is binding— and thus that attachment must be abandoned— demonstrates the absence of bondage when attachment is absent:
"He, indeed, having reached this state of serene bliss, having moved about, and having seen both the auspicious and the evil, returns again..."

"It returns according to its rule and according to its source, as if for the sake of sleep. Whatever it sees there, it does not carry over with it; for this person is unattached. The meaning of this is as follows: this aforementioned *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness), in this state of *saṃprasāda* (serenity) previously described as dream—although the word *saṃprasāda* [is used here]...

Although the term *suṣupti* denotes deep sleep, it is understood here as referring specifically to dreaming, because in deep sleep there is an absence of pleasure (*rati*) and so forth. Having enjoyed pleasure (*ratvā*) with his wife and others, having moved through various places (*caritvā*),
and having seen both meritorious and sinful deeds (*dṛṣṭvaiva puṇyaṃ ca pāpaṃ ca karma*), he [returns] by the very same path through which he departed from that body.

By that very same path, he returns to a human or other body as if for a dream. Whatever meritorious or sinful karma he perceives there in that previous dream, he does not carry it with him. The reason for this is "because he is unattached" (*asaṅga*). Since he was unattached and free from desire (*akāma*) in that previous dream, therefore he does not follow after it.
He goes.

Is it not the case that the absence of desire (*akāmatva*) is unestablished in the dream state? For there is the scriptural hearing: "That immortal one goes wherever he desires" (*sa īyate 'mṛto yatra kāmaḥ*), which indicates the existence of desire; in response to this doubt:
p.

244) There is another section for the purpose of establishing the absence of desire: "Indeed, having moved about in this state of dream, and having seen both merit and evil, he returns again to his place of departure, rushing back according to his original course."

"Only unto the end of waking. Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it; for this person is unattached. "Unto the end of waking" means unto the end of the waking state. The rest is like the dream [section]. For if desire existed in the dream, the action performed while attached to it would persist even in the waking state; yet it does not persist. Indeed, in the dream...

Upon awakening, one who has committed a sin considers himself to have been praised; nor does he think, "I was praised by someone in a dream. Having heard such words from the dreamer, the awakener either censures him or dismisses him.
Therefore, there is indeed no desire in a dream. This very point has also been stated by them: "For this [Self] is unattached."

Regarding the term "puruṣa": non-attachment (*asaṅgatā*) has been stated as the reason for his being a non-agent (*akartṛ*). And it is said: "He goes where he desires, immortal. Attachment is desire; therefore, the reason is established, as stated in the *Upaniṣadbhāṣya*:
"Because of non-attachment, he is a non-agent."
"Is this not unestablished, since desire is seen in dreams, according to the Śruti passage, 'Where one's desire [is]...'?

To refute this, there is the statement beginning with "sa vā... (That indeed...). Thus it is said in the Vārttika. Ānandagiri explains that the words *asaṅga* (non-attachment) and *kāma* (desire) are synonymous.

And thus, since desires exist in the dream state as mere appearances, the manifestation of chariots and so forth should be understood as having the objects of desire belonging to the waking state as their basis. The Śruti also speaks with this manifestation in mind. Nor should it be suspected that because of the statement regarding non-attachment (*asaṅga*), there are no desires even in the waking state; for if there were an absence of desires even in the waking state, [there would likewise be none] in the dream state.

Because that would entail the experience of that [dream object] as such; for it is precisely what is seen in the waking state that appears in the dream, according to the scripture: "Whatever one sees in the waking state, those very things appear in the dream," and "Whatever fear one perceives while awake, that one imagines here through ignorance."

For this very reason, it is said: "Having dwelt and moved about in this state of waking, and having seen both merit and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, toward the state of dream itself. Thus, the term "unattached" (*asaṅga*) does not apply to the passage concerning the waking state.

It is heard [in scripture]. Nor should it be suspected that one wakes up only when [the desire] has reached the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because desire is impossible for that [organ], as it is insentient. This very point was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference" (BS 3.2.41). Nor should it be suspected that the subsequent activity in a dream occurs simply due to the absence of desire, rather than from the presence of desire.
It is by its own light that this [self] sits, moves about, and performs actions, because action is shown to exist in the state of dream;

and since the performance of actions such as seeing deities is possible there, it is untenable for that [dream-self] to be non-conscious or not created by the Self. That too is incorrect, because those very two Selves have entered the cave.

Regarding the word "hi" (for/indeed) here: in reality, agency does not belong to anything at all, because the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient and the self (*ātman*) is devoid of activity. Nor is it the case that the self lacks activity, because activity such as "I am doing" is directly perceived in the self. And thus, with regard to the self, there are various [modifications], for [the text says] "and indeed various. "Various" means manifold transformations.

And because it is established by the Sūtras. Therefore, agency belongs to the Self as its very nature (*svābhāvikam*). Nor should it be argued that if agency were inherent like the heat of fire, it would not cease to exist during states such as deep sleep; for inherent nature does not mean "existing as long as the substance exists," but rather "not being superimposed. [This is evident] in the case of a jar's capacity for cooking or holding water.

For it is universally accepted that even qualities such as heat (hiti) and the like are inherent by virtue of being non-conditional (*anaupādhika*), despite not persisting for the entire duration of the substance; whereas in the case of the jujube (*badara*) and the pilu fruit, their dark and black colors, though persisting for the entire duration of the substance, are merely conditional (*aupādhika*). Nor is agency (*kartṛtva*) superimposed [upon the Self] on the basis of the scriptural passage, "It meditates as it were, it moves as it were."
It cannot be said that [the Self] is perceived as being conditioned (*sopādhika*).
For here, the use of the word "as if" (*iva*) is due to the absence of meditation and so forth, and not due to the absence of agency (*kartṛtva*). Therefore—

Therefore, agency is unconditioned (*anaupādhika*). Likewise, there is a restrictive rule for all [meditations] because there is no contradiction, as established by both scripture and inference; for it has been stated in the Sūtras that the path of the gods (*devayāna*) is to be combined with all meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vijñāna*).
Thus, the claim that there is no inclusion of the path of the gods in the meditation on the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-vijñāna*) is contrary to the Sūtras. Furthermore, ...
Because of this traditional teaching: "The two who drink the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest supreme abode" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad);
and "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad and Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad)—these [texts] refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) characterized by duality.
Because the quality of being a means for establishing Brahman is equal [in all three], and because the knowledge (*vidyā*) is non-different due to the unity of the object of knowledge (*vedyaikya*),
one might think that there should be a combination (*upasaṃhāra*) of the attributes found in the three Upaniṣads.
However, having himself explained that even the three Upaniṣads establish the attribute-less (*nirguṇa*) Brahman, there is no combination of attributes.
Thus, it is quite clear that this presentation is inconsistent with the Sūtra.

Likewise, [the rule] "from desire and so forth elsewhere, and from the abodes and so forth there" applies. Now, regarding the knowledge contained in the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, which begins: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space (ākāśa)," [it continues]: "That indeed is this great, unborn Self, which is this..."

"Consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths; he lies in that space which is within the heart"— based on this [scriptural passage] from the sixth chapter of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, and because of the commonality of the heart being the abode, its being a bridge, and its being the cause of the non-confusion of worlds, one should assume the identity of the knowledge (vidyā) through the identity of the object of knowledge.

Having himself stated that there is a synthesis of the qualities such as "desire" (*kāma*) found in the *Chāndogya* into the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, and likewise a synthesis of the qualities found in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* into the *Chāndogya*,
[the author] says of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "He indeed is not this, not that" (*sa vā eṣa neti*).

(247) Furthermore, the demonstration that there is no combination of qualities here because the passage teaches Brahman with attributes— as established by examining the subsequent sentence beginning with "no"— is likewise inconsistent with the Sūtra.

Nor does this [negation] "not this, not that" constitute a negation of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), for it has been stated that its purpose is merely to establish the distinction between the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). Furthermore, there is no Brahman devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) by virtue of which the statements concerning the quality-less could have any validity; for there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) and because it has never been set forth as a sūtra anywhere. Nor...

Scriptural passages such as "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, the witness, consciousness, alone, and devoid of qualities" provide the authority for its being devoid of qualities. For it is stated in the Sūtra: "Because it is formless, indeed, on account of its being the primary [subject]" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.14), and it should be said that [the Lord] is "devoid of qualities" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.15). Furthermore: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge."

"Knowing the bliss of Brahman," "He indeed is this great, unborn Self," and so forth— by such scriptural passages, [the bliss of Brahman] is revealed, and there is no futility [of the term], precisely because of the designation of that which is distinguished by bliss. Furthermore, by such sūtras as "The one consisting of bliss is the principal [Brahman]" and "Because the intended qualities are appropriate," [it is established that] the bliss belongs to Brahman.

Because its possession of qualities is admitted. Nor is there any contradiction, for even though prohibited qualities are impossible, admitted qualities are possible. Indeed, there is no contradiction between the two statements: "there is no odor in fire" and "there is color.
Likewise, due to the prohibitions such as "soundless" and "touchless," qualities like color and so forth might not exist [in the Self]. [But it is] the Witness, the Conscious One.

The statements "He is alone" and "devoid of qualities" constitute a general negation of qualities; however, this is sublated in certain respects by specific injunctions regarding qualities, such as "He who is all-knowing, the witness, the conscious one, the knower, the time of time, the possessor of qualities, the omniscient," and so forth. This is just as the general prohibition, "One must not kill," is sublated in certain respects by the specific injunction, "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma."
It is sublated;
just as the general scriptural injunction, "One offers into the Āhavanīya fire," is [sublated] by the specific rule, "One offers on the footstep," so it is here. And...

It must be stated that in passages such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," knowledge and the like are understood as the very nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman, not as its attributes (*guṇa*). For, from statements such as "May I become many, may I be born" and "He reflected," it is understood that knowledge is something produced; therefore, it cannot be its [Brahman's] essential nature. Nor can it be said that [knowledge] is merely a modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*avidyā*).

It must be stated that it is indeed another cognition (*jñānāntara*) that is produced, not the cognition of the [Self's] own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*). Or, even if it were the own nature, the production of the cognition in the form of being colored by an object (*viṣayoparaktatva*) would be consistent with scripture. For ignorance (*avidyā*) is equivalent to a hare’s horn; even if it were existent, it could not be perceived therein because of its insentient nature. Otherwise, [it would follow that...].

Furthermore, if the Pradhāna were capable of "seeing," it would result in the inconsistency of the scriptural passage beginning with "Because of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on the Śruti" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5).
As for the argument that, even though this [consciousness] is by nature eternal, its being produced is possible in the form of being colored by an object—that is not correct;
because at the moment of creation, which serves as the cause, no object exists. Nor can it be said that the unmanifest (avyākṛta) exists even then.

It must be stated that form (rūpa) and so forth do indeed exist [prior to creation]; however, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for their existence. Or, even if they did exist, since they would already be present at the time of dissolution (pralaya), it would be impossible for them to arise then. Furthermore, it is illogical to assume that "being produced" (janyatva), which is heard as residing in the act of seeing (īkṣaṇa), actually resides in its object. How then is it said, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"?

There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because—as in the case of "the blue lotus" and so forth—both difference and non-difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality are admitted. And it has been stated by the author of the Sūtras: "But that designation [of the Self as 'blissful,' etc. is due to its having that as its essence, just as in the case of the wise man."

Furthermore, in this context, the word *jñāna* is not derived from the root *jñā* with the suffix *lyuṭ* (ana) denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*). For if that were the case, the word would be accented on the first syllable, as the suffix is udātta; [the forms] would be *saṃjñānam* and *vijñānam*.
It is like [the word] *prajñāna* and others. Furthermore, it is recited with the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable.

Therefore, when the possessive suffix *yac* (corresponding to *matup*) is applied in the sense of "one who possesses this," namely *jñānam asyāsti*, the word becomes *jñāna* with the acute accent on the final syllable according to the rule *citaḥ*. And thus, since the meaning "possessing knowledge" is obtained, by this also it is established that knowledge is indeed a quality (*guṇa*).

Nor is it of the nature of mere knowledge. Therefore, since Brahman does not lack qualities (*nirguṇatva*), the conceptual distinction that "this [text] teaches the qualityless" and "this teaches the qualified" is indeed improper.

Likewise, regarding the statement "and there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse," knowledge depends upon ritual action.

Because the status of being the cause of liberation has been stated [in the Sūtra], the demonstration that liberation arises from knowledge alone, independent of ritual action (*karman*), is inconsistent with the Sūtra. For it is said: "For this very reason, there is dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth; just as knowledge is an auxiliary to ritual action, so too is it for the sake of accomplishing the assistance to its own cause."

By way of cooperation, [knowledge] requires such things as fire and fuel, or the rites of enkindling the fire prescribed by Vedic injunctions such as "O Agni, you are to be praised. When it is not a subordinate part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), then it does not require other auxiliary parts. When knowledge is the cause for the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then all rituals—obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and so forth—are required for the attainment of that human goal.

He says that [knowledge] requires [them] as cooperative factors: "And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural statement regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Knowledge depends upon all ritual actions. Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding sacrifice and so forth: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). For here, previously...

It has been stated: "The wise man, having known that very [Self], should practice wisdom (prajñā) regarding Brahman"; this means that having known it through the authority of scripture (*pramāṇa*), one should perform the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*). In response to the inquiry as to what constitutes the auxiliary factors for that meditation, this is said: "That very [Self]... by the recitation of the Vedas," and so forth.

(250) Here, by the term *vedānuvacana*, a Vedic passage is meant; for it is seen so in such instances as "the *vedānuvacana* of Triśaṅku" and others. It does not, however, mean the study of the Vedas.

Because study (*adhyayana*) satisfies the requirement for a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being itself a means of valid knowledge, and because it would contradict the Sūtra [1.1.2]: "On account of the scriptural statement regarding sacrifice and so forth" (*yajñādi-śruteḥ*);

for since sacrifice cannot be the "beginning" (*ādi*), one must state that it is the recitation of the Veda (*vedānuvacana*) that is the beginning, as in the scriptural passage "recitation of the Veda and so forth" (*vedānuvacanādi-śruteḥ*).
Therefore, [the meaning is established] by the sentence concerning the recitation of the Veda.
The word "vijñāya" (having known) should be supplied and connected [to the text]. Some, however, say that "etaṃ prāptam" means "understood.

In the phrase "vividiṣanti," the act of knowing (*vedana*) is what was previously indicated by the word "prajñā," because we observe the frequent use of the verb "vid" in the sense of "meditation" (*upāsana*).

Furthermore, because it is observed in the Veda that the terms *vidhi* (injunction) and *upāsana* (meditation) are used as distinct entities in the section concerning repetition (*āvṛttyadhikaraṇa*), and because they themselves have stated that [the term] is for the purpose of meditative worship in the form of an injunction; and because in the phrase "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*).

Thus, sacrifices and the like are enjoined as auxiliary factors (*sahakāritvena*). Nor is the instrumental case used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*); what then would it be? It is used in the sense of accompaniment.

This is to be doubted; for it is impossible for sacrifice and the like to be the cause of meditative worship (*upāsti*), and because of the determination that the mind alone is the instrument, as stated in the passage, "It is to be seen by the mind alone. Furthermore, even if an injunction aims at producing valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-jñāna*), it is impossible for non-authoritative acts such as sacrifice to be its cause. Nor is there any obstacle to knowledge [arising from them].

It cannot be argued that sacrifices and the like function as instruments by way of the cessation of sin; for since no non-arising of knowledge is observed even when the causal complex for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*) is present, it is not established that sin acts as an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*). Furthermore, the status of the absence of an obstacle as a cause has been [established] with great effort by others.
Furthermore, by means of that refutation, the causality of sacrifice and the like is cast far away.
Therefore, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) here has the sense of "together with" (*saha*). Consequently, the status of sacrifice and the like as auxiliary causes (*sahakāritva*) is not established.

For this very reason, others have also explained that in passages such as "Having sought the Self through austerity, celibacy, and faith, they conquer the Sun," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). For this same reason, the author of the Sūtras will also explicitly state its status as a cooperative factor (*sahakāritva*) in the words "and by way of being a cooperative factor" (*sahakāritvena ca*). For this very reason, [there is the discussion] regarding the realization of That (*tadadhigama*).
Regarding the two [results] beginning with the north-eastern [direction], there is non-attachment and destruction; because of that designation, the same applies to the other as well.

Having stated the destruction of the prior merits and sins through knowledge by means of the passage "there is no attachment, there is falling away," the author of the Sūtras has stated these two Sūtras as an exception to that. However, only those prior [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is the limit.

Regarding the statement "Agnihotra and so forth are for that purpose alone, because they are seen as such," there is no destruction of the *prārabdha* (commenced) merit and demerit by means of knowledge (*vidyā*). Rather, Agnihotra and the like are not destroyed by knowledge, but their purpose is to serve as causes for liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the fruit of knowledge. For if ritual actions were indeed the producers of knowledge itself, [then they would be destroyed by it].

In that case, since actions have their fruits as their ultimate end, and since [the fruit] does not necessarily cease through knowledge, it would be inconsistent to establish that knowledge is the cause of liberation by way of being an exception to those [actions].
Furthermore, if knowledge were the means to liberation, then sacrifices and other rites would be undertaken for the sake of that [liberation] as its means.

[They] are enjoined. In that case, since engagement in Vedic ritual action is untenable without certainty regarding its fruit, certainty regarding the fruit characterized as knowledge must be stated. And since that knowledge has Brahman as its object, certainty regarding Brahman, which is the object, must also be stated. Nevertheless, because the fruit consisting of certainty regarding Brahman is already established, [it does not need to be enjoined].
The performance of the means [of attainment] follows from this. Furthermore, if there is no certainty [regarding the goal], there will be no engagement in the means because the result is uncertain;

the same should be understood regarding the certainty or uncertainty of liberation (*mokṣa*). This point—that the study [of the Veda] is enjoined for one who desires the comprehension of its meaning—has been established with great effort by those very same [authorities] while refuting that position, so it need not be elaborated further here.

Nor should it be argued that if liberation were achievable through ritual action (*karma*), it would follow that it is impermanent, on the basis of the scriptural passage: "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, even so there the world acquired by merit perishes. For... [the text continues with *athavā*].

For here, it is heard that those who depart without having discovered the Self and these true desires belong to the world produced by mere ritual action devoid of knowledge; likewise elsewhere: "O Gārgī, he who in this world offers oblations, sacrifices, and performs austerities without knowing this Imperishable, [does so in vain]."

"Even if one performs great meritorious action for thousands of years, it comes to an end. If indeed one who knows not thus should perform great meritorious action, it would be his, and from that it surely perishes. Therefore, one should worship the Self alone as the world.
By such passages [the text teaches]: "He who worships the Self alone as the world—his action does not perish," and so forth. In that context, [it refers to] one devoid of knowledge.

This is because it has been established that action alone is perishable, whereas the fruit of action conjoined with knowledge is imperishable. Therefore, it is proven that actions possess the status of being auxiliary factors, like a horse. Just as a right-hand draft horse yoked to the movement of a chariot requires its left-hand counterpart as an auxiliary factor.

In the same way, by that [argument], the status of sacrifice and other rites as causes for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is also refuted. Just as in the expression "he wishes to go by horse," the horse's being a cause for the desire to go is refuted, because in such cases we do not observe the horse to be the cause of the desire to go; whereas in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites, it is observed that they serve precisely as the means to that [desire].

Furthermore, because its status as the direct cause of liberation has been established by the Sūtra itself, its meaning has been explained by those very [commentators]: "The Vedic obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra are for the sake of that very effect; the meaning is that whatever is the effect of that knowledge is indeed the effect of this [rite] as well. Why? Because [the Sūtra says]: "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know Him thus through the recitation of the Vedas (*vedānuvacana*)."
...because of such scriptural indications (*śruti*).
253) Now, an objection: since knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*) have distinct effects, it is impossible for their effects to be one and the same. [For example,] fever and death...
For even in the case of two effects—curd and [the result of] honey—which, when combined with molasses and mantras respectively, are seen to have the effects of satisfaction and nourishment;

similarly, it is logical that action (karma) joined with knowledge also has liberation as its effect. This being so, this statement regarding the unity of the effects refers to matters beyond the present context, by way of mental purification and the desire to know (vividiṣā).

For it is knowledge alone that is figuratively designated as the means to liberation, since it brings about [liberation]. Indeed, for one who knows the undifferentiated Brahman, ritual acts such as the Agnihotra—which involve going and not going—are impossible. This is because, when there is the realization of the Self as a non-agent, one lacks the qualification for scriptures prescribing injunctions and prohibitions; whereas in the case of meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavidyā*), agency has not yet been transcended.

It might be argued that for one who has the capacity to perform the Agnihotra and other rites, even though he is not related [to the sacrifice] through the desire for results, it is possible for those rites to produce the same effect as knowledge, because there is no other purpose for them. This is incorrect;
for how can two distinct meanings be derived from a single scriptural statement or a single sūtra? In some cases, [the rites lead] to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

In some cases, knowledge is the cause; thus it is said that [knowledge] is the cause of the fruit. Or how is there no contradiction between the earlier and later statements, given that while the utility of sacrifices and so forth was stated only with respect to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), their being the direct cause of the fruit is stated in relation to the meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-upāsanā*)? Nor is it the case that even if the meaning of the sentence is simply the causality toward the fruit, [this is incompatible] with the realization of the non-agent self (*akartṛ-ātmabodha*).

It should be stated that, because actions persist until the attainment of their fruits, their utility lies solely in generating the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), as has been declared regarding the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa-vidyā*).
This is because the agency of the Self has been established on the grounds that the scriptures have meaning only if there is an agent (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*).

Because the realization of the Self as a non-agent is not capable of burning away karma due to its being a state of delusion; and because, in the absence of knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman, the utility of the desire to know (vividiṣā) therein is cast far aside. Nor would liberation be impermanent if it were produced by karma.

This must be stated because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is produced is impermanent," and because of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which says, "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes. If indeed... [p. 254]
Even if one performs a great meritorious deed, it perishes; therefore, it surely wastes away.

One should worship the Self alone as the world. For him who worships the Self alone as the world, his work does not perish. [This refers to] the exhaustion at the end of the enjoyment of the fruit of work performed by one who does not know the Self; however, for the knower of Brahman—
Because there is no possibility of the non-eternality of existence resulting from the exhaustion of performed action, due to the demonstration of its [the action's] continued state;

for the [proposed] logic is sublated by scripture. Nor should it be argued: "How can inexhaustibility be established, given that the extremely rapid destruction of action is proven by direct perception? For [action exists] in the form of a subtle state.

This is because it establishes the indestructibility of that which was previously denoted by the word "karma. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this, because in its absence, it would be impossible for an action—which perishes immediately—to produce a fruit at a later time. In its absence, [the scripture states]: "Knowledge and action accompany him."

To whom could the "taking hold" (*anvārambhaṇa*) be said to belong? Or, upon the exhaustion of what action—whatever this person performs here—could the coming back from the other world to this one be said to occur? Furthermore, in the statement, "Those of pleasant conduct enter a pleasant womb," by what means is the attainment of a specific womb being described?

Likewise, it is said that upon the realization of that [Brahman], there is the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of future and past sins. Of what, indeed, could destruction be predicated by knowledge, or of what could non-clinging be asserted? For action perishes at that very moment. Furthermore, of what "good deed" could "attainment" (*upāyana*) be predicated, as expressed in the passage beginning with "of a friend's good deed"?
If it is asked, "How can there be knowledge of, or an offering to, an incorporeal substance?"—the answer is no;
for both are possible through the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra*). Regarding merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), the scripture is the sole [means of knowledge].

Since it is to be realized through direct attainment, its own nature must also be understood solely by means of the scripture (*śāstra*), not through reasoning (*tarka*); for it has been stated that "the Veda is the root of verbal knowledge. Therefore, [the text says]: "A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a wooden pestle, should go before the king and confess his deed; the king should strike him with it; by this killing, he is liberated."

"Sin touches the knower through what is known; one who kills an embryo is accused by the eating of food and so forth; a thief released by the king, and one who breaks a promise after making it. And: "The guest from whose house returns with hopes frustrated, having given his own misdeeds and taken away his merit, departs," and so on.

In scriptural passages, the abandonment and acquisition of merit and demerit are recorded; likewise, the Śruti text beginning with "the works accumulated here" refers to the sphere of the ignorant, as seen in the passage, "Now those who depart from here without having discovered the Self. This is because immediately thereafter, the attainment of all desired fruits is declared for the knower. Even according to that view, [this applies] to the Dahara-vidyā.

For it would result in an inconsistency to claim that the fruit of that [knowledge] is censured by the very same sentence situated within its own context, since it is accepted that qualified knowledge (*saguṇavidyā*) is associated with ritual action (*karman*) in those qualified meditations;
furthermore, in the *Daharādhikaraṇa*, those same [authorities] have established that the fruit of the *dahara-vidyā* is indeed imperishable.
Therefore, even though liberation is to be accomplished through action, because it is established that action is imperishable, the imperishability of liberation is also logically justified.

Likewise, although the equality of the departure [from the body] for both the knower and the ignorant is established in the passage beginning with "And common up to the commencement of the path" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5),...
The assertion by a certain scholar that there is no departure [of the soul] is contrary to the Sūtra; for how indeed [could it be so], when [the Sūtra says]:
"Speech [is merged] in the mind" (p.

By the passage beginning with "from seeing and from hearing," the departure of the individual soul (jīva)—which is designated as the sense organs and the vital breath—along with its subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), is established in relation to the knower. For it is said: "Just as one might depart casting off a well-aimed arrow, even so this embodied self, mounted by the conscious self (prājña-ātman)..."

The scriptural passage beginning with "departing" (*utsarjan*) describes the process of departure (*utkrānti*) in detail; then, by stating "not thus," "not desiring," it establishes that this [departure] pertains to the knower (*vidvat*). Subsequently, introducing the knower with the words "but he who desires," and then declaring "his vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) do not depart," the text negates the departure of such a person. Furthermore...

"A mortal becomes immortal here; he attains Brahman. By this, [the author] states that immortality and the attainment of Brahman are shown to occur right here. Furthermore, up to the commencement of the departure from the body, the departure is the same for both the knower and the non-knower, and immortality is attained without having burned away [the body]. Why? Because no distinction is heard. In the Chāndogya, according to the view of others...

In the sixth chapter, which is intended to establish the non-differentiated Brahman, the teacher begins with the knower, stating, "Thus indeed does a person who has a teacher know," and after declaring the state of *sampatti* (merging/attainment) with the words, "For him there is delay only as long as he is not released, then he shall be merged," [the text proceeds] when the inquiry arises as to by what sequence one attains that merging.

Since the sequence of departure is established by such passages as "Speech merges into the mind," one might ask: is this process the same for everyone? No, he says: "Until the commencement of the path" (*āsṛtyupakramāt*). The "commencement of the path" refers to the period prior to the start of the journey; until then, the process of departure is the same for all. However, regarding the commencement of the path itself, the knower departs through the cranial artery (*mūrdhanyanāḍī*), while the other [the non-knower] departs through other channels.
The distinction is that [this applies] "to the other two."
Regarding what was stated here that for the knower there is immortality and so forth, he says in response: "And immortality without having burnt.

Without having burnt—that is, without having consumed—the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) and the rest, that state of being endowed with vital breaths is called immortality; thus it is said, "then the mortal becomes immortal."
The attainment of Brahman is indeed the attainment of the Brahman within the heart. Why is this so? To this he says:

"Because until the merging into That, there is the designation of transmigratory existence. For it is stated further on: "By that [path], the wise who know Brahman go to the heavenly world from here."

The statement "the liberated ones go upwards" indicates that at the very moment of attaining the undifferentiated Brahman via the path of the gods (*devayāna*), they are described as being liberated from the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) and so forth; this implies that prior to that point, they were still transmigrating beings.
Now, one might ask: when the subtle body exits from the physical body, why is it not perceived by those standing nearby? Why is that?

Or, having raised the doubt that [the subtle body] might not be destroyed by the burning or cutting of the gross body, he says "it is not so" because of its subtlety: "It is subtle, both by measure and because it is perceived as such; therefore, it cannot be destroyed.
Furthermore, regarding the sensation of heat which is perceived during the state of being alive...

Because it has the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) as its substrate, and because the sensation of heat is not perceived in the state of death, the departure of that substrate—the subtle body—is necessary; thus he says: "And for this very reason, the warmth is thus.
As for what was stated—that there is no departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) from the knower, meaning that the departure of the wise one is prohibited—regarding that, he says:
If it be argued that [the soul is not the agent] because of a prohibition, we say no, because [the prohibition refers only to the embodied soul].

This is not a prohibition of the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); rather, it concerns how the Self is understood to depart from the body. For [the answer] is explicit for some. Indeed, for some—the Mādhyandinas—it is explicit because of the use of the ablative case in the phrase, "from him the *prāṇas* do not depart. And the word "from him" (*tasmāt*) refers to the primary subject, namely, the one who has attained excellence.

The body is not the one authorized for the attainment of the supreme good; rather, it is the embodied soul (*jīva*). Therefore, when that soul is about to depart, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) do not depart from it.
The meaning is that they exist together with it. And thus, the departure of that [self] from the body certainly occurs.

Furthermore, in the phrase "of that" (*tasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of a general relationship; however, by means of the ablative case found in another recension (*śākhāntara*), the specific nature of that relationship is established. Nor is it the case that [the self departs] while not desiring, as expressed by the phrase "not desiring" (*na kāmayamāna*).
It should not be said that the statement regarding the departure [of the soul] being connected with the knower is untenable;
for this is not an assertion that the departure is connected with the non-knower. Indeed, the departure from the crown of the head is not possible for the non-knower, as it is said:
