"Going upwards by that, one attains immortality," and so on, beginning with "the kindling of the fire within the abode."

Because the two sūtras state that the departure from the head belongs specifically to the knower; likewise, because of the sūtras, "Knowledge and action follow him" (*taṃ vidyā karmaṇī samanvārabhete*) and "The following is impossible for one who is not a knower," as well as "The separation is like that of a hundred [coins]" (*samanvārambhaṇāt vibhāgaḥ śatavat*), the act of being followed by knowledge and action applies only to the knower.

Furthermore, because the subject matter refers to the wise (*vidvat*); likewise, the attainment of the form of Brahman—expressed as "either that of Prajāpati or that of Brahman"—is not possible for one who lacks knowledge, since the Sūtra, "Jaimini [holds that it is] by means of the Brahman-form, on account of the enunciation and so forth," declares that this is the fruit of knowledge. However, from that world, he returns again to this world.

This is a statement regarding the fact that the aforementioned "returning" belongs to the ignorant person (*avidvat*). For it is stated that the ignorant person returns due to the exhaustion of *karman*, whereas the wise (*vidvat*) merge into Brahman; it is not, however, by means of departure (*utkrānti*) or non-departure (*anutkrānti*).

Nor is the prohibition [of departure] untenable on the grounds that departure from the body is not even a possibility; for since such worldly usage as "Devadatta has died" implies its occurrence, the prohibition is possible. As it is said: "This body indeed dies when abandoned by the living self (jīva); the living self does not die."

Furthermore, it is not at all the case that the absence of departure (*utkrānti*) is being taught here as something previously unknown; rather, it is experienced as established through the question and answer regarding the distribution [of the elements]. For instance:

To the question, "When this person dies, do the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) depart from him or not? Yājñavalkya replied, "No; they are simply absorbed right here. [The opponent asks: "How so? [Yājñavalkya answers: "He swells up, becomes bloated, and lies dead, inflated. In this context, by the word "from him" (*asmāt*), the embodied being (*dehī*) is referred to. "Right here" (*atraiva*).

The phrase "they merge" (samavalīyante) is possible because of the merging of the vital breaths (prāṇas) into the individual soul (jīva), as is established in the passage "He [the soul] with the presiding deity" (sodhyakṣaḥ). It cannot refer to the body, for such a merging is impossible therein. Nor should it be argued that the swelling of the soul is untenable because of the statement "it does not swell" (na sa ucchvayati); for in this context, the word "swells" (ucchrayati) does not mean physical inflation.

But it is indeed an upward movement, according to the traditional rule that the root *ud-vas* signifies both going upward and increasing. "He causes to swell" (*ādhyāyati*) means he makes the body endowed with sound; for the root *dhmā* is transitive, as seen in the expression "they blew the conch shells" (*śaṅkhān dadhmuḥ*). This is evident from the observation that while the body is the object being blown (*apadhmāta*), the conch shell is what has been blown (*ādhmāta*).

The meaning is that he lies dead, separated from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Thus, in this context, the absence of the departure of the vital breaths from the living self (*jīva*)—which is already established—is restated. Nor should it be suspected that this restatement is purposeless; for it serves to establish the state of being Brahman mentioned in the phrase "being Brahman itself. And here, [the text says] "Brahman itself..."
The Vaiśeṣikas do not say that the state of being Brahman (brahmabhāva) for the knower is denoted by the word "sann" (being merged).

This is because the phrase "he attains Brahman" (brahmāpyeti) is stated separately as the attainment of Brahman which is to be accomplished through knowledge (vidyā). Rather, it refers to that merging of the individual soul (jīva)—accompanied by the senses, mind, and vital breath—into Brahman through the elements, as described in the context of the departure [of the soul] from the body.
The attainment of a share is common to both the wise and the ignorant,

as shown by the passage beginning with "Because of the observation of speech and mind, and because of the word" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.1) and ending with "Because of the statement regarding the division" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.13).
That very [process] is being examined and is what is being described here. And that description is given because it serves as the gateway to the attainment of Brahman.

For, in the absence of departure, it is not possible for the soul to go to Brahman by way of the path of the gods. It is precisely for this purpose that the second quarter [of the chapter] examines the process of departure. Furthermore, there is no merging of the individual soul (jīva) into Brahman while accompanied by the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Since it is not possible [for one] to become Brahman without the prohibition of the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) from the living being, that prohibition is also purposeful.

As for the argument that the phrase "being Brahman itself" means "having oneself become Brahman," like the expression "having become a god, he goes to the gods"— even then, the state of being Brahman does not occur for one who has departed with the vital breaths, i.e., for one who is dead.
The prohibition is also meaningful. In response to the inquiry as to when and by what sequence this attainment occurs, it is said: "Then all desires residing in his heart are liberated;
then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman"—here, [the phrase] "all desires are liberated" refers to this.
The phrase "of the one possessing sense-organs" implies "into the vital breaths. For when the cause dissolves, the effect necessarily dissolves in its entirety.
Then, [the text says], "the mortal becomes immortal. Immediately thereafter, the merging of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the individual soul (*jīva*) is stated.
This very point is expressed by a portion of the Sūtra: "and immortality without having burned away [the body]. Its meaning is: "then the mortal..."

In this context, the word "immortality" (*amṛta*) does not denote the fruit of knowledge, because that is mentioned later on. Rather, it refers to the fact that for both the knower and the non-knower, the state of being mere breath (*prāṇatvamātra*) is common; for one who has not fasted—that is, without having burnt away the cause of bondage and without having attained the unmodified Brahman—this alone constitutes his immortality.
The subject matter of the Sūtra (p.
In such passages as "Going upwards by those [rays], he attains immortality," there is the attainment of immortality.

Because it is stated that [attaining Brahman] is preceded by departing, no doubt arises regarding its absence; for here, the phrase "the soul attains Brahman" refers to the soul's merging (*sampatti*) into Brahman through the elements, according to another scriptural passage: "Speech merges into the mind, the mind into breath, breath into heat, and heat into the supreme deity."

One might object: "In that case, it should be said that he has 'become merged' (*sampanna*) in Brahman, rather than 'being Brahman itself' (*brahmaiva san*). Anticipating this doubt—that here "mergence" (*sampatti*) refers to a loss of distinction like milk mixed with water or an iron ball heated by fire, and not merely a state of close contact—the author first addresses the conventional usage of the term "death" regarding the immortality of the individual soul (*jīva*).

He dispels the doubt that [the self] might be without support: "Just as a snake’s slough, dead and cast off, lies upon an anthill, even so does this body lie here; but this [self] is the bodyless, the dead one—breath indeed is Brahman, it is light. Just as a snake’s slough is the skin of a snake, abandoned by the snake because it is separated from life.

"Dead. It lies in an anthill; even so, this body, having been separated from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), lies dead. But the living self (*jīva*), because it has departed from the body or because its identification with the body has ceased, is "bodiless" (*aśarīra*); and because of the absence of connection with the vital breaths and so forth, it is "immortal" (*amṛta*). Through the attainment of non-separation from the vital breaths, the vital breaths [are Brahman]; and through non-separation from Brahman, it is indeed Brahman itself.
"Because it undergoes a division of its radiance, it is indeed light. Thus, the statement "being Brahman itself" has been explained.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what path and endowed with what means one attains Brahman, the text elaborates on the phrase "attains Brahman": "The subtle, ancient, and far-extended path..."

Touched and discovered by me alone, through that [path], even the steadfast knowers of Brahman go from here upwards to the heavenly world, being liberated. Regarding that path, they say it is white and blue, tawny and green, and red. This is the path discovered by Brahman; by it one goes.
p.

262) "The knower of Brahman, the performer of meritorious deeds, and the one who has attained splendor"—this is the path of the gods, the subtle path, so called because it is difficult to perceive due to its extreme subtlety, which passes through the *mūrdhan* (cranial) artery; Yājñavalkya’s statement, "It has touched me, it has touched me," refers to this.

The statement "let him not touch" is because of the connection of the central channel (*mūrdhanyā nāḍī*) with the path of the gods (*devayāna*). "Anuvittaḥ" means fully known; by meditation, [he knows] "the heavenly world"—by which is meant Brahman, the unsurpassed bliss, as indicated by the introductory phrase "he goes even to Brahman. "Vimuktāḥ" refers to those freed from the causes of bondage to the body, both gross and subtle, such as merit (*puṇya*).

And because it is established by scripture that the solar rays possess various forms within that [path] which is called "white" due to its connection with the two sins, the path composed of those [rays] possesses various forms;
and the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "taijasaśca" is for the purpose of indicating a combination of means for the knowledge, as each of these [means] individually [contributes].

He states the attainment of the human goal through the performance of spiritual practice with the passage beginning, "Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance, and into darkness greater than that, as it were, those who delight in knowledge," and so forth. Thus,
when the context is examined from beginning to end, the departure and ascent of the knower are understood.
The prohibition [of returning] is recorded as applying specifically to one who has taken up a physical body; and the destiny of the knower is likewise recorded in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, set out toward the solar orb. Śuka, having attained a speed swifter than that of the wind, entered the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Having displayed his own power, he became one with all beings;
thus it is for one who has become the self of all beings and perceives all beings correctly.
Even the gods are bewildered on the path of the trackless one, who is the guide for those seeking his footprints.

Because the path has departed from its own place, the heart, for one who seeks the goal—that is, one desiring the supreme state—even the deities are bewildered regarding the way; thus, the difficulty of discerning the path is expressed. But it is not that the path does not exist.
For it is said: "Those who do not know the two paths at the time of death become worms, moths, and whatever else is this [lowly] vermin."

Because it is heard that those who have fallen from the two paths go to a lower state, the Sūtra’s statement regarding the absence of departure from the body for the knower has as its subject matter the prohibition concerning the soul's departure from the body.

This is indeed contradictory. Thus, even though it has been established by the Sūtra, "And because that [attainment] is known through the path beginning with light" (Brahmasūtra 4.3.1), that the attainment of Brahman occurs only by way of the path beginning with light and not by any other means, the assertion by some knowers of Brahman that there is no path at all is entirely inconsistent with the Sūtra. Nor is it the case that [the scripture says], "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path."

It should not be argued that because there is a negation of any other path distinct from knowledge in the statement "there exists no other way for going," the path of the gods (*devayāna*) need not be expected; for this [text], like the scriptural passage concerning the knowledge of the Supreme Self—namely, "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here; there is no other path for going"—has as its subject the knowledge of the Self.

Because there is no denial of the path of the gods (*devayāna*). For it is stated in the Sūtra: "But [the two paths are] because of knowledge and action, as they are the subjects under discussion. Thus, since knowledge and action are presented as the respective means for these two paths—the path of the gods and the path of the fathers—mentioned in the passage "Now, neither by one of these two paths," knowledge is also a way on the path of the gods.

Because it is designated as being preceded by knowledge (*pramāpūrvatvena*); for by the very mention of "knowledge" (*vidyā*), the path of the gods (*devayāna*) beginning with that [light] is also obtained.
Since there is no other path for proceeding to Brahman apart from that, it is understood that for the journey to Brahman, only the path of the gods is required; otherwise, there would be no paths.
Because it has been stated that the going is for the purpose of reaching [the goal], the act of going itself cannot be what is intended by "for the sake of reaching" (*narāyaṇāya*).

Rather, it must be said that it refers exclusively to the attainment of Brahman; for when the primary meaning of the word "path" (*panthā*) is possible, it is improper to resort to a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, as it is said: "But those who do not know these two paths become worms."
"Like moths," he says. Now, those who go neither by one of these two paths become these small creatures that return again and again; "be born and die"—this is the third station.

Therefore, that world is not filled. "One should therefore feel aversion" [is said] because those who have fallen away from the two paths must feel a painful aversion toward hearing about the third path. Therefore, the statement regarding the absence of the path of the gods [applies only to them].
This is indeed improper for those who know Brahman.

Likewise, Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord] leads those who do not rely on symbols (apratīkālambana), because there are defects in both cases. Having stated that those who meditate on Brahman attain Brahman, the reason for this is given by the rule "according to his resolve" (*tatkratuś cet*): "Verily, man consists of resolve; as is his resolve in this world, so does he become after departing from here."

"Because it is stated that one attains that which one meditates upon. This being the established meaning of the Sūtra, the statement that those who do not worship the *pratīka* (symbolic forms) attain Hiraṇyagarbha would contradict the Sūtra.

Nor should it be said that their meditation also has Hiraṇyagarbha as its sole object; for this is refuted in the section beginning with "Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere" (*sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt*).

Because of the determination of the state of Brahman for Pāśya; likewise, because of the word "by himself" regarding the manifestation through attainment, and because of the promise of liberation, the manifestation of the nature of the liberated one after attaining Brahman has been stated. When the inquiry arises as to by what nature this manifestation occurs, [the Sūtra states]: "By the nature of Brahman, according to Jaimini, on account of the enunciations and so forth."
There is a consensus [regarding the identity of the Self] through such descriptions as "having true desires and true resolves" due to being freed from evil by means of the Brahman-nature,
and through such forms as "he moves about there, laughing, playing, and rejoicing with women, or chariots, or kinsmen, or friends," and so forth, up to "the omniscient one, the Lord of all."

Having stated the position of Jaimini, and having stated the position of Auḍulomi— that in the state of dissolution there is a merging into that very [Brahman] alone because it is of the nature of that, and that the merging occurs by way of the form of consciousness itself as expressed in the aphorism "Auḍulomi says... because of being of that nature"—
Bādarāyaṇa concludes that there is no contradiction because of the prior existence [of the soul], as shown by the introductory statement.
Even so, although the ultimate nature of reality is admitted to be the essence of pure consciousness alone, from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
there remains the form of Brahman’s sovereignty— which, even prior [to this realization], was untouched by such things as being presented [in scripture] and so forth.

"Because of the refutation [of the objection], the teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers there to be no contradiction. Thus has the position of Bādarāyaṇa been explained by them. And thus, since the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) arises from ignorance, when ignorance is destroyed through knowledge, the entire phenomenal world, which has that [ignorance] as its root, [is likewise destroyed].

It is quite clear that the position—that liberation consists in abiding in the mere nature of the self due to destruction without residue—is not intended by Bādarāyaṇa. Likewise, [this is evident] from the passage: "The serene one, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form. If he...

Even though the passage beginning with "He who desires the world of the fathers, by his mere volition (saṃkalpa) the fathers arise for him," belongs to the Dahara-vidyā, and even though the Sūtra "But [the powers of the Lord] are from volition alone, because of the scriptural statement" depends upon the previously mentioned quality of having true volitions (satya-saṃkalpatva) as expressed in the phrase "by the Brāhma [state]," this [Sūtra] pertains to the Nirguṇa-vidyā, while the preceding Sūtra pertained to the Saguna-vidyā.
The statement that this [text] concerns qualified knowledge (*saguṇavidyā*) is groundless. For this very reason, it says "he has no other lord" (*ananyādhipati*).

Precisely because of this, and because of his power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), as well as the scriptural text stating "he becomes a self-ruler" (*svarāḍ bhavati*), the liberated one has no other lord; the meaning is that no other person becomes his master.

They have also stated that this state of having no other superior (*ananyādhipatitva*) belongs to one who has gone to the world of Hiraṇyagarbha through the meditation on knowledge endowed with qualities (*saguṇavidyopāsanā*). But that is not correct; for since he has two superiors—namely, Hiraṇyagarbha and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)—he lacks the state of having no other superior. Bādari declares this very point [in the sūtra]: "Bādari [says] it is so, for thus [the scripture] says. "Not indeed... [and so forth].
"For one who possesses a body, there is the removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad, Chapter 8).
"But for one dwelling bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad, Chapter 8).

Having stated Bādarāyaṇa’s position—that there is no body for the liberated one because the absence of a body is understood from the scriptural statement—[the author] states Jaimini’s position that there is [a body], on the grounds of the mention of options: "He becomes singlefold, he becomes threefold, he becomes fivefold," and so forth, according to the passage found in the seventh chapter. Thus, the liberated one possesses a body.
Having stated Jaimini’s position— that [the liberated soul] is of both kinds, like the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice— as declared by Bādarāyaṇa,

[it is concluded that] it is of both kinds due to the authority of two scriptural passages. Furthermore, because the liberated one possesses the power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpatva*), for one who has the resolve "I shall become embodied," he becomes embodied.

The state of having a body: Bādarāyaṇa has stated his own position that for one who has the resolve to be bodiless, there is likewise the state of having a body; this has been explained by these [commentators] in the same way. And this is consistent with the unity of the knowledge (*vidyā*) throughout both chapters, and not otherwise, because the two positions are established as distinct based on the difference in knowledge.

Since a fixed rule cannot be established based on mere intention (*saṃkalpa*), such being the case, the seventh chapter teaches the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*). In the eighth chapter, the injunction for the meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vidyā*) and its fruit are stated in various ways, such as "it becomes one," and so forth; this is intended solely as praise for the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman.

The statement beginning with "kīrtitam" (it has been proclaimed) is based on the root [text]. In the sixth chapter, there is the exposition of the Brahman to be meditated upon as being distinct from cause and effect and as being the self of all. And in the seventh [chapter], meditation on that very same [Brahman] in its distributed forms within various [entities] is taught, as well as meditation on it collectively as the Infinite (*bhūman*).
In the eighth [chapter], the place of meditation is described; the qualities of the Brahman to be meditated upon, such as its desires and so forth, are the limbs of the meditation;
certain [details] concern the meditator’s attainment of Brahman by way of the path of the gods (*devayāna*). (Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya, p.

Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Chāndogya-bhāṣya* by him and others that "immediately after [attaining] the state of *prāpti*, there is the attainment of all desires," and so forth, it is established that the three chapters form a single coherent whole (*ekavākyatva*).
Likewise, regarding the sūtra *pradīpavad ādeśas tathā hi darśayati*, what [is the case] in the view that the liberated one possesses multiple bodies?

Regarding the doubt as to whether those bodies possess a self (*sātmaka*) or are devoid of a self (*nirātmaka*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established that, with the exception of this very body, all others are devoid of a self. [The established conclusion is: Just as a single lamp, by virtue of its power of transformation, assumes the state of many lamps and enters into many wicks, so too does the liberated one.

It has been established as a tenet that a single [soul], through its connection with the power of sovereignty (*aiśvarya-śakti*), enters into multiple bodies. This is inconsistent for those who maintain the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). For, regarding the doubt as to whether all bodies are devoid of a soul, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are indeed devoid of a soul, because [the soul] is connected with only one body at a time.

Because the established doctrine—that [the Lord] enters bodies after attaining sovereignty consisting solely in the state of being the sole agent of instruction—is inconsistent with that position; and furthermore, how can sovereignty characterized by the entry into multiple bodies and so forth be admitted for one who is liberated? For by what means could he perceive anything? But it is not [so].

"There is no second, nothing else separate from Him that one might perceive. Regarding the doubt that such scriptural passages as "He becomes one with the One Seer in water, non-dual," which negate specific cognition, [the answer is:
it has indeed been made clear that this depends on either the state of deep sleep (*svāpatti*) or the attainment of liberation (*sampatti*).

It has been stated that this statement regarding the absence of specific cognition refers to either deep sleep (*suṣupti*) or departure from the body (*utkrānti*), because such is understood from the force of the context.
Some maintain here that by the word "attainment" (*sampatti*), the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) is meant; [the former view holds] with reference to that.
They say that the statement regarding the absence of specific cognition refers to this; however, for them, a contradiction between what precedes and what follows would result.
On page 268, by the sūtra "Jaimini [holds that the liberated soul possesses] omniscience on account of the enunciation and so forth," the omniscience of the liberated one was stated. Now...

"It is said that there is an absence of knowledge. Why say more? Whatever [categories] are accepted by various [schools] as their own unique [tenets], all of them are indeed included within the Sūtras; for nowhere in the Sūtras are words expressive of those [unique tenets] to be found.
Thus, there is likewise a contradiction with the Sūtras elsewhere as well, but I shall desist here for fear of being too prolix.

Thus, since commentaries following the Sūtras have perished and existing works do not follow the Sūtras, this commentary conforming to the Sūtras is now commenced. In that regard, regarding the injunction for study, "The Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied," the suffix -tavya in the word *adhyetavya* indicates that the Veda is the object to be refined by the act of study.

Because origination and so forth are impossible; or even if they were possible, because [the result] would be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*) would be redundant. Furthermore, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) is something that enters into the means of accomplishment. However, the status of the Veda as a means—unlike that of rice grains—is not perceived through context (*prakaraṇa*) or other such means, because the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) is taught as an independent rule (*anārabhyādhīta*). Likewise...

And by this very [injunction], the understanding of its status as a means must be stated: "One should effect the desired result by means of the Veda (svādhyāya) as refined by study. This is just as in the case of "one should choose a domestic priest," where it is understood that one should effect the desired result by means of a domestic priest as refined by the act of choosing. And thus, because the Veda is to be adopted as a means, the singularity residing in it [is significant].

The phrase "is intended to be significant" means that the injunction for the study of the Veda applies to a single [Veda] alone. Otherwise, just as in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), since the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text) would be the object of the injunction as something to be refined (*saṃskārya*), the singularity inherent in it would be unintended as significant; consequently, just as with the cleansing of all cups, there would be the study of all Vedas.

[One] would obtain [the fruit]. And thus, when there arises the inquiry as to what the door to that desired [fruit] is in the case of the injunction "one should perform the desired [fruit] through the study of one's own Veda" (*svādhyāyena iṣṭaṃ kuryāt*), since it is illogical to postulate an unseen result when a seen result exists, it is concluded that the comprehension of meaning (*arthāvabodha*) alone is the door to the desired [fruit]. Furthermore, because that [comprehension of meaning] is a cause of prosperity and the supreme good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*) by means of [leading to] ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), [it serves as the door].
Because it is logically established that [the study of the Veda] serves as a means to human goals (*puruṣārtha*).
For instance, in cases such as the study of the *rājasūya* sacrifice and other such texts, there is no visible purpose for a Brāhmaṇa or others.
Because performance [of the injunction] is impossible, in that case, by necessity, it culminates in human purpose through means such as recitation (*japa*).
However, where a visible means is possible, there it culminates in human purpose precisely through that visible means. And thus, the injunction for study [culminates in] the comprehension of meaning.
Since the comprehension of meaning depends on [prior study], and since inquiry into doubtful matters requires such inquiry,
inquiry itself is implied by the injunction to study. In that regard, all the meanings of the Veda must be investigated immediately after the study.

In this regard, because it is the first section (*kāṇḍa*), Jaimini first undertook an investigation into its subject matter. Through that very investigation, the injunctions for knowledge (*vidyā-vidhi*) were also largely investigated; however, Brahman, which is the object of that [knowledge], had not yet been investigated. Since that [Brahman] is supremely subtle, it might be considered unfit for investigation; therefore, he undertook its investigation as the primary task.

The venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa promises [the following]: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*). Nor does this contradict the fact that the inquiry into Brahman is suitable for the injunction to study, as stated in such passages as: "For the sake of knowing that, one should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) who is established in Brahman."

It should not be argued that the rule for the separate instruction of Brahman is purposeless; for the performance of knowledge does not become established merely from the study of the Mīmāṃsā regarding ritual action. Even if the meaning of the doubtful scriptural statements were determined by that alone, the practical application would still remain unknown without the synthesis of the auxiliary elements (aṅgas) found across various recensional branches (śākhās). Rather, however—

Just as the performance of rituals is carried out by learning the application through the study of the *Kalpasūtras* and the verbal instructions on specific rites imparted by those who possess direct knowledge of them, so too here, one should attain the most effective knowledge of the Vidyā from a teacher alone; such is the teaching of the scriptures.

In this context, such a Brahman—characterized by these specific qualities and presided over by various teachers possessing mastery of the respective vidyās—is the object of worship; these are the preceding and subsequent auxiliary elements of the meditation, and such is the nature of the worshiper.

This is established through the practice of knowledge even without such instruction as: "The vow is of this kind, the locus of worship is of this kind, the destination of the worshiper is of this kind, and the attainment of the fruit is of this kind. Since the injunction for that instruction is purposeful, the injunction for the study of these various [texts] is the motivator for inquiry. Its perishable...

Because [the injunction to study] culminates merely in the act of grasping [the text], however, it is the very injunctions regarding sacrifices (*kratu-vidhi*)—which are themselves taught by the injunction to study—that imply an inquiry into Dharma, since the Dharma that is their own object must be known before it can be performed. This is the view held [by some]. According to their opinion, just like the injunctions regarding sacrifices, the injunction for knowledge (*vidyā-vidhi*) also serves as the motivator for inquiry.
The inquiry into Brahman must likewise be undertaken now.
It should not be argued that the inquiry into Brahman need not be undertaken now because there is no performance of ritual knowledge (*vidyā*) at this time;

for if that were so, it would follow by parity of reasoning that the inquiry into the *agnihotra* and other rites should also not be undertaken now because there is no performance of those rites. If [you say...]

Since it is stated in the Smṛti, "Having understood [the nature of] actions, one should undertake whatever one desires," and since the performance of rituals is mandatory for those in other stages of life (āśramas), the inquiry into them is equally necessary for knowledge (vidyā). Even though, for one who investigates Brahman as the reality, the performance of the Agnihotra and other rites is impossible due to the absence of maintaining the sacred fires and so forth;

Since knowledge is common to all stages of life (*āśrama*), it is indeed appropriate for the student (*brahmacārin*) as well. Furthermore, because meditations connected with subordinate elements such as the *Udgītha* are to be performed at the very time of ritual practice— as they fall under the jurisdiction of one who is already qualified for those rites— the inquiry into Brahman, which constitutes their essence, must likewise be undertaken now.

Now, by the word "atha" (then), the immediate succession to the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) is expressed; yet this does not imply an absence of the requirement for such immediate succession, because [the Vedānta] has the scripture as its source (*śāstrayonitvāt*). With respect to the heart, because it concerns human beings, and because it is a subordinate element, it is a statement regarding the human goal (*puruṣārthavāda*).
Jaimini [says] it is "as in other cases. [The knowledge of Brahman] is recognized in all Vedānta texts because there is no difference in the injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth.

Because there is the existence of various sounds and so forth; but [the sin] is destroyed because the scriptural words regarding the taking up [of the fruit] remain as the residue, as in the case of the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing; this has been stated. Nor is it [the case that the sin remains] even for one who holds an office, because of the performance [of penance] after falling and because of the non-experience [of the fruit].

Some [teachers] maintain that [the *Brahma-sūtras*] follow immediately after [the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtras*], because in such sūtras as "Even when preceded by [another action], one attains the state" (*Upapūrvamapi tveke bhāvam...*), there is a necessary mention of immediate succession based on the reliance upon principles established in the previous system (*pūrvatantra*), such as the authority of the Veda, the distinction [of actions], and the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*). For this very reason, they constitute the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās.

Common usage (*prasiddhi*) is also consistent [with this]. Therefore, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Since the Veda (*svādhyāya*) has its meaning intended to be expressed and Brahman has been fully defined, it follows that an inquiry into them must be undertaken. Thus, there arises the doubt as to whether Brahman is to be investigated or not.

The initial position is that it is not so; for the entire Veda has already been investigated in the *Pūrvatantra*, and Brahman is also the subject matter of the Veda. Nor is it unestablished that the subject matter of the entire Veda has been investigated.
Therefore, [Brahman] should be investigated in the manner described through service to the Guru.
That which is designated as the *liṅga* by the scriptures bestows the fruit of Brahman and absolute liberation.
Through the grace of the inseparable power of consciousness, one shall attain liberation;
the act of hearing, as prescribed by the scriptural injunctions, is that which is to be heard from the words of the sacred texts.
The knowledge derived from linguistic compositions and that which arises from human speech do not possess the quality of being the sole cause for the human goal (puruṣārtha) in this context.
Therefore, Vedic knowledge directly bestows liberation upon human beings.
Regarding this matter, many treatises have been composed, as shown in the commentaries (*bhāṣya*).
There exists no Vedic commentary for the Tantric systems.
And this composition of the commentary, preceded by the recitation for peace, [is as follows].
It is to be understood that those who are detached from the multitude of sense objects attain this through service to the Guru;
therein, the wise have shown the *Śaṃ no mitra* and other such mantras.
But how could there be any connection for the Vīraśaivas with such a meaning?
(272) Here, this path of tradition is being expounded by Nīlakaṇṭha,
through the yoga of instruction with the nectar of the guru’s grace in Vīraśaivism.

Sprouted by initiation and designated by the terms "individual soul" (jīva) and "Brahman," the identity of the subtle body (liṅga) and its support (aṅga) is like the instruction of a Great Saying (mahāvākya).
From this great five-syllabled mantra, the wise one should discern its meaning:
by the word *namaḥ* (salutation), there is the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*); by *śiva*, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*);
and by *āya*, the attainment of unity—therefore, the mantra is remembered as "five-syllabled."
Thus, in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Brahma [Purāṇa], through the investigation of the meaning of the mantra,
and by understanding those meanings as taught in the Āgamas through oral instruction;
This meaning of the gross five-syllabled mantra, as proclaimed by the words of the Vedas,
should be grasped by those seeking liberation through a clear discernment of the meaning of the *kārikās*.
Therefore, the ancient collection of commentaries was not approved by Śambhu;
for at the break of day, Sāmba Śiva himself directly instructed me to explain the collection of Vyāsa’s sūtras in accordance with Vīraśaivism.
"May he of pure intellect explain [this], for through his effort,
an understanding arises from such an investigation of the meanings of the scriptures in the form of these kārikās."
Having studied [this] through the great compassion of the Guru, one attains liberation.
And this five-syllabled mantra is employed for the purpose of pacification.
Therefore, that goal is attained through the investigation of the meaning of the verses;
for he who himself masters and propagates the meaning of the verses [attains it].
I have again borne his pair of feet upon my head; may this Karikā,
though harsh, bestow the state of Śiva.
Having heard it, one should give to the reciter the very sacrificial fee prescribed in the Vedas:
wealth and grain to a householder, and the earth filled with crops.
One should give her, adorned with ornaments, to those who are dispassionate according to their instruction;
the wise man should cause her limbs to be enjoyed by a thousand or even a hundred [such men].
The knower, at the end of the Śāmbhava state, attains union with Śambhu.

Thus ends the fourth instruction in the *Kriyāsāra*, within the *Nigamāgamasārasaṅgraha* composed by Nīlakaṇṭha, who is proficient in the one hundred and one topics concerning the secrets of the illustrious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
